t: Sustainability in vocational education and training: national and international experiences
c: Hermann, R, Kress, H & Olesen, J (eds.) 2024, Sustainability in vocational education and training: national and international experiences, Federal Institute for Vocational Education and Training, Bonn.
s:
This series of papers position sustainability as a central driver of transformation in vocational education and training. 

They show climate change, resource scarcity and shifting labour market demands require VET systems to equip learners with competencies that support sustainable economic and social development. 

The text highlights Germany’s structured approach, including the integration of environmental protection and sustainability into all dual training regulations since 2021 and the long-term use of pilot projects to test and refine practical innovations. 

These projects link research institutions with companies to develop teaching materials, workplace tasks and organisational models that embed sustainability in daily training practice. 

The series also stresses the need for trainers who can translate regulatory requirements into meaningful learning and who see themselves as active contributors to socio-ecological change. 

International cooperation is presented as essential, with countries sharing diverse experiences and strategies for embedding sustainability in TVET. 

The series aims to consolidate these perspectives across macro, meso- and micro levels to support a global shift towards sustainable skills development.

t: The myth of livelihoods through urban mining: The case of e-waste pickers in Cape Town
c: Chitaka, T. Y., Moyo, T., Gihring, K., & Schenck, C. (2022). The myth of livelihoods through urban mining: The case of e-waste pickers in Cape Town. South African Journal of Science. https://doi.org/10.17159/sajs.2022/12456
s:
By diverting discarded electronics into the secondary resource stream, E‑waste pickers play an important role in South Africa’s formal and informal economies. However, a survey of 110 e‑waste pickers in Cape Town shows that their participation is driven by necessity rather than choice. Many reported that the only positive aspect of their work is earning an income. 

This study found that e‑waste alone cannot sustain a livelihood: 83.3% of respondents earned below the minimum wage, and 22.9% earned below the food poverty line.  

This means that most pickers collect a wide range of recyclables to survive. They often work long hours in harsh, hazardous conditions that threaten their health and safety and also involved in a range of e‑waste activities, including collection, dismantling and limited processing. 

E‑waste picking functions as a survivalist strategy rather than a viable livelihood. Low and unstable earnings, combined with limited skills, prevent waste pickers from moving up the value chain or transitioning into formal employment. Given the lack of alternatives, the study argues that the waste sector needs to create pathways to decent work so that workers can secure more stable and dignified livelihoods.

t: Building a carbon dioxide removal science–policy partnership for southern Africa
c: Monteiro, P. M., & Midgley, G. F. (2023). Building a carbon dioxide removal science–policy partnership for southern Africa. South African Journal of Science, 119(9/10). https://doi.org/10.17159/sajs.2023/16320
s:
Removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere is increasingly recognised as essential for keeping the planet within a safe climate range by the end of this century. 

This article makes the case for a regionally focused, coordinated carbon dioxide removal (CDR) CDR centred science–policy platform for southern Africa that can also contribute to global climate action. 

The authors argue that CDR presents both opportunities and risks, which can be navigated using that a structured regional approach to responsible development, supporting innovation and ensuring that interventions align with social and environmental priorities. 

They outline the rationale for a new strategic compact that brings together science, government, innovation and business to position South Africa as a leader in CDR research, governance and implementation. 

Such a platform would help the country shape regional responses, influence global debates and build long term capacity for climate resilience. 

They emphasise that coordinated action is vital if CDR is to meaningfully contribute to reducing carbon dioxide while avoiding unintended consequences.

t: Imperatives for an agricultural green economy in South Africa
c: Musvoto, C., Nortje, K., de Wet, B., Mahumani, B. K., & Nahman, A. (2015). Imperatives for an agricultural green economy in South Africa. South African Journal of Science, 111(1/2), 1-8. https://doi.org/10.17159/sajs.2015/20140026
s:
Global development faces major social, economic and environmental pressures, including climate change, rising food demand, persistent poverty and widespread ecological degradation. 

These challenges have prompted a shift towards the idea of a green economy, which aims to improve human well-being and social equity while reducing environmental risks. 

South Africa has committed to green economic growth, with agriculture is expected to play a central role in driving this transition. 

Agriculture has the potential to address several sustainable development concerns, yet it also faces constraints linked to resource scarcity, environmental impacts and climate change. 

For agriculture to support a green economy, it must remain productive, contribute to economic growth and avoid undermining environmental, social and cultural systems. 

Because the green economy is still an emerging concept both globally and in South Africa, the information base and policy frameworks needed to guide this transition are not yet fully developed. 

This article analyses and synthesises green economy principles and agricultural priorities to outline the core features of an agricultural green economy and the practices that are needed to support it.

t: The justice and policy implications of clean energy transition in Africa
c: Nsafon, B.E.K., Same, N.N., Yakub, A.O., Chaulagain, D., Kumar, N.M. and Huh, J‑S. (2023) ‘The justice and policy implications of clean energy transition in Africa’, *Frontiers in Environmental Science*, 11, 1089391. Available at: [https://doi.org/10.3389/fenvs.2023.1089391](https://doi.org/10.3389/fenvs.2023.1089391).
s:
Africa is often viewed as a key player in the global energy transition because it holds both significant fossil fuel reserves and many of the minerals critical for renewable energy technologies, transport and electronics. 

However, the continent still faces low energy access rates and deep socio-economic vulnerabilities. 

To ensure that no group is left behind, the authors argue that Africa’s shift to a low-carbon future must be guided by principles of justice, fairness and inclusion. 

Despite many African countries have adopted ambitious transition plans, some projects that are labelled as clean energy, create environmental, social and economic risks for communities that are already exposed to climate impacts. 

The authors look at the policy implications of a just transition and present evidence that Africa’s energy security, economic growth and affordable access priorities must be central to any clean energy pathway. 

They conclude that the most realistic and effective route for transforming African economies is for strategies to support poverty reduction and long-term resilience to go hand in hand with an incremental transition focused on low-carbon development.

t: Repositioning the Renewable Energy Independent Power Producer Procurement Programme: Localization Lessons for the Just Energy Transition in South Africa
c: Maponya, F. M. (2026). Repositioning the Renewable Energy Independent Power Producer Procurement Programme: Localization Lessons for the Just Energy Transition in South Africa. Asian Journal of Management, Entrepreneurship and Social Science, 6(02), 36-51. https://doi.org/10.63922/ajmesc.v6i02.1535
k: Renewable Energy Independent Power Producer Procurement Programme
s:
This article assesses South Africa’s Renewable Energy Independent Power Producer Procurement Programme (REIPPPP) to identify lessons for socio-economic development and localisation within the just energy transition. 

The REIPPPP was designed as a competitive, market-driven mechanism to attract the private sector to invest in renewable energy connected to the national grid. 

More than a decade later, its contribution to an inclusive and locally grounded transition remains contested. 

This article analyses the programme’s socio-economic commitments, which include job creation, enterprise development, long-term skills building and community trusts. These are often undermined by passive compliance, capture by elites, weak policy alignment and fragmented institutional coordination. 

Although renewable energy capacity has expanded, the sector is dominated by foreign companies. Local producers face barriers such as limited finance, insufficient skills, technological gaps, strong international competition and policy uncertainty. 

A developmental state approach is needed to strengthen localisation in the REIPPPP; the article recommends industrial policy reforms, improved access to capital, participatory socio-economic processes and stronger institutional oversight and coordination.

t: Just Energy Transition Partnerships in the context of Africa-Europe relations: reflections from South Africa, Nigeria and Senegal, Ukȧmȧ.
c: Elisabeth Hege, Chukwumerije Okereke, Sébastien Treyer, Youba Sokona, Ann Kingiri, Niels Keijzer, Fatima Denton (2022).  Just Energy Transition Partnerships in the context of Africa-Europe relations: reflections from South Africa, Nigeria and Senegal, Ukȧmȧ.
s:
Just Energy Transition Partnerships (JETPs) have become an important framework for shaping energy cooperation between Africa and Europe, especially in South Africa, Nigeria and Senegal. 

Each country faces different transition pressures: South Africa must address coal dependence and Eskom’s debt, Nigeria struggles with severe energy access gaps, and Senegal seeks energy sovereignty as it manages new gas discoveries. 

Contrasting priorities complicate cooperation. 

African governments emphasise industrialisation, development and affordable energy, while European partners push for rapid decarbonisation and warn against locking in new fossil fuel infrastructure. 

The authors argue national priorities should drive credible JETPs, based on strong evidence and grounded in distributive, procedural and restorative justice. Inclusive dialogue, independent research and local capacity are essential for designing realistic pathways. 

Gas remains a contested transition option, while renewables are becoming increasingly competitive. 

Effective partnerships require coordinated donors, transparent governance and clear links between climate and development outcomes. 

Contextualising the transition as a development opportunity in local value chains, innovation and universal energy access can strengthen Africa–EU relations and build long term political support.

t: The JETPs of South Africa and Indonesia A Blueprint for the Move Away from Coal?
c: Seiler, A, Brown, H & Matthews, S (2023) The JETPs of South Africa and Indonesia: A blueprint for the move away from coal? CGD Policy Paper 302, Center for Global Development, Washington DC.
s:
This paper analyses the Just Energy Transition Partnerships (JETPs) of South Africa and Indonesia as emerging models for accelerating a shift away from coal in countries with deep structural dependence on coal-based power. 

It outlines how both JETPs combine national decarbonisation strategies with long-term international partnerships intended to support economic restructuring, social protection and energy system reform. 

The authors highlight the note challenges each country faces, including entrenched coal interests, weak policy alignment, constrained fiscal space, governance issues and slow renewable energy deployment. 

The paper shows that both countries have high emissions intensity, large untapped renewable potential and substantial transition risks. 

While the JETPs provide a coordinated framework for investment, technology cooperation and just transition measures, the authors argue that gaps in financing, implementation readiness, supply chain development and political commitment may hinder progress. 

They conclude that although the JETPs offer a potential blueprint for other coal-dependent economies, their success depends on coherent policies, transparent cost management, strong governance, effective social protection and the ability of international partners to deliver promised financial and technical support.

t: Ensuring a Just Energy Transition through Hydrogen:  How the G20 can Support Africa
c: Grobbelaar N and Ngubevana L (2022) Ensuring a just energy transition through hydrogen: How the G20 can support Africa. SAIIA Policy Insights 122, Johannesburg.
s:
This policy insight examines how Africa can position itself as a major producer of green hydrogen and how the G20 can support this shift. 

It highlights that Africa’s strong solar resources, existing port and gas infrastructure, and established regional power pools create favourable conditions for large-scale green hydrogen production. 

The authors show that G20 members increasingly view green hydrogen as essential for decarbonising hard to abate sectors and for achieving net zero commitments. 

Africa can leverage this momentum by integrating green hydrogen into regional energy systems, strengthening industrial development and reducing reliance on fossil fuels. 

The African Continental Free Trade Area can further support skills mobility, services and trade linked to hydrogen value chains. 

The paper stresses that Africa must balance export opportunities with domestic energy security and industrialisation goals. 

The authors that coordinated policy frameworks, investment in enabling infrastructure and international cooperation will be critical to ensuring that green hydrogen contributes to a just energy transition on the continent.

t: A Systems Thinking Approach to a Transition Towards Renewable Energy in South Africa
c: Mgoduso, LT (2021) A systems thinking approach to a transition towards renewable energy in South Africa. MPhil dissertation, University of Cambridge.
s:
This dissertation examines South Africa’s transition from a coal dependent electricity system to renewable energy using a systems thinking approach. 

It highlights how the country’s reliance on coal, combined with governance failures, policy inconsistency and Eskom’s financial and operational crises, has undermined energy security and delayed decarbonisation. 

The research reviews the historical development of the electricity sector, the evolution of climate and energy policy, and the structural barriers that have limited renewable energy deployment. 

Through interviews and causal loop diagramming, the study identifies the interconnected social, economic, institutional and technical factors shaping the transition. 

It emphasises the socio economic risks of coal phaseout, including job losses and community disruption, and stresses the need for a just transition that protects workers and supports regional development. 

The dissertation proposes intervention strategies such as unbundling Eskom, enabling a competitive electricity market, strengthening governance and developing a comprehensive Just Transition Plan. 

A Theory of Change framework is presented to guide coordinated action among government, industry, labour and civil society. 

The study concludes that a systems approach is essential for navigating complexity and designing a fair and effective transition to a green economy.

t: Socio-economic considerations for a Paris Agreement-compatible coal transition in South Africa
c: Burton, J, Marquard, A & McCall, B (2019) Socio economic considerations for a Paris Agreement compatible coal transition in South Africa. Climate Transparency Policy Paper, University of Cape Town.
s:
This policy brief examines the socio economic implications of phasing out coal in South Africa in line with a Paris Agreement compatible emissions pathway. 

It highlights how decades of state support entrenched coal in electricity generation, liquid fuels and exports, creating deep structural dependence. 

However, coal is now increasingly uncompetitive, and a least cost energy pathway shows a rapid decline in coal use driven by cheaper renewable energy. 

A Paris aligned pathway requires coal phaseout in electricity and liquid fuels by around 2040, with renewables and flexible capacity replacing coal generation. 

The brief stresses that South Africa’s high unemployment, poverty and regional dependence on coal mining make a just transition essential. 

Coal dependent provinces such as Mpumalanga face significant risks, including job losses, declining export revenues and stranded assets. 

The authors argue that transition planning must include worker support, social protection, economic diversification and investment in new sectors. 

They outline elements of a just transition package that aligns climate mitigation with development priorities and protects vulnerable workers and communities while enabling a shift to a sustainable energy system.

t: Gender inclusivity towards a just energy transition in South Africa
c: Geen, V (2025) Gender inclusivity towards a just energy transition in South Africa. Master of Management in Energy Leadership research report, University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg.
s:
This research report examines how gender inclusivity can be advanced within South Africa’s just energy transition. 

Using energy justice theory and an adapted engendered energy justice framework, the study explores whether women are meaningfully included as participants and beneficiaries in the shift to clean energy. 

The report highlights that South Africa’s transition is accelerating, driven by climate commitments, the Climate Change Act and the need to move away from the Minerals and Energy Complex. 

However, women remain underrepresented in the energy sector and face structural, institutional and societal barriers that limit their participation. 

Through interviews with key informants, the study finds that gender considerations are largely absent from current transition planning, despite women forming a significant share of the population and being disproportionately affected by inequality. 

The author argues that gender mainstreaming, improved data, inclusive decision making and a long term energy vision are essential to ensure that women are not left behind. 

It concludes that integrating gender justice into the just transition is necessary for equitable outcomes and recommends a national dialogue to embed gender inclusivity in policy and practice.

t: The Impact of the Green Transition on Jobs in South Africa
c: Davidson, K, David, A, De Lannoy, A, Grotte, J, Jana, A, Leibbrandt, M, Nell, A & Visagie, J (2025) The impact of the green transition on jobs in South Africa. SALDRU Working Paper 318, University of Cape Town, Cape Town.
s:
This working paper analyses how South Africa’s green transition will affect employment across regions and sectors. 

It highlights that the country’s shift from a carbon intensive economy is urgent due to climate risks, declining coal competitiveness and the need to meet its Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC). 

The authors emphasise that the transition must be just and equitable, particularly because coal dependent provinces such as Mpumalanga face concentrated risks, including job losses and economic disruption. 

Using a combined bottom up and top down framework, the study identifies green occupations and maps their distribution across provinces and municipalities. 

It shows that the impacts of the transition will vary widely across locations, with some areas likely to experience significant job displacement while others may benefit from emerging green opportunities. 

The paper argues that understanding this spatial variation is essential for designing targeted, place based policies that support workers and communities. 

It concludes that South Africa needs evidence based planning to manage labour market disruption, build new skills and ensure that the green transition contributes to inclusive development.

t: The Role of Trade Unions in Shaping the Just Energy Transition in South Africa: A Case Study of Komati Power Station
c: Sekano, Lesego.   University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg (South Africa) ProQuest Dissertations & Theses,  2024. 32527677
s:
South Africa’s Just Energy Transition (JET) marks a major shift from coal to renewable energy and requires strong social inclusion to succeed. 

This study examines the role of trade unions in shaping the transition using Komati Power Station as a case study. Mpumalanga the province in which it is located, is one of the regions most affected by coal mine closures. 

Using a qualitative approach, the research explores how unions influence policy negotiations and advocate for workers and surrounding communities during the decommissioning process. 

Interviews with union representatives, workers and policymakers show that unions focus on job security, reskilling and fair social outcomes, but their priorities often differ from those of environmental groups and government officials. 

The study finds that effective collaboration between unions and government is essential to ensure that the transition supports both economic and environmental justice. It also highlights that preventing negative impacts on coal dependent communities is central to achieving a genuinely just transition. 

Overall, the research demonstrates that labour movements play a critical role in shaping policy and protecting workers’ interests as South Africa moves towards a cleaner energy future.

t: The end of coal? Planning a “just transition” in South Africa
c: Strambo, C, Burton, J & Atteridge, A (2019) The end of coal? Planning a “just transition” in South Africa. Stockholm Environment Institute, Stockholm.
s:
This report examines the implications of South Africa’s inevitable shift away from coal and outlines what is required to plan a just transition. 

Coal remains central to electricity generation, liquid fuels and regional economies, particularly in Mpumalanga, where mining and coal fired power stations are highly concentrated. 

The report highlights that closures of ageing plants and declining export demand will have significant socio economic impacts, including job losses, reduced municipal revenues and disruption to local economies. 

It stresses that unmanaged change could deepen poverty and inequality, while a well planned transition could create new opportunities. 

Key challenges include labour mobility, skills transferability, environmental rehabilitation and the need for economic diversification. 

The report argues that existing institutions and policy mechanisms are insufficiently coordinated to manage the transition and that subnational governments must play a stronger role. 

It calls for early planning, credible strategies for worker support, investment in new sectors and transparent governance to ensure that communities are not left behind. 

The authors conclude that a just transition requires inclusive dialogue, clear institutional responsibilities and long term planning to navigate the decline of coal.

t: Assessing coal mine closures and mining community profiles for the ‘just transition’ in South Africa
c: Cole, M.J., Mthenjane, M. & van Zyl, A.T. (2023) ‘Assessing coal mine closures and mining community profiles for the “just transition” in South Africa’, Journal of the Southern African Institute of Mining and Metallurgy, 123(6), pp. 329–342. https://doi.org/10.17159/2411-9717/2689/2023
s:
This report analyses the scale and timing of coal mine and power station closures in South Africa and assesses the vulnerability of the 69 host communities and 21 municipalities that will be directly affected. 

It finds that the transition away from coal will largely follow the natural ageing of mines and plants rather than premature shutdowns, with five power stations and 15 mines likely to close by 2030 and a further four stations and 23 mines by 2040. 

Although this aligns with climate commitments, the socio economic consequences for the 2.5 million residents of mining communities will be severe. 

These areas already face low income, weak employment, limited education outcomes and widespread municipal financial distress. 

The report argues that a just transition must be grounded in local realities, including spatial, temporal and skills mismatches between declining coal jobs and emerging opportunities. 

It stresses that South Africa’s approach must balance climate ambition with energy security and economic stability, and that planning must prioritise community resilience, municipal capacity and long term regional development.

t: Skills futures in Africa
c: McGrath, S. (2022) ‘Skills futures in Africa’, Prospects, 52(3–4), pp. 325–341. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11125-022-09622-9
s:
McGrath explores how African countries can do skills training in a rapidly changing world arguing that skills development cannot focus only on narrow technical training. 

Instead, it must support broader human development, including the ability to adapt, think critically, and participate fully in society. 

McGrath points out that many African skills systems still reflect old colonial structures and do not respond well to current economic, social and technological changes. He stresses that skills planning must be rooted in local realities, shaped by community needs and connected to wider development goals such as inclusion, sustainability and decent work. 

He calls for stronger partnerships between governments, education providers, employers and communities to build flexible, future focused skills systems. 

McGrath argues that skills futures in Africa depend on reimagining education and training so that it supports resilience, opportunity and meaningful participation in a changing world.

t: Just Energy Transition of South Africa in a Post-COVID Era
c: Bohlmann, H.R., Bohlmann, J.A., Chitiga-Mabugu, M. & Inglesi-Lotz, R. (2023) ‘Just Energy Transition of South Africa in a post-COVID era’, Sustainability, 15(14), 10854. https://doi.org/10.3390/su151410854
s:
Bohlmann and colleagues look at how how South Africa’s Just Energy Transition (JET) is unfolding in the aftermath of COVID 19, a time of economic strain, rising unemployment and deepening inequality. 

They use economic modelling to explore how shifting from coal to cleaner energy sources will affect jobs, growth and household welfare. 

They find that the transition can support long term economic benefits, including new investment and employment in renewable energy, but that these gains are uneven and depend heavily on policy choices. 

Coal dependent regions and low income households face the greatest risks, especially if the transition happens rapidly without adequate support. 

They stress that South Africa needs strong social protection, targeted regional development and skills programmes to ensure that vulnerable workers and communities are not left behind. 

A successful JET requires coordinated planning across government, industry and society so that the shift to clean energy strengthens economic recovery and improves livelihoods rather than worsening existing inequalities.

t: The regional implications of just transition in the world's most coal-dependent economy: The case of Mpumalanga, South Africa
c: Nel, E., Marais, L. & Mqotyana, Z. (2023) ‘The regional implications of just transition in the world’s most coal dependent economy: The case of Mpumalanga, South Africa’, Frontiers in Sustainable Cities, 4, 1059312. https://doi.org/10.3389/frsc.2022.1059312
s:
The article examines the regional implications of a just energy transition in Mpumalanga, South Africa, the country’s most coal dependent province. 

It highlights how decades of reliance on coal have created a mono economy that now faces severe disruption as global and national commitments to decarbonisation accelerate. 

The study shows that mine closures and the decline of coal fired power stations will have significant social and economic consequences for workers and communities, many of whom lack alternative employment pathways. It draws on international and South African evidence to assess how regional resilience and economic diversification can be strengthened. 

The authors argue that external financial support for renewable energy is valuable but insufficient without targeted planning, strong governance and investment certainty. 

They emphasise the need for mechanisms that protect vulnerable groups, support reskilling and prevent the deepening of inequality. 

The paper concludes that a just transition in Mpumalanga requires coordinated action to manage economic restructuring, attract new industries and ensure that affected communities are included in decision making.

t: What role for social policies in the framework of the just transition in South Africa?
c: Annecke, W. and Wolpe, P. (2022) ‘What role for social policies in the framework of the just transition in South Africa?’, AFD Research Papers, 230, pp. 1–33. Available at: https://shs.cairn.info/journal-afd-research-papers-2022-230-page-1?lang=en
s:
The article examines how social policies can support a just transition in South Africa as the country moves away from its coal dependent economy. 

It outlines how poverty, inequality and unemployment remain entrenched legacies of apartheid and argues that any transition to a low carbon economy must protect vulnerable groups who face job losses and livelihood disruption. 

The authors distinguish between affirmative approaches that redistribute risks within the current economic system and transformative approaches that seek structural change. 

They highlight three dimensions of justice that shape transition outcomes: procedural justice through inclusive decision making, distributive justice through labour market and industrial policies, and restorative justice that addresses past and present harms. 

The paper shows that South Africa’s political economy, dominated by the minerals energy complex, limits ambition and slows implementation. 

It reviews national policies and institutions, including the Presidential Climate Commission, and assesses the role of social protection in supporting workers and communities. 

A case study of Steve Tshwete Municipality illustrates both the challenges of coal region dependence and emerging opportunities for diversification. 

The authors conclude that social policies are essential to ensuring that the transition is fair and improves wellbeing.

t: Addressing climate goals and the SDGs through a just energy transition? Empirical evidence from Germany and South Africa
c: Hägele, R., Iacobuţă, G.I. and Tops, J. (2022) ‘Addressing climate goals and the SDGs through a just energy transition? Empirical evidence from Germany and South Africa’, Journal of Integrative Environmental Sciences, 19(1), pp. 85–120.  https://doi.org/10.1080/1943815X.2022.2108459
s:
The article analyses how Germany and South Africa attempt to align climate commitments with the Sustainable Development Goals through a just energy transition. 

It shows that phasing out coal presents complex environmental, economic and social challenges that require coordinated policy responses across sectors and levels of government. 

Using a qualitative approach based on literature, interviews and policy analysis, the authors examine how each country designs and implements measures intended to reduce emissions while safeguarding development priorities. 

They find that both countries face significant obstacles, including job losses, inequality and pressures linked to the water energy food land nexus. 

The study highlights that achieving coherence between climate action and broader development goals depends on inclusive decision making, careful assessment of impacts and strong institutional coordination. 

It concludes that just transition pathways must integrate energy justice principles, ensure that vulnerable groups are protected and strengthen governance systems that can manage the social and economic consequences of coal phase out.

t: Taking stock of the just transition from coal in South Africa
c: Strambo, C., Patel, M. and Maimele, S. (2024) Taking stock of the just transition from coal in South Africa. Stockholm Environment Institute. https://doi.org/10.51414/sei2024.034
s:
The working paper reviews how the idea of a just transition has developed in South Africa as the country confronts the decline of its coal sector. 

It shows that coal has shaped local economies, employment and public institutions for decades, making the transition socially and politically complex. 

The authors explain that although the just transition has gained broad acceptance, different actors interpret it in conflicting ways. 

Some view it as an opportunity for structural transformation that supports workers and communities, while others use it narrowly to justify decarbonisation without addressing inequality or local needs. 

The paper highlights the risks of top down decision making, limited transparency and uneven influence over project selection. It stresses that procedural justice, inclusive governance and clear allocation of resources are essential for legitimacy. 

As coal plants reach the end of their operational life, South Africa faces a critical moment in shaping transition pathways. 

The authors argue that without careful planning, community engagement and investment in alternative livelihoods, the transition may entrench existing vulnerabilities rather than reduce them.

t: Workforce Transition in South Africa’s Just Energy Transition
c: Tamasiga, P. (2025) Workforce Transition in South Africa’s Just Energy Transition: An Analysis of Needs, Policy Gaps and Socioeconomic Implications. Policy Brief, 39. doi: 10.51414/sei2024.034.
s:
This policy brief examines how South Africa can manage workforce transitions as the country moves towards a low carbon economy. It argues that the success of the Just Energy Transition depends on understanding the real needs of the workers and communities who are affected by the decline of coal and other carbon intensive sectors. 

The brief notes gaps in current policy, including limited coordination between national strategies, uneven support for skills development and insufficient planning for local economic diversification. It stresses that workers face complex risks such as job losses, reduced income and income insecurity as well as potential community instability.

The analysis calls for stronger alignment between labour, energy and industrial policies, supported by targeted investment in reskilling and social protection. It also emphasises the importance of place based planning to ensure that transition measures respond to local realities rather than applying generic national solutions. 

The brief concludes that a fair and effective transition requires long term commitment, inclusive governance and sustained support for workers, households and regional economies.

t: The green economy learning assessment South Africa: Lessons for higher education, skills and work-based learning
c: Rosenberg, E., Lotz-Sisitka, H.B. and Ramsarup, P. (2018) ‘The Green Economy Learning Assessment South Africa’, Higher Education, Skills and Work-Based Learning, 8(3), pp. 243–258. doi:10.1108/heswbl-03-2018-0041.
s:
This paper examines how South Africa’s post school education and training system is responding to the skills demands of a growing green economy. 

It uses a Green Economy Learning Assessment to analyse the extent to which national policies, institutions and learning pathways support the development of green skills across sectors such as energy, water and waste. 

The authors find that although South Africa has strong policy intent, implementation remains uneven and fragmented. 

Many education and training institutions lack the capacity, resources and industry partnerships needed to deliver relevant programmes at scale.

The study indicates that gaps in curriculum alignment, limited opportunities for work based learning and weak coordination between government departments are responsible for skills planning and environmental policy. 

Building a capable green workforce requires systemic reform, including clearer national direction, stronger institutional collaboration and investment in educator development. 

The authors conclude that South Africa must integrate green skills more deliberately into its skills ecosystem to support inclusive, sustainable economic growth.

t:
Sector Education and Training Authorities role in Ensuring Just Transition to a
Greener Economy through Skills Planning
c: Josopu, T. (2024) Sector Education and Training Authorities role in ensuring Just Transition to a Greener Economy through Skills Planning. Available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5208050 (Accessed: 23 March 2026). doi: 10.2139/ssrn.5208050.
s:
Josopu explores how South Africa’s Sector Education and Training Authorities (SETAs) can strengthen their role in supporting a Just Transition to a greener economy through more effective skills planning. 

He argues that SETAs occupy a strategic position because they link industry needs, labour market intelligence and skills development funding. However, their current planning processes are not yet fully aligned with the emerging demands of green industries or the broader objectives of a low carbon transition.

The analysis highlights several constraints including fragmented data systems, limited coordination across SETAs and insufficient integration of green skills into sector skills plans. 

It also notes that many SETAs lack the technical capacity to anticipate future skills needs in rapidly evolving green sectors. He calls for stronger national guidance, improved labour market forecasting and deeper collaboration between SETAs, government departments and industry stakeholders. 

Josopu concludes that SETAs can play a decisive role in ensuring a fair and inclusive transition, but only if skills planning becomes more forward looking, coherent and responsive to environmental and economic change.

t: Is our skills system ready for a sustainability transition?
c: Allais, S. (2024) Is our skills system ready for a sustainability transition? South African Journal of Science, 120(9/10), Art. #19157. https://doi.org/10.17159/sajs.2024/19157
s:
Allais argues that South Africa’s current skills system is only partly prepared for a sustainability transition. She explains that while universities and private providers are developing new courses linked to green technologies and emerging occupations, the system still struggles to respond to short term needs. 

Funding mechanisms are slow and fragmented; policymakers often lack insight into employers’ short- and medium-term needs.

Skills alone cannot guarantee a just transition: moving away from a carbon based economy demands deep structural change, coordinated government leadership and long term investment in expertise. 

The system also fails to distinguish between immediate training needs and the development of specialised knowledge to support innovation. As a result, education institutions tend to offer short courses rather than building sustained capacity.

She concludes that although there is promising activity, the skills system remains too clumsy and under coordinated to meet the complexity of the transition. What is needed is better planning, clearer priorities and stronger alignment between government, industry and education for the country to develop the expertise that a socially just and sustainable future demands.

t: Sustainability in Vocational Education and Training – National and  International Experiences
c: Hermann, R., Kress, H. and Olesen, J. (eds) (2024) Sustainability in vocational education and training: National and international experiences. Bonn: Verlag Barbara Budrich. Available at: https://www.bibb.de/dienst/publikationen/de/19901.
s:
This edited volume brings together national and international experiences that show how sustainability is becoming a central priority in vocational education and training. 

The contributors highlight that countries are approaching sustainability in diverse ways, while sharing common aims: strengthening green skills, aligning training with climate goals and preparing workforces for rapid economic and technological change. 

The publication documents the role of the German Office for International Cooperation in Vocational Education and Training (GOVET) supporting this shift.

Case studies from regions including Latin America, Africa, Central Asia and Europe illustrate how systems are embedding sustainability at institutional, curricular and workplace levels. They show that progress depends on coordinated policy, strong partnerships and the ability to translate global sustainability goals into local training practice. 

The editors argue that VET systems must offer more than short courses to build long term capacity if they are to respond effectively to climate challenges and support inclusive development. 

The volume provides a broad platform for dialogue and offers concrete examples that can guide policymakers, practitioners and researchers working to integrate sustainability into VET.

t: Energy skills roadmap South Africa 2023
c: SANEA, Wits REAL and AELC (2023) South African Energy Skills Roadmap 2023. Johannesburg: South African National Energy Association. Available at: https://www.sanea.org.za (Accessed: 31 March 2026).
s:
The 2023 South African Energy Skills Roadmap sets out a coordinated plan to ensure the country has the human capacity needed for a just energy transition. 

The roadmap responds to the fragmented nature of existing skills initiatives and the absence of a unified long-term strategy. 

It draws on a baseline review of more than 200 documents and wide stakeholder consultation across government, business, labour, civil society and research institutions.

The roadmap identifies four major forces shaping future skills needs: decarbonisation, decentralisation, digitalisation and shifts in market structure. 

These trends will transform current jobs and create new occupations, requiring an integrated approach to skills planning rather than siloed interventions. 

The report stresses that South Africa must build a responsive ecosystem that aligns short term training with long term capability development, supports regional transitions and anticipates uncertainty in the energy landscape.

Overall, the roadmap provides a structured foundation for planning future energy skills and highlights “no regret” actions that can strengthen workforce readiness as the energy transition accelerates.

t: Just Transition and the Labour Market in South Africa: Measuring Individual and Household Coal Economy Dependence
c: Bhorat, H., Kupeta, T., Martin, L. and Steenkamp, F. (2023) Just transition and the labour market in South Africa: Measuring individual and household coal economy dependence. Cape Town: Development Policy Research Unit, University of Cape Town.
s:
The report provides a detailed quantitative assessment of South Africa’s coal labour market to inform just transition planning. 

It shows that coal remains central to national energy supply and emissions, with production and employment heavily concentrated in Mpumalanga. 

Using multiple datasets, the authors estimate that in 2019 the coal mining industry employed between 76 000 and 108 000 workers, with a further 30 000 employed in coal based electricity generation. 

Most workers are Black African men aged 25–44 with relatively high levels of secondary education, and the majority hold formal, stable jobs with benefits. 

The report highlights the regional dependence on coal, noting that several municipalities rely on the sector for a significant share of employment. 

It also identifies 46 000 coal linked households in Mpumalanga, many of which rely on a single coal income and have limited alternative employment options. 

The authors classify workers into groups facing different transition risks, ranging from high skilled workers likely to find new opportunities to low skilled workers who will require income support. 

The report concludes that a just transition will require targeted interventions that reflect the diverse skills, vulnerabilities and spatial realities of coal dependent communities.

t: Skills for a just-transition to a green Future
c: Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH (2023) Skills for a just transition to a green future. Bonn: GIZ.
s:
This GIZ publication explores how countries can build the skills base needed for a fair and inclusive shift to a green economy. It argues that a just transition is not only a technological challenge but a social one that depends on preparing workers, communities and training systems for structural change. 

The report shows how green transitions reshape labour markets by creating new occupations, transforming existing ones and phasing out carbon intensive jobs. Because of this, skills planning must be protective, coordinated and grounded in evidence.

The authors emphasise that TVET systems need to integrate sustainability across curricula, workplace learning and institutional strategies. They also stress the importance of social dialogue with workers and employers jointly shaping training pathways with transition support. 

Case studies from partner countries show that successful approaches combine long term capacity building with short term measures such as reskilling, career guidance and local economic diversification.

Skills development is the cornerstone of a just transition:  without targeted investment in people, green policies risk deepening inequality rather than promoting inclusive growth.

t: Company upcycles used vapes into power banks
c: Hudson, P. (2025) On the couch: Company upcycles used vapes into power banks. CapeTalk, 14 August. Available at: https://omny.fm/shows/afternoons-with-pippa-hudson/on-the-couch-company-upcycles-used-vapes-into-power-banks (Accessed: 31 March 2026).
s:
This interview on Cape Talk, Lunch with Pippa Hudson profiles One More Time, a Cape Town based start-up founded by Dante Roumega and Gus Robins, which upcycles discarded vape cartridges into functional power banks. 

Millions of single use vapes end up in landfills each year, despite containing rechargeable lithium ion batteries that still hold significant capacity. 

The company collects used vapes, extracts the batteries, tests them for safety and performance, and repurposes them into compact, affordable power banks.

The conversation highlights the environmental urgency behind the project. Single use vapes combine plastics, metals, electronics and chemicals, making them difficult to recycle and harmful when dumped. 

By recovering the batteries, One More Time diverts waste from landfills and demonstrates how circular economy thinking can be applied to everyday consumer products. 

The founders also discuss public awareness, regulatory gaps and the potential to scale their model through partnerships with retailers and waste management organisations.

t:
Public Perceptions and Attitudes Relating to Climate Change and the Just Transition in South Africa:
Results from a 2023 nationally representative survey
c: Roberts, B., Struwig, J., Zondi, T., Gordon, S., Dunn, S., Fundisi, E., Dlamini, S. and Bohler Muller, N. (2025) Public perceptions and attitudes relating to climate change and the just transition in South Africa: Results from a 2023 nationally representative survey. Pretoria: Human Sciences Research Council.
s:
The report presents findings from a nationally representative 2023 survey examining how South Africans understand climate change and the just transition. 

It shows that awareness of climate change is widespread, although levels of detailed knowledge vary across demographic groups. 

Most respondents recognise that climate change is already affecting their lives through extreme weather, rising costs and pressure on public services. 

The survey finds strong support for action to reduce emissions, provided that measures do not worsen poverty or unemployment. 

Public attitudes towards the just transition emphasise fairness, job creation and government accountability. 

Respondents express concern about the potential loss of coal related jobs but also show openness to new opportunities in renewable energy and green industries if training and support are available. 

Trust in government and institutions is identified as a key factor shaping willingness to support transition policies. 

The report concludes that effective communication, targeted skills development and visible social protection measures are essential to build public confidence in South Africa’s transition pathway.

t: Towards low-carbon energy state in South Africa: a survey of energy availability and sustainability
c: Adedeji, P.A., Akinlabi, S., Madushele, N. and Olatunji, O.O. (2018) Towards a low carbon energy state in South Africa: A survey of energy availability and sustainability. EAI Endorsed Transactions on Energy Web. https://doi.org/10.4108/eai.13-7-2018.161751
s:
This study investigates South Africa’s progress towards a low carbon energy system by examining current patterns of energy availability, consumption and sustainability. 

Adedeji and colleagues underline South Africa’s dependence on coal, which continues to dominate electricity generation and contributes significantly to greenhouse gas emissions. Their survey shows that although renewable energy technologies are expanding, their contribution is still limited by policy uncertainty, infrastructure constraints and slow investment cycles.

The public and industry are concerned about energy reliability, rising costs and the long term viability of coal based power. They argue that these pressures create both urgency and opportunity for accelerating the transition to cleaner energy sources. 

The study emphasises that achieving a low carbon future needs coordinated policy, improved grid capacity, stronger incentives for renewable deployment and sustained investment in research and innovation.

They conclude that South Africa has the technical potential to shift towards a more sustainable energy mix, but this depends on decisive action to address structural barriers and support large scale adoption of low carbon technologies.

t: Identification of Skills Needed for the Hydrogen Economy
c: Rakaibe, T., Simiyu, D., Tlokolo, B., Marema, A., Mbam, V. and Pandarum, A. (2024) Identification of skills needed for the hydrogen economy: Research report. Labour Market Intelligence Research Programme, Department of Higher Education and Training.
s:
The report identifies the skills South Africa needs to build a competitive and inclusive hydrogen economy. 

It explains that green hydrogen is central to the country’s long term decarbonisation strategy and offers opportunities for industrial development, export growth and job creation. 

The authors map the hydrogen value chain and outline the occupations required across production, storage, transport and end use applications. 

They find that demand will grow for engineers, technicians, artisans and operators with specialised competencies in electrolysis, renewable energy integration, safety management and hydrogen handling. 

The report highlights significant gaps in current training provision, noting that most programmes do not yet include hydrogen specific content. 

It stresses the need for coordinated curriculum development, industry partnerships and investment in TVET and higher education capacity. 

The study also emphasises the importance of reskilling workers from carbon intensive sectors to ensure a just transition. 

It concludes that South Africa must act quickly to align skills planning with emerging hydrogen projects to secure local participation and avoid dependence on imported expertise.

t: South African Renewable Energy Masterplan (SAREM): An Inclusive Industrial Development Plan for the Renewable Energy and Storage Value Chains by 2030
c: Department of Trade, Industry and Competition (2025) South African Renewable Energy Masterplan (SAREM): An inclusive industrial development plan for the renewable energy and storage value chains by 2030. Pretoria: Government of South Africa.
s:
The South African Renewable Energy Masterplan (SAREM) sets out a coordinated industrial development strategy to build competitive, inclusive and locally anchored value chains for renewable energy and storage technologies by 2030. 

Developed through extensive consultation with industry, labour, government and civil society, the plan identifies priority interventions to expand manufacturing capacity, deepen localisation and create decent jobs across solar PV, wind, battery storage and related components.

According to the masterplan, South Africa has strong potential to position itself as a regional manufacturing hub, but needs stable policy, targeted incentives and improved coordination across to do so. 

To ensure that the transition benefits workers, SMMEs and historically marginalised groups, the plan emphasises that industrialisation must go hand in hand with skills development, enterprise support and transformation measures.

The plan outlines concrete actions, including demand side certainty through procurement pipelines, investment in industrial infrastructure, support for technology upgrading and the development of local supplier networks. It frames renewable energy not only as a climate imperative but as a strategic opportunity to drive re industrialisation, energy security and inclusive economic growth.

t: Sector Jobs Resilience Plan: Metals Value Chain
c: Montmasson Clair, G., Makgetla, N., Maseko, N. and Patel, M. (2020) Sector Jobs Resilience Plan: Metals value chain. Pretoria: Trade & Industrial Policy Strategies (TIPS) for the Department of Environment, Forestry and Fisheries.
s:
Montmasson Clair and colleagues analyse the full value chain, from mining and smelting to fabrication and downstream manufacturing. They explain that as global markets move towards cleaner production, the sector faces both challenges and new opportunities.

The report highlights that energy intensive processes, especially smelting, are vulnerable to rising electricity costs, carbon related trade measures and tightening environmental regulations. At the same time, demand for metals used in renewable energy, electric vehicles and green infrastructure is expected to grow. 

South Africa must act proactively to secure these opportunities by improving energy efficiency, expanding access to low carbon power, upgrading technology and strengthening skills development.

The plan emphasises the need for social dialogue, targeted support for affected workers and coordinated industrial policy to manage restructuring. It concludes that a just transition in the metals value chain requires balancing decarbonisation with economic resilience, job protection and inclusive growth.

t: Supply and Demand of Artisans in South Africa Labour Market Intelligence research programme
c: Mzabalazo Advisory Services (2022) Supply and demand of artisans in South Africa. Labour Market Intelligence Research Programme, Department of Higher Education and Training.
s:
The report assesses the supply and demand of artisans in South Africa and examines how the country can strengthen its artisan pipeline to support industrial development and the transition to a greener economy. 

It shows that artisans remain critical to core sectors such as manufacturing, construction, energy and transport, yet persistent shortages continue to constrain growth. 

The study identifies misalignment between training output and labour market needs, with some trades oversupplied while others face chronic gaps. 

It highlights structural challenges including uneven workplace training opportunities, limited employer participation, and variable quality across training providers. 

The report notes that the shift toward renewable energy, energy efficiency and new technologies will increase demand for mechanical, electrical and electro technical artisans with updated competencies. 

It stresses the need for coordinated planning, improved data systems and stronger partnerships between industry, SETAs and public training institutions. 

The authors conclude that South Africa must expand and modernise artisan training, ensure better matching between supply and demand, and integrate green skills into curricula to prepare the workforce for a just transition.

t: Skills for a Just Transition to a Green Future: Measuring the South African TVET System and providing input to support its development.
c:
Freimann, K. and Magnus, G. (2023) Skills for a just transition to a green future: Measuring the South African TVET system and providing input to support its development. Paper presented at the International Research Conference on Skills for a Just Transition, Centre for Researching Education and Labour (REAL), University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg, 11–12 May.
Education and Labour (REAL), University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg, 11–12 May.
s:
Freimann and Magnus examine how well the South African TVET system is positioned to support a just transition to a green future, drawing on evidence generated through the GIZ Career Path Development for Employment (CPD4E) project. 

They assess the system’s capacity across institutions, programmes, governance structures and labour market linkages, highlighting both strengths and structural constraints. They argue that although sustainability has begun to enter policy discourse, it is not yet embedded in curricula, lecturer training or workplace based learning at the scale required for emerging green occupations.

Freimann and Magnus identify gaps in occupational standards, limited coordination between industry and training providers and uneven access to equipment and practical learning environments. 

They emphasise that the just transition demands not only new technical skills but also transversal competencies such as systems thinking, problem solving and adaptability. 

The paper proposes targeted interventions, including curriculum renewal, lecturer upskilling, stronger employer partnerships and improved labour market intelligence to anticipate future green skills needs.

The authors position the TVET system as a critical lever for an inclusive transition, but one that requires systemic reform and deliberate investment to meet the demands of a rapidly changing economy.

t: Skills for green transformation:  toolkit, dashboard, training concept
c: GIZ Competence Centre Education, TVET and Labour Markets (2023) Series of Exchanges on Green Skills and Jobs – 5th event: “To green or not to green… Skills for Green Transformation: Toolkit, Dashboard, Training Concept”. Online event held on 6 June.
s:
This fifth event in the GIZ “Series of Exchanges on Green Skills and Jobs” focuses on practical tools and approaches that TVET systems, policymakers and practitioners can use to support green transformation. Hosted online by the GIZ Competence Centre for Education, TVET and Labour Markets, the session introduces three core resources: a Green Skills Toolkit, a Green Transformation Dashboard and a Training Concept designed to help countries and institutions integrate sustainability into skills development.

The discussion points out that the green transformation requires more than adding isolated environmental modules.  It demands systemic change across curricula, occupational standards, labour market intelligence and institutional strategy. 

The toolkit guides the identification of green skills needs, mapping value chains and designing responsive training interventions. 

The dashboard offers a structured way to track progress and visualise indicators related to green jobs, policy readiness and sectoral shifts. The training concept supports capacity building for educators, planners and decision makers.

Participants from multiple countries share experiences of applying these tools, emphasising the importance of collaboration, data driven planning and cross sector dialogue. 

The event positions these resources as practical enablers for embedding green skills in TVET systems worldwide.

t: Just Energy Transition Mechanisms for Planning: Summary Note
c: Centre for Researching Education and Labour (REAL) (2024) Just Energy Transition Mechanisms for Planning: Summary note. Johannesburg: University of the Witwatersrand.
s:
This REAL summary note outlines key mechanisms that South Africa can use to plan effectively for a just energy transition.  It focuses on institutional coordination, evidence based decision making and regional implementation. 

The summary emphasises that the transition is not only a technical shift in the energy system but a structural economic transformation that must be deliberately managed to protect workers, communities and vulnerable regions.

The authors highlight several planning mechanisms, e.g. such as spatial mapping, labour market modelling, social impact assessment and multi stakeholder governance, that help identify where risks and opportunities are concentrated. 

Planning must be proactive, integrated across government departments and grounded in transparent data. The note stresses that local contexts differ significantly, meaning that transition pathways must be tailored to specific provinces and municipalities, particularly coal dependent areas.

The summary also underscores the importance of social dialogue, participatory planning and clear institutional mandates to avoid fragmentation. 

It concludes that South Africa needs a coherent planning architecture that links national strategy with local implementation, ensuring that the transition is fair, inclusive and developmental.

t: Employment and Labour Market Analysis (ELMA) in South Africa: Focus on Just Transition
c: GIZ (2024) Employment and Labour Market Analysis (ELMA) in South Africa: Focus on Just Transition. Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH.
s:
This Employment and Labour Market Analysis (ELMA) report provides a structured assessment of how South Africa’s labour market is positioned to navigate the economic and employment shifts associated with the just transition. 

Using a combination of quantitative labour market data and qualitative stakeholder insights, it identifies which sectors, occupations and regions are most exposed to transition risks and where new opportunities are likely to emerge. The authors highlight that coal dependent provinces face the greatest vulnerability, because of concentrated employment, limited economic diversification and high levels of informal work.

At the same time, the report points to significant job creation potential in renewable energy, green manufacturing, environmental services and emerging hydrogen related industries. 

However, achieving these opportunities requires targeted skills development, improved labour market information systems and stronger coordination between government, training institutions and employers. 

The analysis stresses that workers in declining sectors need early support through reskilling, income protection and mobility pathways.

This study positions labour market planning as a central pillar of a just transition, arguing that without deliberate, data driven interventions, structural inequalities could become worse instead of improving.

t: Learning Pathways In The Context Of A Just Energy Transition
c: Ramsarup, P., Allais, S., Hepplethwaite, V., Francis, D., Marock, C. and Sibiya, T. (2024) Learning pathways in the context of a just energy transition. Pretoria: Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH, July.
s:
This report examines how South Africa’s learning and skills ecosystem can support workers, youth and communities as the country moves through a just energy transition. 

Ramsarup and colleagues argue that the transition will reshape occupational structures across the energy system, requiring new technical capabilities, stronger transversal skills and more flexible pathways that allow people to move between learning, work and reskilling opportunities.

The authors map existing learning pathways across schooling, TVET, higher education and workplace learning, identifying fragmentation, uneven quality and weak articulation as major barriers.   

Many emerging green occupations do not yet have clear qualification routes, while others require updated curricula, improved practical training and stronger industry partnerships. 

Planning must be grounded in labour market intelligence and responsive to regional realities, particularly in coal dependent provinces where workers face the greatest disruption.

The study calls for a coordinated national framework that links education, skills planning, industrial policy and social protection.

It concludes that a just transition requires not only new skills but also equitable access to learning opportunities that enable mobility, resilience and long term inclusion.

t: Guidelines on  Green Employment Diagnostics for a Just Transition:  Revised Edition
c: International Labour Organization (ILO) (2025) Guidelines on green employment diagnostics for a just transition: Revised edition. 2nd ed. Geneva: ILO, June.
s:
The ILO’s revised Guidelines on Green Employment Diagnostics provide an updated framework to help governments, social partners and practitioners analyse how labour markets are affected by environmental transitions and to design policies that support a just transition. 

The 2025 edition strengthens the methodological tools introduced in earlier versions, offering clearer steps for diagnosing green employment potential, identifying vulnerable workers and sectors, as well as for assessing institutional readiness for transition planning.

The guidelines emphasise that green employment diagnostics must integrate economic, social and environmental dimensions, combining labour market data with sectoral, technological and policy analysis. 

They outline practical approaches for mapping green and greening occupations, evaluating skills needs and identifying barriers to decent work in emerging green sectors. 

The revised edition also expands guidance on social dialogue, stakeholder engagement and gender responsive analysis, recognising that inclusive processes are essential for credible transition strategies.

Guidelines position diagnostics as a foundational step for countries seeking to align climate ambition with employment outcomes. By providing a structured, evidence based methodology, they support policymakers in designing coherent, equitable and forward looking policies for a just transition.

t: The Just Energy Transition  Partnership Crossroads
c: Csanadi, A. and Helmeci, D. (2025) The Just Energy Transition Partnership crossroads. Washington, DC: Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, October.
s:
Csanadi and Helmeci analyse the evolving political, financial and geopolitical dynamics shaping the Just Energy Transition Partnership (JETP), with a particular focus on South Africa’s experience as the first country to implement the model. 

The report argues that the JETP framework which is designed to mobilise large scale concessional finance for decarbonisation, has reached a crossroads. While it has generated global interest and inspired similar agreements in other countries, its implementation has been slowed by governance challenges, misaligned expectations between donors and recipients, as well as domestic political constraints.

The authors note that South Africa’s energy crisis, institutional fragmentation and fiscal pressures complicate the rollout of JETP aligned investments. At the same time, donor countries face their own political pressures, shifting priorities and budgetary limits. 

The report stresses that without clearer accountability mechanisms, stronger coordination and more flexible financing instruments, the JETP risks losing credibility as a model for climate cooperation.

Ultimately, the authors argue that the partnership still holds significant potential, but only if it evolves into a more transparent, country driven and development aligned mechanism that balances climate ambition with social and economic realities.

t: Press Release:  South Africa's Just Energy Transition Project Management Unit Acknowledges the United States’ Withdrawal from the Just Energy Transition Partnership
c: Just Energy Transition Partnership, Climate finance, International partners, Energy transition, Policy response, South Africa, JET PMU
s:
This press release from South Africa’s Just Energy Transition Project Management Unit (JET PMU) responds to the United States’ withdrawal from the Just Energy Transition Partnership (JETP). 

The PMU acknowledges the decision while emphasising that South Africa remains committed to its just transition objectives and to implementing the JET Investment Plan. 

It underscores that the JETP is a multi partner initiative, supported by several International Partners Group (IPG) members, and that the withdrawal of one partner does not halt the country’s transition efforts.

The PMU draws attention to the ongoing collaboration with remaining partners and stresses that South Africa’s transition is driven by domestic priorities: energy security, economic diversification, social protection for affected workers and communities, and long term climate resilience. 

It also notes that the withdrawal underscores the need for predictable, long term climate finance and for strengthening South Africa’s own institutional capacity to manage transition investments.

The PMU says this is a challenge not a derailment, reaffirming that the just transition will continue through coordinated national planning, stakeholder engagement and diversified international cooperation.

t: Leaders’ Summary: Jobs and Skills for the New Economy – An Action Agenda for a People‑Centred Climate Transition
c: Steer, L., Samans, R., Labonia, T., Steventon, M., Haddaoui, C., Sanan, I., Jobim, E., Harsono, A., Connolly, K. and Metzger, E. (2025) Jobs and skills for the new economy: An action agenda for a people centered climate transition – Leaders’ summary. London: Systemiq; Washington, DC: World Resources Institute.
s:
This leaders’ summary sets out a global action agenda for ensuring that climate transitions generate inclusive, high quality employment and equip workers with the skills they need for a rapidly changing economy. 

Steer and colleagues argue that the world is entering a decisive decade in which climate ambition must be matched by large scale investment in people, institutions and labour market systems. 

While the transition will create millions of new jobs, it will also disrupt existing sectors, requiring proactive planning to avoid deepening inequality.

This report identifies three pillars for a people centred transition: scaling up skills systems to prepare workers for green and digital jobs, strengthening social protection and labour market policies to support workers in declining sectors; and aligning industrial, climate and employment strategies to drive equitable economic transformation. 

The authors emphasise that countries need coordinated governance, long term financing and strong social dialogue to effectively manage these shifts.

Skills development and worker centred policies are essential foundations for achieving climate goals while promoting shared prosperity.

t: Jobs and Skills for the New Economy: An Action Agenda for a People‑Centered Climate Transition
c: Steer, L., Samans, R., Labonia, T., Steventon, M., Haddaoui, C., Sanan, I., Jobim, E., Harsono, A., Connolly, K. and Metzger, E. (2025) Jobs and skills for the new economy: An action agenda for a people centered climate transition. London: Systemiq; Washington, DC: World Resources Institute.
s:
This report sets out a comprehensive global action agenda to ensure that climate transitions deliver inclusive, high quality employment and equip societies with the skills needed for a rapidly evolving economy. Steer and colleagues argue that the world is entering a decisive period in which climate ambition must be matched by large scale investment in people, institutions and labour market systems. 

While the transition will generate significant new employment opportunities, particularly in clean energy, green manufacturing, digital services and climate resilient infrastructure, it will also disrupt carbon intensive sectors, forcing proactive planning to avoid increasing inequality.

The authors propose a three pillar framework for a people centred transition: transforming skills systems to prepare workers for green and digital jobs, strengthening social protection and labour market policies to support workers in declining sectors and aligning industrial, climate and employment strategies to drive equitable economic transformation. 

They emphasise that coordinated governance, long term financing and strong social dialogue are essential for managing these shifts effectively.

The report positions human centred policy as the foundation for achieving climate goals while promoting shared prosperity.

t: Evidence Brief: Green Skills
c: Stein, M. (2025) Evidence Brief: Green Skills. Technical coordination: Büdke, C., Ouma, E. and von Seydlitz, L. Bonn: Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH
s:
This evidence brief synthesises current international research and practice on green skills, offering policymakers, training institutions and labour market actors a concise overview of what is required to support effective green transitions. 

Stein argues that green skills extend far beyond narrow technical competencies to encompass a blend of foundational, transversal and occupation specific capabilities that enable workers and organisations to adapt to environmental, technological and economic change.

The brief highlights three core insights. First, green transitions reshape entire value chains, meaning that skills needs emerge not only in new green sectors but also within traditional industries as they undergo decarbonisation. Second, countries need strong labour market intelligence systems to anticipate demand and guide curriculum reform, investment and workforce planning. Third, successful green skills strategies depend on coordinated governance, social dialogue and capacity building across TVET systems, employers and public institutions.

Stein outlines practical entry points for action, including integrating sustainability into occupational standards, strengthening educator training, expanding workplace based learning and embedding green competencies across all levels of education and training. 

The brief positions green skills as a foundational enabler of inclusive, resilient and future ready economies.

t:
A Framework for a Just
Transition in South Africa
c: Presidential Climate Commission (2022) A Framework for a Just Transition in South Africa. Pretoria: PCC.
s:
The Presidential Climate Commission’s (PCC) Framework for a Just Transition in South Africa sets out the country’s first comprehensive vision for managing the social, economic and environmental dimensions of the shift to a low carbon economy. 

The framework indicates that the transition must prioritise people and regions most affected by decarbonisation, particularly coal dependent workers and communities, and at the same time unlock new opportunities in renewable energy, green manufacturing and climate resilient development.

The PCC outlines three core principles: distributive justice, ensuring fair allocation of risks and benefits, restorative justice, addressing historical inequalities and environmental harm and finally, procedural justice, guaranteeing meaningful participation in decision making. 

It also identifies priority interventions, including social protection measures, skills development pathways, economic diversification strategies and strengthened local planning in transition affected municipalities.

The framework emphasises that a just transition requires coordinated governance, long term financing and transparent social dialogue across government, labour, business and civil society. It positions the transition not only as a climate imperative but as an opportunity to build a more inclusive, resilient and sustainable economy.

t: Coal Kills: An analytical framework to support a move away from coal and towards a just transition in South Africa
c: Munnik, V. 2019. Coal Kills: An analytical framework to support a move away from coal and towards a just transition in South Africa. Johannesburg: Life After Coal/Greenpeace Africa.
s:
The Coal Kills report sets out a clear analytical framework for understanding why South Africa must move away from coal and how a just transition can be achieved. 

The report shows how coal harms people, ecosystems and the economy through air pollution, water contamination, land degradation and greenhouse gas emissions. 

It highlights the severe health impacts in coal affected regions, especially the Highveld, where communities face chronic illness and premature death linked to emissions from power stations and mines.

Munnik explains how South Africa’s political economy keeps the country locked into coal. He describes a powerful network of state entities, mining companies and industrial users that shapes policy and slows the shift to renewable energy. 

The report argues that a just transition must protect workers, support affected communities and repair damaged environments. It calls for inclusive planning, transparent decision making and investment in new industries that can replace coal based livelihoods. 

The framework offers a practical guide for policymakers, researchers and civil society working to build a fair and sustainable energy future.

t: National GHG Inventory Report for South Africa: 2000 - 2020
c: Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment. 2022. National GHG Inventory Report for South Africa: 2000–2020. Pretoria: DFFE.
s:
It tracks emissions from energy, industrial processes, agriculture, waste and land use, and shows how national totals have changed in response to economic activity, policy shifts and structural trends. 

The energy sector remains the dominant source of emissions because of South Africa’s reliance on coal for electricity and liquid fuels. 

Industrial processes and product use form the second largest category, driven by minerals processing and chemicals production.

The inventory notes gradual improvements in data quality and reporting methods, reflecting South Africa’s commitment to international transparency requirements under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). It also notes the influence of economic cycles, energy demand, technology changes and mitigation measures on emissions levels. While total emissions remain high, the report shows early signs of decoupling as renewable energy begins to enter the grid and efficiency measures take effect.
