The inventory provides an evidence base for planning mitigation actions, tracking progress and informing South Africa’s climate commitments.

t: South Africa’s Green Economy Transition: Implications for Reorienting the Economy Towards a Low Carbon Growth Trajectory
c: Kaggwa, M, Mutanga, S S, Nhamo, G and Simelane, T. 2013. South Africa’s Green Economy Transition: Implications for Reorienting the Economy Towards a Low Carbon Growth Trajectory. Pretoria: HSRC Press.
s:
South Africa’s Green Economy Transition: Implications for Reorienting the Economy Towards a Low Carbon Growth Trajectory examines how the country can shift from a resource intensive development model to one that supports sustainable, inclusive and low carbon growth. 

The authors argue that South Africa’s economic structure is heavily shaped by energy intensive industries, coal dependence and historical inequalities, which together limit competitiveness and resilience. 

The report outlines the opportunities offered by a green economy, including new industries, improved resource efficiency and stronger environmental governance.

The authors emphasise that a successful transition requires coordinated policy, targeted investment and institutional reform. 

They point to the need to align industrial policy, energy planning and environmental regulation so that economic growth does not deepen ecological damage or social vulnerability. 

They stress that green sectors such as renewable energy, sustainable agriculture, waste management and ecosystem restoration can create jobs while reducing emissions and resource use. 

They conclude that South Africa must adopt a long term, integrated approach that supports innovation, builds human capabilities and ensures that the benefits of a low carbon transition are shared across society.

t: Impact Case Study: Sustainable Local Development in Nomzamo Agri Village, Ermelo, Mpumalanga. South Africa
c: ASDU, Embassy of France in South Africa Lesotho and Malawi, New Zealand High Commission and Royal Danish Embassy Pretoria. n.d. Impact Case Study: Sustainable Local Development in Nomzamo Agri Village, Ermelo, Mpumalanga. South Africa: ASDU.
s:
This case study shows how a community driven agricultural initiative can support local development, food security and economic resilience in a coal dependent region. 

The Nomzamo Agri Village was established to provide smallholder farmers with land, training and access to markets, enabling households to generate income while strengthening local food systems. It showcases the project’s role in building practical skills, promoting cooperative models and improving community cohesion.

The case study places the initiative within the broader context of Mpumalanga’s transition challenges, noting that coal affected communities face unemployment, land degradation and limited economic alternatives. 

By demonstrating how agriculture can create livelihoods and restore degraded land, the project offers a practical example of how local development can support a just transition. 

Sustained investment, institutional support and community participation are essential for scaling similar initiatives and ensuring long term social and environmental benefits.

t: Multistakeholder Conference on South Africa’s Just Transition: Chair’s Summary, 6 May 2022
c: Presidential Climate Commission. 2022. Multistakeholder Conference on South Africa’s Just Transition: Chair’s Summary, 6 May 2022. Pretoria: PCC.
s:
The conference focused on how South Africa can move towards a low carbon, climate resilient and socially inclusive economy while protecting workers and supporting vulnerable communities. 

Delegates emphasised that the transition must be people centred, transparent and grounded in social dialogue. They highlighted the need for clear planning, predictable policy and strong institutional coordination to guide investment and manage the decline of coal dependent sectors.

The summary notes broad support for diversifying local economies, expanding renewable energy, strengthening skills development and ensuring that affected workers and communities have access to social protection and new opportunities. 

Participants stressed that justice must be central to the transition, with particular attention to youth, women and historically marginalised groups. 

The Chair concluded that a just transition requires long term commitment, inclusive governance and practical partnerships that link national policy with local implementation.

t: Sector Skills Plan 2026–27
c: Chemical Industries Education and Training Authority (CHIETA). 2025. Sector Skills Plan 2026–27. Pretoria: CHIETA.
s:
The Chair’s Summary of the Multistakeholder Conference on South Africa’s Just Transition held on 6 May 2022 captures the main agreements, concerns and priorities conveyed by government, labour, business, civil society and community representatives. 

The CHIETA Sector Skills Plan 2026–27 outlines, among other things, how the chemical industries sector must prepare its workforce for South Africa’s just energy transition. 

The plan shows that the shift towards cleaner energy, stricter environmental standards and low carbon industrial processes is reshaping skills demand across the sector. 

It indicates growing needs in green chemistry, emissions monitoring, waste minimisation, process optimisation and the safe handling of alternative fuels and cleaner technologies. 

Digitalisation and automation are also accelerating, requiring workers who can operate advanced systems and support energy efficient production.

The SSP stresses that the transition will only be just if workers, youth and communities gain access to new opportunities created by low carbon growth. It calls for expanded learnerships, reskilling programmes and workplace based learning that prepare technicians, artisans and operators for emerging green roles. 

The plan also emphasises collaboration between industry, training institutions and government to ensure qualifications align with future energy and environmental requirements. 

By linking skills development to decarbonisation pathways, the SSP positions the chemical sector as a key contributor to South Africa’s climate commitments and a more inclusive, sustainable economy.

t: South Africa’s Just Energy Transition Investment Plan (JET IP) for the Initial Period 2023–2027
c: Government of South Africa. (2022). South Africa’s Just Energy Transition Investment Plan (JET IP) for the Initial Period 2023–2027. Pretoria: Government of South Africa.
s:
The Just Energy Transition Investment Plan (JET IP) 2023–2027 sets out South Africa’s investment needs for the first phase of its transition from a coal based energy system to a low carbon, climate resilient and socially inclusive economy. 

The plan identifies priority investments in the electricity sector, new energy vehicles and green hydrogen, supported by cross cutting measures such as skills development, municipal strengthening and social protection. 

It stresses that the transition must be just, with clear support for workers and communities in coal dependent regions as new industries emerge and coal plants retire.

The JET IP outlines the scale of investment required to modernise the grid, accelerate renewable energy deployment and enable economic diversification in Mpumalanga. 

It underscores the importance of public and private finance working together to unlock long term, affordable capital. 

The plan also recognises the need for strong governance, transparent decision making and meaningful community participation to ensure that the benefits of the transition are shared fairly. 

The JET IP provides a strategic framework for mobilising finance, guiding implementation and aligning South Africa’s climate commitments with inclusive development.

t: EWSETA Sector Skills Plan 2023/24
c: EWSETA (2023) Sector Skills Plan 2023/24. Energy and Water Sector Education and Training Authority.
s:
As the country shifts from coal based energy to cleaner, decentralised and digitised systems, demand is rising for advanced technical and professional capabilities. The SSP identifies critical shortages in occupations such as electrical engineers, energy engineers, industrial engineers, environmental scientists, and civil engineering technologists. 

These occupations are essential for planning, installing, operating and maintaining renewable energy technologies, grid modernisation, hydrogen systems as well as energy efficient infrastructure.

The transition also requires new competencies in decarbonisation, systems integration, green hydrogen production and emerging technologies linked to the Fourth Industrial Revolution. 

EWSETA stresses the need for reskilling and upskilling workers affected by the decline of coal based industries, supported through apprenticeships, RPL and workplace based learning. 

Partnerships with industry, higher education, and research institutions are central to building a pipeline of qualified practitioners.

t: Green Transport Strategy for South Africa: 2018–2050
c: Department of Transport (2018) Green Transport Strategy for South Africa: 2018–2050. Pretoria: Government of South Africa.
s:
South Africa’s Green Transport Strategy (2018–2050) outlines a long term plan to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.  

The sector is responsible for 10.8% of national emissions, with road transport contributing more than 90%. 

The strategy commits to a 5% reduction in transport emissions by 2050 and prioritises shifting passengers from private cars to public and non motorised transport, and freight from road to rail. 

It promotes cleaner fuels, electric mobility and alternative technologies such as biogas and hydrogen fuel cells. 

Spatial inequality, fragmented urban form and inadequate public transport increase travel distances, costs and emissions so the strategy calls for integrated planning, regulatory reform, fuel economy standards, carbon pricing and incentives to accelerate low carbon choices. 

It positions green transport as essential for economic efficiency, improved air quality and public health. 

Achieving a just transition will require behavioural change, strong governance and sustained investment from both the public and private sectors.

t: Gender in a Just Urban Transition
c: Sartori, S. (2024) Gender in a Just Urban Transition. Bangkok: Friedrich Ebert Stiftung.
s:
This discussion paper examines how gender equality must be embedded in just urban transitions as cities confront climate change, rapid urbanisation and rising energy demand. 

With more than half of the world’s population now living in cities and the fastest growth occurring in Africa and Asia, the paper argues that if they are not deliberately designed to be inclusive, urban transition processes risk reinforcing existing gender and social inequalities. 

Cities consume two thirds of global energy and generate more than 70% of greenhouse gas emissions, making them central to countering and managing climate change. 

The paper highlights that women are particularly vulnerable because they tend to have limited access to services and work in the informal sector, often facing disproportionate safety concerns and exclusion from decision making. 

It draws on insights from the 2023 Gender Lab held during the Just Transition Forum Asia, where stakeholders explored practical entry points for gender responsive planning. 

These include improving women’s participation in governance, integrating gender analysis into urban energy and mobility planning, and supporting women’s economic empowerment in emerging green sectors. 

Current gaps in equality and inclusion must be addressed and similarly, urban transitions must actively promote social justice.

t: Electric Vehicle White Paper
c: Department of Trade, Industry and Competition (2023) Electric Vehicle White Paper. Pretoria: Government of South Africa.
s:
South Africa’s Electric Vehicle (EV) White Paper sets out a national plan to shift the automotive industry and domestic market towards electric mobility, and at the same time protecting jobs and industrial capacity. 

It emphasises the urgency of reducing greenhouse gas emissions, meeting changing export market requirements and addressing energy insecurity. It stresses that the transition must support economic growth rather than trigger de industrialisation. 

The strategy focuses on building a competitive domestic EV production ecosystem, expanding the battery value chain and ensuring that small and medium enterprises can participate. 

It outlines measures to close the price gap between internal combustion engine vehicles and EVs, expand charging infrastructure, strengthen grid capacity and increase public and corporate procurement of locally produced EVs. 

The paper frames the transition as an opportunity to deepen localisation, secure investment and create new skills pathways. 

It also emphasises that a just transition must place workers and vulnerable groups at the centre of planning and ensure that the benefits of new technologies are shared. 

The approach relies on coordinated policy, targeted incentives and strong alignment between government, industry and labour.

t: Challenges and opportunities for Just Energy Transition Partnerships in Africa
c: Tamasiga, P. (2024) Challenges and opportunities for Just Energy Transition Partnerships in Africa. Megatrends Afrika Policy Brief 30.
s:
This policy brief examines the role of Just Energy Transition Partnerships in supporting African countries as they shift from coal to cleaner energy systems. 

It argues that although JETPs offer a promising alternative to slow multilateral climate negotiations, their social dimension has received far less attention than technical and financial considerations. 

Using South Africa and Senegal as case studies, the brief highlights how JETPs can mobilise investment for renewable energy, grid modernisation and new technologies, but face persistent challenges. 

These include inadequate funding relative to transition needs, heavy reliance on loans that increase debt burdens, weak governance and institutional capacity, and limited access to clean energy for low income communities. 

The brief stresses that without stronger social protection, job transition planning and community engagement, JETPs risk deepening existing inequalities. 

It identifies opportunities to strengthen governance, improve transparency, integrate demand side measures, and use public finance to de risk private investment. 

A people centred approach is essential for ensuring that the benefits of decarbonisation are shared fairly and that vulnerable groups are not left behind.

t: Workforce transition in South Africa’s Just Energy Transition: An analysis of needs, policy gaps and socioeconomic implications
c: Tamasiga, P. (2025) Workforce transition in South Africa’s Just Energy Transition: An analysis of needs, policy gaps and socioeconomic implications. Megatrends Afrika Policy Brief 39.
s:
This policy brief analyses whether South Africa’s Just Energy Transition can balance decarbonisation with socioeconomic justice. 

It focuses on the country’s deep dependence on coal, which supports more than 120,000 direct jobs, and shows how coal reliant municipalities in Mpumalanga face severe risks due to limited economic diversification, low skills and weak social protection. 

Although renewable energy jobs are increasing, many are short term, lack benefits and offer little job security compared with employment in coal mining and processing. 

Skills mismatches, fragmented training pathways and uneven regional investment further undermine a fair transition. 

Stakeholder interviews reveal concerns about inadequate funding for skills development, weak municipal capacity and limited community participation in decision making. 

Without stronger social protection, job quality measures and targeted reskilling, the transition could deepen inequality. 

It recommends job guarantee schemes, expanded social insurance, scaled reskilling programmes and community led governance structures to ensure that workers and coal dependent communities are not left behind. 

Overall, the brief stresses that a people centred approach is essential for aligning climate goals with economic stability.

t: Financing South Africa’s energy transition: making the just aspects count more
c: Tamasiga, P. and Sokona, Y. (2025) Financing South Africa’s energy transition: making the just aspects count more. Ukåmå.
s:
This brief argues that South Africa’s energy transition cannot succeed through infrastructure investment alone and must place far greater emphasis on social measures that protect workers and coal dependent communities. 

Although the Just Energy Transition Investment Plan identifies six priority areas, funding patterns remain heavily skewed toward electricity infrastructure and green hydrogen, while social interventions such as skills development, social protection and local economic diversification remain underfunded. 

Stakeholder interviews highlight deep concerns about job losses across the coal value chain, weak social safety nets and limited alternative employment pathways. 

Mpumalanga, the region most affected by coal decline, has received only a small fraction of its estimated funding needs. 

The JETP financing model has structural problems including the dominance of loans over grants, donor driven allocation patterns and high administrative costs absorbed by international agencies. 

TVET programmes need to be scaled up, and social protection strengthened through income support or job guarantees, with increased local participation in renewable energy value chains. 

Unless social investments are prioritised alongside infrastructure, South Africa risks an unjust transition that leaves vulnerable communities behind.

t: Just Transition Blueprint, Congress of South African Trade Unions
c: COSATU 2022, Just Transition Blueprint, Congress of South African Trade Unions, viewed April 2026, https://mediadon.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/COSATU-Just-Transition-Blueprint-Full-version.pdf
s:
COSATU’s Just Transition Blueprint argues that South Africa’s shift to a low carbon economy must protect workers, communities and public services and accelerate climate action. 

The transition cannot be left to the market, because this would deepen unemployment and inequality. 

Instead, it calls for a state led industrial strategy that expands renewable energy, modernises the grid and secures affordable electricity for households and industry. 

There is a need for strong social dialogue so that workers in coal dependent regions are not abandoned. 

It proposes retraining, income protection and local economic diversification to prevent large scale job losses. 

COSATU also emphasises public ownership of key energy assets to prevent privatisation from undermining labour rights and energy security and sees the just energy transition as an opportunity to rebuild manufacturing capacity, strengthen public transport and improve environmental health. 

It frames the just transition as a social compact that balances climate commitments with economic justice and long term national development.

t: Equipping South Africa’s workforce for a just transition through up skilling and reskilling: Mpumalanga case study summary draft report
c: Wits REAL & Rhodes University ELRC (2025) Equipping South Africa’s workforce for a just transition through up skilling and reskilling: Mpumalanga case study summary draft report. International Labour Organization.
s:
As Mpumalanga shifts away from coal, this report looks at how the province can prepare its workforce for South Africa’s just energy transition. 

It identifies the risks facing intermediate and low skilled workers in coal mining, coal based power generation and internal combustion engine vehicle services, noting that many of these jobs are likely to decline. 

The study also identifies growth opportunities in renewable energy, electric mobility, sustainable agriculture and critical minerals. 

It maps at risk occupations such as electricians, automotive mechanics, mechanical technicians, mine and quarry workers and truck drivers, and links them to emerging roles including solar PV installers, high voltage electricians, mechatronics technicians and agricultural workers. 

The report stresses the need for demand driven training, flexible learning pathways and coordinated planning across government, industry, labour and education institutions. 

It also highlights major data gaps and limited worker engagement, calling for more detailed occupational analysis and inclusive consultation. 

Proactive reskilling and upskilling are essential to protect livelihoods and support Mpumalanga’s economic transformation.

t: Equipping South Africa’s workforce for a just transition through up skilling and reskilling: Eastern Cape case study summary draft report
c: International Labour Organization, Wits REAL and Rhodes University ELRC (2025) Equipping South Africa’s workforce for a just transition through up skilling and reskilling: Eastern Cape case study summary draft report. Geneva: ILO.
s:
The report examines how the Eastern Cape can prepare its workforce for South Africa’s just energy transition by identifying occupations at risk and mapping realistic reskilling and upskilling pathways. 

The JET IP aims to guide the shift to a just, low carbon, climate resilient economy and society by 2050 but workers who may lose jobs as the energy system changes must be supported. 

There are significant risks in internal combustion engine manufacturing and related aftercare roles, including automotive mechanics, diesel mechanics, metal machinists and toolmakers. 

However, there is also strong growth potential in renewable energy, new energy vehicles, green hydrogen, advanced manufacturing and agriculture. 

High demand occupations include high voltage electricians, millwrights, welders as well as mechanical and electrical engineering technicians. 

The focus should be on demand driven training, flexible learning pathways and alignment with emerging value chains. 

Worker engagement is limited, compounded by major data gaps suggesting deeper research and inclusive consultation. 

Strategic workforce planning, multi skilling and targeted skills development are essential to ensuring a fair transition and for strengthening economic resilience in the province.

t: The electric vehicle ecosystem and associated value chains
c: GreenCape (2021) The electric vehicle ecosystem and associated value chains. Cape Town: GreenCape.
s:
The report outlines how South Africa’s electric vehicle (EV) ecosystem is developing across manufacturing, battery value chains, charging infrastructure, energy supply and consumer demand. 

The automotive sector remains central to the economy, contributing 27.6% of manufacturing output in 2019 and employing up to 900 000 people directly and indirectly. As global markets shift, local original equipment manufacturers (OEMsa0 are preparing to pivot from internal combustion engine production to electric vehicles to remain competitive. 

Although South Africa currently assembles imported battery cells rather than producing them, EVs require far more mineral inputs than internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles, creating opportunities in copper, nickel, cobalt and lithium value chains. 

Charging infrastructure remains limited, with about 280 public stations nationally, mostly using Combined Charging System (CCS) connectors. 

Barriers to EV uptake include high vehicle costs, slow charging times and limited home and public charging options. 

The report identifies opportunities for the City of Cape Town in manufacturing, skills development, renewable energy integration and supportive regulation. 

Coordinated policy, investment and skills planning will be essential to build a viable EV industry and support South Africa’s transition to low carbon mobility.

t: GIZ’s latest foresight work on geopolitics and sustainable development. Futures4Europe
c: Kummerow, J, Geisselmann, J and Hunger, M (2025) GIZ’s latest foresight work on geopolitics and sustainable development. Futures4Europe. Available at: https://www.futures4europe.eu/post/gizs-latest-foresight-work-on-geopolitics-and-sustainable-development-hnto7 (Accessed 2 April 2026).
s:
The blog outlines GIZ’s latest foresight work, which examines how geopolitical shifts will shape sustainable development and the global agenda over the next decade. 

It notes that the world has been described as being in a state of “perma-crisis” and argues that GIZ must anticipate political and economic disruptions to remain resilient. 

The 2024 foresight report draws on contributions from more than 100 staff members and over 30 external experts, combining workshops, interviews and secondary research. 

It presents four scenarios based on the Manoa School archetypes, ranging from intensified bloc confrontation to transformative multilateral cooperation. These scenarios explore tensions between economic growth and green transitions, the fragility of global governance and the potential for new development agendas. 

Each scenario includes wildcards, such as “billionaires with God complex” or “AI goes rogue”, to test organisational preparedness. 

The report aims to help GIZ identify risks, opportunities and strategic choices, and has already prompted widespread internal engagement. 

It concludes that strategic foresight must inform long-term planning, strengthen organisational resilience and support more adaptive approaches to international cooperation.

t: Gender Response Guide: How to increase women’s participation in the emerging green hydrogen economy in South Africa.
c: Urban Earth (2025) Gender Response Guide: How to increase women’s participation in the emerging green hydrogen economy in South Africa. Pretoria: Department of Mineral Resources and Energy and GIZ.
s:
The guide sets out practical actions to increase women’s participation in South Africa’s emerging green hydrogen economy. 

Women currently make up only 33.2% of the renewable energy sector in South Africa and face barriers at entry, retention and leadership levels. 

These include gender stereotypes in STEM education, limited access to information, poor visibility of career pathways, restricted access to funding and a lack of family friendly workplace policies. 

Women often feel isolated in a male dominated sector with black women facing additional socio economic barriers. 

To address these challenges, the guide proposes interventions across four thematic areas: networking, job opportunities, leadership and ownership and research as well as skills development. 

Targets include 40% women speakers at hydrogen events by 2025, 45% women across all job levels by 2030 and 55% women in postgraduate research by 2030. 

The guide emphasises the need for mentoring, transparent recruitment and promotion processes, gender responsive workplace policies and stronger support for women owned enterprises. 

It positions gender inclusion as essential for a fair and sustainable green hydrogen economy.

t: Gender sensitivity training: For facilitators, moderators and trainers
c: TRi Facts (2025) Gender sensitivity training: For facilitators, moderators and trainers. International PtX Hub and H2.SA, supported by GIZ.
s:
The manual provides practical guidance to help facilitators, moderators and trainers design and run events that are gender sensitive and inclusive. 

Gender responsive facilitation is essential because women and non binary participants are often overlooked in technical and energy related spaces. 

When women make up less than a critical mass, usually around 30% of the group, their contributions are more likely to be ignored or interrupted. 

It explains key concepts such as gender, gender norms, intersectionality, gender mainstreaming and allyship, emphasising how social expectations shape participation and power dynamics. 

The manual provides detailed checklists for planning, running and evaluating workshops.  These cover logistics, inclusive language, speaker selection, multimedia use, networking design and accessibility. 

It also provides pointers for virtual and in person events, highlighting issues such as safety, family responsibilities and representation in visuals. 

It encourages facilitators to reflect on their own biases, create balanced agendas and ensure equal opportunities to speak. 

Gender sensitive facilitation is a strategic tool that improves participation, strengthens learning outcomes and supports more equitable engagement in the renewable energy and green hydrogen sectors.

t: Strengthening skills for a Just Transition: Recommendations to support collaboration
c: Presidential Climate Commission (2025) Strengthening skills for a Just Transition: Recommendations to support collaboration. Pretoria: PCC.
s:
The report sets out the strategic skills priorities needed to support South Africa’s Just Transition and strengthen the role of the Presidential Climate Commission in coordinating this work. 

The transition must be inclusive and equitable with economic diversification, social inclusion and environmental sustainability. 

National policy frameworks consistently highlight the need for reskilling and upskilling adult workers, improving foundational education, aligning training with future labour market needs and building a coordinated skills ecosystem. 

Challenges persist, including fragmented systems, weak anticipation of occupational change and limited inclusion. 

To address these, it proposes four collective action priorities: strengthening collaboration and governance, improving understanding of occupational needs, enabling demand led education and training, and supporting education to work transitions. 

Coordinated action across government, business, communities and training institutions is essential. 

Quick wins include fast tracking solar skills, reskilling coal workers, expanding RPL and bridging programmes, mobilising CET and TVET hubs and scaling climate care jobs. 

These actions aim to create early momentum while longer term systems are developed to ensure a fair and effective transition.

t: Greening technical and vocational education and training: A practical guide for institutions
c: UNESCO UNEVOC (2017) Greening technical and vocational education and training: A practical guide for institutions. Paris: UNESCO.
s:
A practical framework to help TVET institutions integrate sustainability into their systems, programmes and culture. 

Greening TVET is essential because institutions must prepare learners for the jobs that exist now and also for those of the future, particularly as economies shift to low carbon pathways. 

The guide advocates a whole institution approach that embeds sustainability across governance, teaching, campus operations, research and community engagement. 

It sets out a four step process: understanding the greening concept, planning an institutional greening strategy, implementing the plan and monitoring progress. 

TVET institutions need to align with global frameworks such as the SDGs and Education for Sustainable Development; greening enhances employability by equipping learners with green skills and supporting transitions into emerging sectors. 

Disadvantaged groups require targeted support to access green jobs. 

Practical tools include assessment templates, planning checklists and examples of institutional greening plans. 

Greening TVET is a strategic response to climate change, labour market shifts and the need for sustainable development.

t: Youth Employment Programmes in South Africa: Impact, Challenges and Future Directions
c: Chitiga Mabugu, M.R., Bohlmann, J., Meniago, C., Omotoso, K.O., Mabugu, R.E. and Monareng, T. (2025) ‘Youth Employment Programmes in South Africa: Impact, Challenges and Future Directions’, in Mabugu, R.E. and Ronconi, L. (eds) Youth Employment Programmes in Africa. London: Routledge, pp. xxx–xxx
s:
The chapter argues that South Africa’s youth employment programmes have expanded but still struggle to create sustained labour market inclusion. 

Public employment programmes, skills training and wage subsidies have delivered short term gains yet remain fragmented and quality is uneven. 

Weak coordination, limited employer participation and inconsistent alignment with real labour market demand reduce their long term impact. 

The authors highlight that structural barriers, including slow economic growth and persistent spatial inequality, continue to limit opportunities for young people. 

They call for stronger monitoring systems, better targeting and a shift towards integrated pathways that link training, workplace exposure and progression into decent work. 

To ensure that young people can access emerging opportunities in a changing economy, they conclude that youth employment policy must be embedded in broader economic reforms, including industrial diversification and a just energy transition.

t: The risks and returns of innovative finance for social change
c: Intellidex (2021) The risks and returns of innovative finance for social change. Johannesburg: Intellidex SIBs Research Series.
s:
Social impact bonds (SIBs) operate as a results based financing tool that shifts financial risk from the state to investors while aiming to improve social outcomes. 

This report assesses two early South African SIBs and shows that investors provide upfront capital to non profit service providers, who must meet predefined outcome targets to trigger repayment. If targets are not met, investors may lose their capital. 

The report highlights that SIBs can strengthen accountability, improve data systems and encourage collaboration between government, investors and implementing partners. 

However, SIBs introduce new risks, including complex contracting, high transaction costs and uncertainty about long term sustainability. 

The authors argue that while SIBs can support innovation in social service delivery, they are not a universal solution and require strong governance, clear metrics and credible independent evaluation. 

SIBs may complement public funding in areas such as youth employment and early childhood development, but only when designed with realistic outcomes and robust monitoring.

t: South African Renewable Energy Masterplan (SAREM): Draft for Public Consultation
c: Department of Mineral Resources and Energy, Department of Trade, Industry and Competition and Department of Science and Innovation (2023) South African Renewable Energy Masterplan (SAREM): Draft for Public Consultation. Pretoria: Government of South Africa.
s:
The draft South African Renewable Energy Masterplan (SAREM) positions renewable energy and storage as central to economic recovery, industrial growth and a just transition. 

Rapidly expanding demand for solar, wind and battery technologies creates an opportunity to rebuild domestic manufacturing capacity, deepen local value chains and stimulate investment. 

The draft plan stresses that South Africa’s past stop start procurement cycles undermined industrialisation, and argues for predictable demand, clear localisation targets and coordinated industrial policy. 

It highlights the need to widen access to renewable energy, strengthen transformation across the value chain and direct new projects into just transition hotspots such as Mpumalanga. 

Skills development is a critical enabler, with shortages already constraining growth. 

The draft plan proposes a coordinated skills pipeline, expanded work based learning and stronger support for technology commercialisation to bridge the “valley of death”. 

Overall, the draft SAREM aims to align demand, industrial development, inclusion and capability building to ensure that renewable energy contributes to broad based socio economic development.

t: The South African Green Hydrogen TVET Ecosystem Just Transition Strategic Framework: Synthesis Report
c: SAIIA, DHET & DSI 2022, The South African Green Hydrogen TVET Ecosystem Just Transition Strategic Framework: Synthesis Report, South African Institute of International Affairs, Johannesburg.
s:
The report positions green hydrogen as a major opportunity for South Africa to build a new energy industrial system anchored in renewable power. 

It explains that hydrogen can decarbonise sectors such as long haul transport, iron and steel, long duration storage and liquid fuels. 

South Africa’s strong renewable resources, mineral endowment and manufacturing capability give it a competitive advantage in producing green hydrogen and derivative products. 

Hydrogen is used for both for energy and as a material in industry and could therefore help to build a new energy and industrial system. Because people around the world need hydrogen, South Africa can potentially export products like green ammonia and fuel-cell parts.

It also stresses the need for a TVET ecosystem that can anticipate skills demand and support a just transition for workers. 

Aligning TVET colleges with hydrogen related industries will improve labour absorption and enable workers to shift from declining fossil fuel sectors into emerging green value chains. 

It concludes that coordinated planning, investment and skills governance are essential for positioning South Africa for inclusive growth in a green hydrogen economy.

t: South African Energy Skills Roadmap 2023
c: SANEA, AELC, REAL & BRICS Business Council (2023) South African Energy Skills Roadmap 2023. Johannesburg: South African National Energy Association.
s:
The energy transition demands a coordinated, future focused skills system that can respond to rapid technological, economic and social change. 

South Africa’s Energy Skills Roadmap explains that the sector is shaped by major trends including decarbonisation, decentralisation, digitalisation and evolving markets, all of which shift job profiles and create new occupational demands. 

It highlights that traditional engineering skills remain important but are no longer sufficient, as the transition requires stronger socio economic capabilities, policy expertise and transversal skills. 

Current education and training provision is uneven, with universities offering adequate traditional qualifications with TVET colleges lagging behind local renewable energy needs. 

It stresses that skills planning must be flexible, integrated and geographically sensitive, particularly in regions affected by coal decline. 

The roadmap calls for anticipatory planning, improved labour market intelligence and a single coordinating entity to align government, industry and education providers. 

Without systemic reform and investment in foundational and specialised skills, South Africa risks missing both the economic and social opportunities of a just energy transition.

t: The socioeconomic implications of renewable energy and low carbon trajectories in South Africa
c: Caetano, T. and Thurlow, J. (2014) The socioeconomic implications of renewable energy and low carbon trajectories in South Africa. In: Inequality and Climate Change. Pretoria: HSRC Press.
s:
South Africa’s shift to a low carbon economy creates both opportunities and risks, with renewable energy investment offering potential gains in employment, regional development and reduced inequality. 

Coal dependence has produced high emissions and deep social disparities, and that climate commitments require a rapid diversification of the energy mix. 

Modelling of different electricity build scenarios indicates that renewable energy pathways generate more construction and manufacturing jobs than coal, although long term operations jobs remain fewer. These gains are uneven across skill levels, which reinforces the need for targeted skills development. 

Expanding technical training in renewable technologies, strengthening labour market mobility and improving access to STEM education are essential to ensure that workers can transition into new roles. 

Women and people with disabilities remain under represented in energy related occupations, and that without deliberate inclusion strategies the transition may reproduce existing inequalities. 

A just energy transition therefore requires coordinated policy that links decarbonisation with skills planning, social protection and inclusive labour market reforms. 

Strengthening local manufacturing, supporting vulnerable workers and investing in community level training can help ensure that the benefits of the transition are shared more equitably.

t: Analysing the transition away from coal in South Africa using a linked energy economic model
c: Merven, B., Hartley, F., McCall, B., Burton, J. and Schers, J. (2020) Analysing the transition away from coal in South Africa using a linked energy economic model. Pretoria: University of Cape Town Energy Systems Research Group.
s:
South Africa’s transition away from coal will not protect jobs in the long term unless there is a deliberate and parallel process for skills development and inclusive planning. 

The modelling shows that rising coal costs, declining export demand and the retirement of ageing coal plants make continued coal investment economically damaging. 

A constrained energy pathway that forces new coal capacity leads to higher electricity prices and weaker economic performance, which ultimately reduces employment across the wider economy. 

A least cost pathway dominated by renewables performs better for growth and job creation, particularly through construction, operations and associated value chains. 

However, these gains require a workforce able to shift into new roles. 

Without targeted reskilling, workers in coal dependent regions face significant displacement. 

The analysis underscores the need for structured transition support that is inclusive, including training for renewable technologies, grid operations and emerging energy services.

t: Implementation Handbook for Eco Industrial Parks
c: UNIDO (2017) Implementation Handbook for Eco Industrial Parks. Vienna: United Nations Industrial Development Organization.
s:
An eco industrial park is defined as a community of manufacturing and service businesses located on a common property. Member businesses look for enhanced environmental, economic and social performance through collaboration when managing environmental and resource issues.

This handbook explains how to plan, develop and operate eco industrial parks (EIPs) so they deliver economic, environmental and social benefits. 

The United Nations Industrial Development Organisation (UNIDO) sets out an approach covering scoping, awareness raising, policy support, park management, technical measures to boost resource efficiency and industrial synergies, performance monitoring and capacity building. 

It stresses stakeholder engagement, clear park leadership, financial sustainability and iterative improvement so projects can move from pilot actions to scalable programmes. 

Resource efficient and cleaner production (RECP) reduces inputs and waste while industrial synergies enable shared utilities, services and by product exchanges that lower costs and risks for companies in the industrial park. 

The handbook also links EIPs to sustainable cities by showing how parks can process municipal waste, supply low carbon energy and provide social infrastructure that supports local employment and skills development.

t: The Global Eco Industrial Parks Programme.
c: NCPC SA, UNIDO and the dtic (2021) The Global Eco Industrial Parks Programme. Pretoria: NCPC SA.
s:
The Global Eco Industrial Parks Programme (GEIPP) supports South African industrial parks to improve resource productivity and strengthen economic, environmental and social performance. 

It promotes practical interventions such as resource efficient and cleaner production, industrial synergies, shared utilities and strengthened park governance. 

The National Cleaner Production Centre South Africa (NCPC SA) will pilot EIP practices in three government parks, working with park managers and tenant companies to identify quick wins and investable projects that boost competitiveness and resilience. 

The approach prioritises stakeholder engagement, capacity building and measurable performance monitoring so parks can attract investment and create local employment while reducing energy, water and waste footprints. 

Early actions focus on energy management, water stewardship and waste exchanges alongside governance reforms to ensure financial sustainability and community benefits. 

The handbook frames EIPs as a continuous improvement process that combines technical measures with management reforms to deliver tangible economic savings and social outcomes.

t: Quantifying the macro  and socio economic benefits of a transition to renewable energy in South Africa
c: Merven B, Ireland G, Hartley F, Arndt C, Hughes A, Ahjum F, McCall B and Caetano T (2018) Quantifying the macro  and socio economic benefits of a transition to renewable energy in South Africa. SA TIED Working Paper 19, June 2018.
s:
This working paper models the macroeconomic and social benefits of shifting South Africa's power sector towards renewable energy using a linked energy economy framework called SATIMGE. 

The authors combine a TIMES energy model with a dynamic general equilibrium model to test least cost technology mixes under realistic constraints for capacity, reliability and emissions. 

Results show a transition from coal to a system dominated by solar PV, wind and flexible gas and storage by 2050, with variable renewable energy supplying a large share of generation and power sector emissions falling substantially. 
The findings indicate that by 2050, South Africa's power sector is set to shift away from coal towards a an energy mix that is mainly solar photovoltaic, wind, flexible gas and energy storage. 

As a result, renewable energy will contribute a significant portion of electricity generation, leading to a marked reduction in emissions from the power sector.

The analysis emphasises the importance of when and how much to invest, how electricity prices change over time and the potential drawbacks of limiting renewable energy development.

It also demonstrates that, with appropriate assumptions on technology costs and system flexibility, a renewable led pathway can meet demand growth while supporting economic objectives. 

The paper provides policy relevant insights on planning, reserve margins, distributed generation limits and the importance of linking energy system choices to broader economic outcomes.

t: Just Transition Policy Brief: Skills Development for a Just Transition
c: International Labour Organization (2022) Just Transition Policy Brief: Skills Development for a Just Transition. Geneva: ILO.
s:
The ILO’s Just Transition Policy Brief highlights how skills development underpins an equitable shift to environmentally sustainable economies. 

It stresses that climate commitments across energy, agriculture, manufacturing, transport and construction cannot be met without the skills that emerging green sectors need. 

Job creation potential is significant, yet uneven, but millions of workers will require reskilling as carbon intensive industries decline. 

Weak coordination between environmental, labour and education policies remains a major barrier, particularly in countries where skills systems are fragmented or under resourced. The brief emphasises the need for coherent national and sectoral strategies, stronger social dialogue, and systematic skills anticipation mechanisms to align training with labour market demand. 

It also calls for inclusive approaches that prioritise women, young people, low skilled workers, people with disabilities, migrants and rural communities. 

Public private partnerships, improved TVET systems and investment in teachers and trainers are critical to ensuring that the green transition is both effective and just.

t: Just Energy Transition Implementation Plan 2023–2027
c: The Presidency, Republic of South Africa (2023) Just Energy Transition Implementation Plan 2023–2027. Pretoria.
s:
The JET Implementation Plan 2023–2027 (JITP) sets a practical five year roadmap for decarbonising South Africa while protecting workers and communities and supporting economic growth. 

It assigns six core portfolios, namely Electricity; Mpumalanga Just Transition; New Energy Vehicles; Green Hydrogen; Skills and Municipalities. 

It establishes a Project Management Unit (PMU) in the Presidency to coordinate planning, finance and monitoring. The plan prioritises rapid private sector deployment of renewable energy alongside urgent transmission and distribution upgrades as well as repurposing and repowering at retiring coal sites to deliver local jobs and enterprise opportunities. 

It proposes a JET Projects’ Register and a JET Funding Platform to match grant makers with community and project needs

It embeds the Theory of Change approach with monitoring framework to track outcomes which recognises fiscal constraints and the need for higher grant funding

The JITP stresses co-creation with labour, business and civil society to promote distributive and procedural justice during the transition. 

It aims to help South Africa meet its decarbonisation commitments while supporting inclusive economic growth, energy security and employment at a pace, scale and cost that match the country’s socio-economic needs and affordability.

The six JET Portfolios are: Electricity; Mpumalanga Just Transition; New Energy Vehicles (NEVs); Green Hydrogen (GH2); Skills; and Municipalities.

t: Just Energy Transition Implementation Plan Quarterly Progress Report 30 June 2025
c: The Presidency, Republic of South Africa (2025) Just Energy Transition Implementation Plan Quarterly Progress Report 30 June 2025. Pretoria.
s:
The Quarterly Progress Report to 30 June 2025 reviews year two of JET Implementation Plan (JITP) and shows steady institutional progress while noting financing and delivery challenges. 

The JET Project Management Unit (PMU) in the Presidency is fully operational and runs a monitoring, evaluation and learning framework, an online grants register and a funding platform that is actively matching JET projects with grant funding. This has seen some early grant matche successes.

Lead institutions and secretariats for the six portfolios are in place as are building project pipelines, with the Electricity Portfolio prioritising transmission upgrades; an updated ACT Investment Plan to manage retiring coal plants is in place. 

International partners have pledged USD 12.8 billion to support the JET, but the roll-out of concessional loans has been limited by Eskom’s borrowing moratorium and wider financial constraints. 

It remains necessary to accelerate grant deployment to secure community benefits and attract further private sector investment.

The JET Skills Desk has been established along with and an advisory forum to align training with new energy value chains.

t: Sector Skills Plan 2024/2025
c: merSETA (2023) Sector Skills Plan 2024/2025. Johannesburg.
s:
The merSETA Sector Skills Plan 2024/2025 (SSP) sets out a practical skills response for the manufacturing, engineering and related services sectors to support industrial recovery, localisation and inclusive employment. 

It draws on workplace data, primary research and national statistics to identify hard to fill vacancies, priority occupations and the skills gaps that constrain growth. 

The plan prioritises workplace learning, apprenticeships, artisan recognition of prior learning and simulation training to expand training capacity and improve job readiness. 

It commits to strengthening partnerships with employers, TVET colleges and higher education institutions to align curricula with industry needs and to scale workplace based learning. 

The SSP emphasises targeted actions to increase participation by youth, women and people with disabilities and to use monitoring and evaluation to refine interventions. 

Skills development as central to industrialisation, community development and adapting to new technologies so that the sector can respond to economic shocks and create sustainable employment.

The merSETA will continue to focus on skills aligned to localisation, industrialisation, community development, new technologies, the changing world of work and prioritising participation by women, the youth and persons with disabilities.

t: Beyond the “decarbonised minerals–energy complex”: Rethinking financialisation and state–capital relations in South Africa’s green hydrogen transition
c: Smith, R.N. (2025) ‘Beyond the “decarbonised minerals–energy complex”: Rethinking financialisation and state–capital relations in South Africa’s green hydrogen transition’, New Agenda, Issue 99, 17 December 2025. African Journals Online
s:
Smith examines South Africa’s green hydrogen ambitions and argues that prevailing framings of a consolidated “decarbonised minerals–energy complex” overstate the current dominance of finance capital and underplay important gaps in practice. 

Drawing on recent critical literature and initial fieldwork, Smith shows that the hydrogen sector is characterised by a persistent financing gap and institutional fragmentation within the state, which together limit private financial participation and slow the creation of investible projects. 

Instead of describing financialisation as complete, the article argues that the government is trying to put the right conditions in place for investment, but it is held back by competing mandates and poor coordination.

Smith therefore calls for renewed empirical inquiry and a rethinking of political economy paradigms so analysis and policy can better reflect how state-capital relations are being constructed in practice, so that interventions can address the specific barriers to scaling green hydrogen investment in South Africa. 

The piece locates these arguments within debates on development finance, industrial strategy and the politics of energy transition.

t: Presidential Climate Commission Annual Review 01 April 2023–31 March 2024
c: Presidential Climate Commission (2024) Presidential Climate Commission Annual Review 01 April 2023–31 March 2024. Pretoria.
s:
The Presidential Climate Commission (PCC) Annual Review 2023–24 assesses the PCC’s work to advance a just transition that balances decarbonisation with jobs, livelihoods and resilience. 

The report describes institutional consolidation as the PCC moves towards Schedule 3 public entity status, and it summarises research, advisory and activities across energy, skills, adaptation and finance. 

Key priorities include recommendations on the electricity mix and grid investment, building municipal and the Mpumalanga pipelines for just transition projects, designing a just transition financing mechanism, as well as strengthening monitoring, evaluation and learning to track progress. 

Skills, employment and social protection remain central to managing coal affected regions and to enabling green industrialisation. 

The review documents donor and partner support, early work on climate resilient development pathways, and plans to finalise guidance on emissions trajectories and the Climate Response Fund. 

Inclusive stakeholder engagement and the need to accelerate finance deployment and capacity building are stressed to ensure that transition benefits are widely shared and implementation can be scaled.

To achieve a just transition, we need to decarbonise our economy at a pace and scale that is sustainable and advances development outcomes (jobs, livelihoods and human development).

t: Powering Futures: The Green Skilling Opportunity
c: National Business Initiative and Boston Consulting Group (2024) Powering Futures: The Green Skilling Opportunity. Johannesburg.
s:
The report frames skilling as central to a just energy transition and sets out a demand led approach to aligning workforce development with confirmed project pipelines. 

It quantifies near term and long term job needs, estimating the need for between 120,000 and 200,000 jobs by 2030 and between 400,000 and 600,000 over 25 years, and identifies where and when training must scale. 

The analysis breaks down occupations by value chain step and project phase so training providers can match intake to hiring windows. 

It recommends an ecosystem model that combines employer engagement, TVET and higher education alignment, workplace learning, SMME support and with a strong leader to coordinate local delivery. 

The report highlights solar, construction, transmission, battery storage, green hydrogen and new energy vehicles as priority value chains and maps short term geographic hot spots. 

It calls for learner centric, low barrier pathways, simulation training and artisan recognition of prior learning to speed up placement and improve inclusion for youth, women and marginalised communities. 

The emphasis is on practical, phased implementation to de risk projects and maximise local economic benefit.

t: JET Skills Desk launch programme: Preliminary programme for the official launch of the JET Skills Desk and National JET Skills Advisory Forum
c: Department of Higher Education and Training (2025) JET Skills Desk launch programme: Preliminary programme for the official launch of the JET Skills Desk and National JET Skills Advisory Forum. Pretoria.
s: Preliminary programme for the launch of the Just Energy Transition (JET) Skills Desk, National JET Skills Advisory Forum and a multi donor initiative to coordinate skilling for a just energy transition. The launch will outline governance and indicate how the JET Skills desk will link national leadership with donors and industry, introduce Skills Development Zones and prioritise employer partnerships, TVET capacity, workplace learning and broadly inclusive access.

t: Presidential Climate Commission Annual Report 2024–2025
c: Presidential Climate Commission (2025) Presidential Climate Commission Annual Report 2024–2025. Pretoria.
s:
The Presidential Climate Commission (PCC) Annual Report 2024–2025 reviews the PCC’s transition into a statutory body and its work to steer South Africa towards a just, low carbon, climate resilient economy. 

The report outlines institutional strengthening, governance changes and a streamlined secretariat. It also sets out the PCC’s research and advisory work on mitigation, adaptation, finance and skills.

It highlights progress on national climate legislation, monitoring and evaluation systems, and provincial studies that inform local just transition planning. 

The PCC reports on efforts to mobilise climate finance, design a Just Transition Financing Mechanism and build municipal and regional project pipelines, with particular attention to Mpumalanga and coal-affected communities.

Skills development and social protection are central to securing livelihoods and enabling green industrialisation. 

The report stresses inclusive stakeholder engagement to build consensus and calls for accelerated deployment of finance capacity building and targeted skilling to ensure transition benefits are widely shared and so that implementation can be scaled up.

t: Reducing Inequalities Through Just Energy Transitions: From Equality Neutral to Equality Positive. Maximising the Distributional Effects of the South Africa Just Energy Transition Partnership
c: van Veldhuizen, M. and Ochs, A. (2024) Reducing Inequalities Through Just Energy Transitions: From Equality Neutral to Equality Positive. Maximising the Distributional Effects of the South Africa Just Energy Transition Partnership. Berlin.
s:
South Africa’s energy transition offers a strategic opportunity to reduce entrenched inequality if policies are designed to be equality positive rather than merely neutral.

 The country is still coal dependent and faces unequal exposure to pollution and unreliable energy access, which deepen poverty and constrain livelihoods. 

The transition will eliminate many coal and related manufacturing jobs while creating hundreds of thousands of roles across renewables, retrofitting and energy efficiency, so targeted reskilling and place based economic development are essential. 

The study evaluates instruments such as carbon pricing, revenue recycling, progressive tariffs and support for small scale renewables for their distributive effects and recommends design choices that protect vulnerable households while maximising local benefits. 

It emphasises skills interventions that combine technical training with soft skills micro credentials and enterprise support, and calls for stronger localisation, mine rehabilitation and community participation in project design. 

The authors propose quantitative and qualitative indicators to assess equality positive outcomes and identify priority areas for development cooperation to ensure the Just Energy Transition delivers inclusive growth and durable livelihoods.

t: Skills for the green transformation Toolkit
c: GIZ, n.d. Skills for the green transformation Toolkit. Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH.
s:
This Toolkit presents eight practical approaches to align vocational, higher and continuing education for a just energy transition. It is an interactive PDF that allows users to navigate content by topic and links to additional resources.

It guides policymakers, institutions and trainers through demand led curriculum design, industry partnerships, living labs and green campus initiatives to build technical, transversal and transformative green skills. 

The toolkit emphasises labour market mapping, modular learning pathways and inclusive strategies to support women, youth and marginalised groups while reducing displacement from shifting job profiles. 

It outlines processes for curriculum co creation, employer engagement and financing models that combine public support with employer co investment to scale training. 

It includes project examples, competency frameworks, trainer guides and monitoring indicators to measure employment outcomes and equity. 

The toolkit is designed for use alongside a digital dashboard that maps relevant projects and resources to help stakeholders implement context specific programmes and accelerate local capacity building for green jobs.

t: Feasibility Study: Skills for a Green and Just Energy Transition
c: PLANCO INTEGRATION RENAC JG AFRIKA Consortium, 2025. Feasibility Study: Skills for a Green and Just Energy Transition. Main report. Hamburg: PLANCO INTEGRATION RENAC JG AFRIKA Consortium on behalf of SARETEC.
s:
This feasibility study assesses how seven South African TVET colleges can support a skills response to a green and just energy transition. 

It evaluates college readiness using criteria for employment relevance, financial sustainability, staff competence and organisational setup, through site visits, interviews and facility inspections. 

Most colleges had equipment for a merSETA solar PV pilot but had not started practical training, so only West Coast College provided meaningful pilot experience. 

The report finds weak industry engagement limited practical training and low graduate employment outcomes, and it highlights procurement delays, trainer shortages and ICT platform problems that hinder rollout. 

Management systems are generally functional but show limited strategic orientation towards renewable energy opportunities. 

The study recommends targeted investments in practical facilities and trainer capacity, stronger employer partnerships, improved procurement and monitoring systems, and low threshold measures to raise awareness and use of renewable technologies on campuses. 

These measures aim to scale demand led training, improve graduate employability and ensure TVET institutions can deliver inclusive upskilling for the transition.

t: Skills4JET Feasibility Study: TVET Annexes
c: SARETEC and KfW (2024) Skills4JET Feasibility Study: TVET Annexes. South African Renewable Energy Technology Centre.
s: The annexure sets out a structured evaluation template that scores colleges on employment relevance, gender inclusion, practical training capacity, industry cooperation, follow up and tracer studies, material availability and financial sustainability. It includes, as appropriate, the raw data.

t: South Africa’s Just Energy Transition Investment Plan (JET IP) 2023–2027: at a glance
c: The Presidency, Republic of South Africa. 2023. South Africa’s Just Energy Transition Investment Plan (JET IP) 2023–2027: at a glance. Pretoria: The Presidency.
s:
This is a summary of South Africa’s Just Energy Transition Investment Plan (JET IP) 2023–2027, a five year, practical programme to decarbonise the economy while protecting workers and communities and building new industrial opportunities. 

It identifies three priority sectors — electricity, new energy vehicles and green hydrogen — and two cross cutting areas, skills development and municipal capacity. 

Initial financing needs are in the region of ZAR 1.48 trillion for 2023–2027; concessional and private finance to catalyse larger investments and support affected regions will be mobilised.

Implementation will use national institutions, Treasury managed sovereign agreements and intermediary development banks to channel funds, and it emphasises governance, monitoring and social safeguards to ensure a just transition and local economic diversification. 

The JET IP invites international partners and private investors to co finance grid upgrades, renewable generation, municipal modernisation and targeted skills hubs and pilot skills zones to prepare the workforce for green industries.

The JET IP requires initial funding of around ZAR 1.5 trillion over five years 2023-2027. 

The International Partners Group undertook to mobilise US$8.5 billion over five years to support South Africa's just energy transition.

t: South Africa’s Just Energy Transition Investment Plan (JET IP) 2023–2027
c: The Presidency, Republic of South Africa (2023) South Africa’s Just Energy Transition Investment Plan (JET IP) 2023–2027. Pretoria: The Presidency.
s:
South Africa’s Just Energy Transition Investment Plan (JET IP) sets out priority investments for 2023–2027 that are designed to shift the economy towards low carbon, climate resilient growth and at the same time protect workers and communities. 

The plan targets the electricity, new energy vehicle and green hydrogen sectors and includes cross-cutting support for skills development and municipal capacity. 

It estimates an initial funding need of about ZAR 1.48 trillion over five years and identifies catalytic roles for concessional finance to leverage private investment. 

The International Partners Group (IPG) offered an initial US$8.5 billion to catalyse grid upgrades, renewable generation and community support, with most funds directed to electricity infrastructure. 

The JET IP emphasises strong governance, phased implementation, and targeted skills interventions such as a national skills hub and pilot Skills Development Zones to reskill workers and prepare youth for green jobs. 

If it is funded and delivered at scale, the plan should help South Africa meet its Paris Agreement climate pledge and strengthen its 2030 Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC), while supporting industrialisation and inclusive economic growth.

t: Terms of Reference: TVET and labour market support for the Just Transition in South Africa
c: GIZ (2024) Terms of Reference: TVET and labour market support for the Just Transition in South Africa. Bonn: GIZ.
s:
These GIZ Terms of Reference (ToR)set out a comprehensive programme for strengthening TVET and labour market systems for South Africa’s just transition. 


The document frames a multi year CPD4E project that aims to improve youth employment in low carbon sectors by aligning curricula with industry demand, scaling training for new energy vehicles and green hydrogen, and supporting SMME development in affected regions. 

The ToR specify measurable outputs and targets including training of trainers, pilot projects in Skills Development Zones, gender and disability inclusion, and labour market intelligence products. 

They detail work packages for curriculum development, demand studies, capacity building, and SARETEC support alongside governance, data protection and costing requirements. 

They emphasises coordination with the Department of Higher Education and Training (DHET), sector education and training authorities (SETAs), the Quality Council on Trades and Occupations (QCTO) and local partners to ensure accreditation and workplace relevance. 

The approach combines national oversight with regional pilots and private sector engagement to create pathways from learning to earning while protecting vulnerable workers and communities. 

Clear milestones and monitoring arrangements aim to translate investment into scalable training models and local job creation that support a fair green economy.

t: Joint statement from the International Partners Group on the US withdrawal from the Just Energy Transition Partnership in South Africa
c: Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (2025) Joint statement from the International Partners Group on the US withdrawal from the Just Energy Transition Partnership in South Africa. London: FCDO.
s:
South Africa’s International Partners Group (IPG ) issued a joint statement after the United States withdrew from the Just Energy Transition Partnership. 

They explain that the IPG remains committed to supporting South Africa’s shift away from coal and to accelerating low emission, climate resilient development. 

It notes that substantial IPG funding has already been disbursed and that total international pledges have grown beyond the original commitment, with partners exploring ways to cover activities previously supported by the US. 

The statement emphasises continued collaboration with the South African government to allocate existing funds towards grid upgrades renewable generation municipal capacity building and social support for affected communities. 

It frames the partnership as resilient despite the withdrawal and signals ongoing political technical and financial backing from remaining IPG members and other development partners. 

The IPG’s collective effort is central to delivering a just transition that protects workers and promotes inclusive economic opportunities while mobilising concessional finance and private investment for catalytic infrastructure and skills interventions.

t: Sector Skills Plan 2025–2030
c: W&RSETA (2024) Sector Skills Plan 2025–2030. Wholesale and Retail Sector Education and Training Authority.
s:
W&RSETA’s Sector Skills Plan 2025–2030 sets a strategic roadmap to align wholesale and retail skills provision with evolving labour market needs and national development priorities. 

The plan combines quantitative and qualitative research to map sector profiles identify hard to fill vacancies and emerging occupations and assess skills supply and demand. 

It prioritises digital literacy data analytics sustainable supply chain management and circular economy competencies while emphasising youth employment SMME support and inclusion of people with disabilities. 

The SSP outlines targeted interventions including tracer studies graduate placement evaluations and pilot projects in skills development zones to strengthen pathways from learning to earning. 

It proposes partnerships with TVET colleges universities industry and government to develop PIVOTAL programmes and accredited curricula and to scale training for priority occupations. 

Monitoring and evaluation frameworks and M&E data are central to the plan to ensure accountability and iterative improvement.

t: South African Renewable Energy Masterplan (SAREM): Draft for public consultation
c: Department of Mineral Resources and Energy et al., 2023. South African Renewable Energy Masterplan (SAREM): Draft for public consultation, Pretoria: DMRE.
s:
The draft South African Renewable Energy Masterplan (SAREM) is a consultative document that sets out a practical, action-oriented pathway to industrialise renewable energy and storage value chains by 2030, to both expand access and support a just transition.

It prioritises four pillars: securing sustained demand and system readiness; driving localisation and industrial policy to grow manufacturing and services; promoting inclusive development through transformation, supplier support and targeted procurement in just transition hotspots; and building skills and technology commercialisation capacity. 

The plan recommends catalytic interventions such as quarterly public and private procurement pipelines, reactivation of the 12i tax incentive, a Transformation Fund for new entrants, targeted procurement for Mpumalanga and designated renewable energy development zones (REDZs)

It also proposes a digital skills match making platform called PowerUp to link education providers with industry. 

SAREM emphasises measurable targets, coordinated trade and industrial measures, and strengthened incubation and certification facilities to attract investment and create decent jobs across the value chain.

The SAREM articulates a vision, objectives and an action plan for South Africa to tap into these opportunities. 

It aims to leverage the rising demand for renewable energy and storage technologies, with a focus on solar energy, wind energy, lithium ion battery and vanadium based battery technologies, to unlock the industrial and inclusive development of associated value chains in the country.

t: The reconceptualised Human Resource Development Strategy of South Africa 2024–2033
c: Human Resources Development Council, 2024. The reconceptualised Human Resource Development Strategy of South Africa 2024–2033, Pretoria: HRDC.
s:
The reconceptualised Human Resource Development Strategy of South Africa (HRDS SA) 2024–2033 sets a focused, long term framework to align education training and skills with national development goals and the Just Energy Transition. 

It focuses on four priority areas with the greatest potential impact. These are improving early learning and school outcomes, boosting youth employability and reducing NEET rates by strengthening the post-school skills pipeline through TVET and higher education, and coordinating a Master Skills Plan that links industry master plans to demand-led training.

The strategy emphasises collective accountability across government industry labour and civil society.

It commits to measurable five year implementation milestones for improving work readiness and addressing sectoral skills shortages, including those arising from the transition to low carbon energy systems. 

The strategy emphasises the need for targeted interventions in foundational literacy numeracy and science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM), expanded ECD practitioner training, and clearer pathways from education to green jobs to ensure that South Africa sees the benefits for of the energy transition for employment and industry.

The HRDS-SA identifies the challenges South Africa must address over the next five years to strengthen human resource development. It aims to ensure the country has the people and skills that civil society and the economy need, and to reduce mismatches between skills supply and demand.

The HRDS SA is an anchor for good practice and a pledge of political and collective will and commitment.

t: Master Skills Plan of South Africa (2024 – 2030)
c: Department of Higher Education and Training, 2024. Master Skills Plan of South Africa (2024 – 2030) March 2024, Pretoria: DHET.
s:
The Master Skills Plan (MSP) 2024–2030 sets a concise, action focused framework for aligning South Africa’s education and training system with national development goals. 

TMSP is the implementation vehicle for the Human Resource Development Strategy of South Africa and seeks to reduce fragmentation by clarifying institutional roles, improving coordination and prioritising high impact interventions. 

The MSP stresses early childhood development and schooling as foundational to long term human capital and adopts a Pareto approach to concentrate effort on a limited set of interventions that deliver the greatest benefit. 

The MSP is central for coordination and decentralised for implementation so that national, provincial and local stakeholders integrate its priorities into budgets and plans. 

It calls for demand led skills planning, stronger workplace learning, and targeted support for TVET and STEM pathways to address persistent skills shortages and high youth unemployment. 

The plan emphasises measurable milestones, improved monitoring and evaluation, and collective ownership by government, industry and civil society to ensure the country captures the employment and industrial opportunities of a just energy transition.

t: CPD4E: Interventions with TVET Colleges, July 2024
c: GIZ South Africa (2024) CPD4E: Interventions with TVET Colleges, July 2024.
s:
The CPD4E programme strengthens TVET capacity and supports demand side enterprise development to improve youth employment in a decarbonising economy. 

It includes lecturer and practitioner training in renewable energy technologies and mentoring, as well as the development of short skills programmes and new occupational profiles.  It incorporates the work placements and internships for graduates in SMEs. 

It supports SMME incubation through IRM hubs, business mentoring and green economy toolkits to scale local enterprises and create jobs and improve employment prospects of young South Africans in a decarbonised economy. 

The CPD4E programme promotes a just transition and inclusive employment creation by supporting the supply and demand side to understand and address the emerging opportunities for enterprise and skills development. 

Activities include EPC and energy efficiency training, gender focused lecturer development, certificate of compliance training, and targeted reskilling for workers at risk of job loss, all coordinated with national partners to align training with labour market needs.

t: Overview: South African H2 Projects
c: GIZ H2.SA (2024) Overview: South African H2 Projects. January 2024.
s:
The presentation Overview: South African H2 Projects maps the South Africa’s hydrogen that have been announced, and summarises their characteristics and development stages. 

Nine Strategic Integrated Projects (SIPs) have been gazetted, including Prieska Power Reserve, Upilanga Solar and GH2 Park, Boegoebaai and Hive Hydrogen, which have capacities ranging from single digit kilotonnes to multi GW scale and focuses on ammonia, methanol, sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and domestic hydrogen. 

It also lists numerous non SIP initiatives such as Enertrag Postmasburg, Saldanha Bay GH projects and IPM refuelling stations, and maps production, technology and manufacturing sites nationwide. 

The presentation outlines project development steps from opportunity assessment and feasibility through front end engineering, permitting as well as engineering, procurement and construction management (EPCM) to commissioning and operations

Technical and regulatory considerations including power supply options, water sourcing, environmental assessments and compliance with codes are also included. 

The presentation also sets out advanced production projects and site level capacities to support planning and investment decisions.

t: Wind energy and green hydrogen production: a sustainable vision for the province of Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada
