c: Pourvaziri Z, Sabau G L & Haghiri M (2026), Wind energy and green hydrogen production: a sustainable vision for the province of Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada, Academia Green Energy, vol. 3.
s:
The article examines how Newfoundland and Labrador can use its strong wind resources to support a sustainable energy transition through green hydrogen production. 

It argues that wind powered electrolysis offers a practical pathway to reduce emissions, strengthen energy security and diversify the province’s energy mix. 

The study uses a narrative literature review to assess technological, social and economic factors shaping this transition. 

It notes the role of new knowledge, including advances in electrolysis, catalysts, artificial intelligence and supply chain optimisation. 

It also stresses the importance of values, policies and financial strategies that guide investment, public acceptance and long term planning. 

From a practical perspective, the article notes that material conditions such as geography, renewable resource availability and infrastructure readiness determine what is achievable. 

It concludes that Newfoundland and Labrador has significant potential to develop a competitive green hydrogen sector, but that success depends on coordinated policy, investment, community engagement and the ability to integrate wind energy with emerging hydrogen technologies.

t: How can the transition to a low carbon economy and society be made more just in South Africa?
c: Machaieie J (2026) How can the transition to a low carbon economy and society be made more just in South Africa?, Dublin City University.
s:
The paper examines how South Africa can pursue a low carbon transition in a way that protects workers and communities dependent on coal. 

It traces the origins of the just transition concept, noting its roots in trade union efforts to secure support for workers affected by environmental regulation. 

The author argues that a just transition in South Africa must prioritise employment creation for coal miners and broader community development. 

The paper outlines the structure of the national energy sector, highlighting the dominance of coal and the slow but growing contribution of renewable energy initiatives such as the Renewable Energy Independent Power Producer Procurement Programme (REIPPPP) and the Green Economy Accord. 

It compares South Africa’s situation with Germany and Poland, showing how labour market dynamics, governance and funding shape transition outcomes. 

The analysis concludes that South Africa faces significant challenges due to structural unemployment, high dependence on coal and limited economic diversification. 

A just transition will require social dialogue, targeted support for workers, investment in new industries and differentiated regional strategies that address local needs.

t: Exploring the unique contribution of green hydrogen and Power to X in South Africa’s Just Transition: Workshop Report
c: GIZ 2022, Exploring the unique contribution of green hydrogen and Power to X in South Africa’s Just Transition: Workshop Report, Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit, Pretoria.
s:
The report outlines workshop discussions about how green hydrogen and Power to X technologies can support South Africa’s just transition. 

Participants from research institutions, civil society and government reviewed ongoing initiatives at the intersection of hydrogen and justice, noting the wide range of activities already underway. 

The workshop noted South Africa’s strong potential to develop a green hydrogen economy and the need to understand how this emerging sector can contribute to social and economic priorities. 

Stocktaking revealed projects linked to decarbonisation, skills development, industrial transformation and community engagement. 

Participants identified gaps such as limited community capacity, unclear land use models, environmental concerns, coordination challenges and the need for stronger information sharing. 

They proposed interventions including value chain analysis, training, policy alignment, environmental assessment and demonstration projects. 

The report concludes that regular exchanges are needed to strengthen collaboration and ensure hydrogen related activities support a fair transition for workers and communities. 

It also notes that GIZ will assess which proposed actions align with its programme objectives and explore opportunities for future implementation.

t: H2 and PtX for a Just Transition: Exploratory Consultation and Design Workshop
c: GIZ (2022) H2 and PtX for a Just Transition: Exploratory Consultation and Design Workshop, Pretoria, 4 August.
s:
A consultative workshop brought together government, research institutes and civil society to align activities on the just energy transition with emerging opportunities in green hydrogen and Power to X. 

Organisations reported work on coal region diversification, skills development, social impact assessment and environmental safeguards. 

Several highlighted the need to link technical modelling with labour market planning, particularly through the TVET ecosystem. 

Green hydrogen was framed as a potential driver of new industrial value chains, requiring coordinated policy, investment and skills strategies. GIZ’s portfolio supports this through technical studies, capacity building, stakeholder dialogue and pilot projects. 

Crosscutting priorities included community inclusion, gender considerations, mine rehabilitation and local economic development. 

The workshop identified gaps in governance, skills anticipation and financing mechanisms, reinforcing the need for integrated planning across institutions to ensure that hydrogen related growth contributes to a fair and inclusive transition.

t: South Africa’s Hydrogen Strategy
c: Salma, T and Tsafos, N (2022) South Africa’s Hydrogen Strategy, Center for Strategic and International Studies, 4 April.
s:
South Africa’s hydrogen strategy positions green hydrogen as a driver of economic growth, industrial renewal and a just transition away from coal. 

The Hydrogen Society Roadmap sets targets for large scale electrolysis capacity and annual hydrogen production by 2030, supported by catalytic projects such as the Platinum Valley, COALCO₂ X, sustainable aviation fuels and the Boegoebaai export hub. 

These initiatives aim to stimulate domestic demand, build integrated value chains and leverage the country’s strengths in platinum group metals, Fischer Tropsch expertise and renewable resources. 

The strategy also relies on foreign investment, concessional finance and international partnerships to accelerate development. 

Hydrogen hubs in Durban, Johannesburg and Limpopo are expected to anchor early deployment, supported by existing infrastructure and potential off takers. 

The strategy links decarbonisation with employment creation and regional development, positioning hydrogen as a pathway to reduce emissions while expanding industrial capabilities and supporting a fair transition for affected workers and communities.

t: Renewable energy sources: Jobs created, skills required and identified gaps, education and training
c: Malamatenios, C (2016) Renewable energy sources: Jobs created, skills required and identified gaps, education and training, Renewable Energy and Environmental Sustainability, 1, 23.
s:
The article analyses how renewable energy deployment generates employment and the skills required to support sector growth. 

It shows that renewables create more jobs per unit of installed capacity than fossil fuel technologies, with solar PV, wind and biomass offering the highest labour intensity across different stages of the value chain. 

Using Greece as a case study, the article quantifies direct and indirect jobs per megawatt and illustrates how policy uncertainty can sharply reduce employment. 

It identifies four main sub sectors in the renewable energy industry, viz., equipment manufacturing, project development, construction and installation, and operations and maintenance.  Each requires a wide range of technical and professional occupations. 

Persistent shortages of engineers, technicians and specialised trainers are highlighted, alongside gaps in non technical roles such as legal advisors and inspectors. 

The article stresses that education and training systems often struggle to respond to rapid changes in labour demand. 

It argues for coordinated skills strategies, stronger social dialogue and updated curricula to ensure that training provision aligns with industry needs and supports workforce mobility.

t: The hydrogen economy and jobs of the future
c: Bezdek, R H (2019) The hydrogen economy and jobs of the future, Renewable Energy and Environmental Sustainability, 4, 1.
s:
The article examines how the growth of the hydrogen and fuel cell industries is likely to generate substantial new employment across a wide range of occupations. 

It outlines the current state of the hydrogen economy, noting rapid market expansion driven by industrial demand, regulatory pressures and interest in clean energy applications. 

Despite this growth, the paper highlights a major constraint: most hydrogen is still produced from fossil fuels, limiting its environmental benefits and slowing progress toward a fully sustainable hydrogen economy. 

The study identifies emerging job categories across technical, managerial and professional roles, many of which do not yet exist in formal occupational classifications. 

It provides indicative salary levels and minimum education requirements, showing that opportunities range from technicians with on the job training to engineers and specialists with advanced degrees. 

The article argues that education and training systems must adapt quickly to meet evolving skills needs and that communities can position themselves to attract hydrogen related industries. 

It concludes by identifying research gaps, particularly in forecasting job numbers, defining new occupations and aligning curricula with future workforce demands.

t: Unlocking South Africa’s Hydrogen Potential
c: Strategy& and PwC 2020, Unlocking South Africa’s Hydrogen Potential, PwC, Johannesburg.
s:
The PwC Unlocking South Africa’s Hydrogen Potential report argues that hydrogen is central to achieving global decarbonisation because it can store renewable energy, decarbonise hard to electrify sectors, and provide industrial heat and feedstock. 

It explains why grey and blue hydrogen fall short and presents green hydrogen, produced through renewable-powered electrolysis, as the long-term solution as costs drop and electrolyser technology matures.

The report details hydrogen’s applications across transport, rail, shipping, aviation, buildings, power systems, and heavy industry, emphasising its role in grid buffering, long duration storage, synthetic fuels, and industrial decarbonisation. 

It notes global pilots in fuel cell vehicles, hydrogen trains, ammonia fuelled ships, and synthetic aviation fuels.

For South Africa, the report identifies major opportunities in green hydrogen production, export, industrial decarbonisation, fuel cell manufacturing, Fuel Cell Electric Vehicle (FCEV) uptake, and new hydrogen enabled industries. South Africa’s renewable resources, rich platinum group metal (PGM) resources, existing industrial capabilities, and port infrastructure position it to become a competitive producer and exporter. 

The report stresses the need for a national hydrogen strategy, coordinated policy, investment incentives, carbon pricing clarity, and large scale infrastructure to unlock economic and employment benefits.

t: South Africa’s massive hydrogen valley project is a step closer – here’s what you need to know
c: BusinessTech (2021) South Africa’s massive hydrogen valley project is a step closer – here’s what you need to know, 12 October.
s:
This BusinessTech article reports on progress toward establishing South Africa’s first hydrogen valley, following the release of the Hydrogen Valley Feasibility Study by the Department of Science and Innovation and its partners. 

The initiative aims to create an integrated hydrogen ecosystem stretching from Mokopane in Limpopo, through Johannesburg, to Durban. 

The valley is positioned as a catalyst for industrial revitalisation, green technology deployment and export oriented hydrogen production. It aligns with the National Hydrogen Society Roadmap and the Economic Reconstruction and Recovery Plan. 

Anglo American, Bambili Energy and ENGIE highlight the valley’s potential to stimulate new industries, support PGM beneficiation and accelerate commercialisation of hydrogen technologies. 

The feasibility study identifies nine initial projects across mobility, industry and construction, including the conversion of heavy duty trucks to fuel cell systems. 

Stakeholders emphasise the role of public private partnerships, the importance of green hydrogen in reducing dependence on fossil fuels and the opportunity for South Africa to participate competitively in global hydrogen markets. 

The initiative is also linked to national policies on climate response and mineral beneficiation.

t: South Africa Hydrogen Valley Final Report
c: Department of Science and Innovation (2021) South Africa Hydrogen Valley Final Report, Pretoria.
s:
The South Africa Hydrogen Valley Final Report outlines a coordinated plan to establish three catalytic green hydrogen hubs in Johannesburg, Durban/Richards Bay and Mogalakwena/Limpopo. 

These hubs were selected for their strong potential hydrogen demand, renewable energy resources and alignment with South Africa’s just transition objectives. 

The study estimates that hydrogen demand across the valley could reach up to 185 kilotonnes by 2030, driven by industrial feedstock substitution, heavy duty mobility, mining applications and public buildings. 

Green hydrogen production costs are expected to fall to around USD 4 per kilogram by 2030, although still above those for grey hydrogen, with transport adding further cost. 

The report highlights significant socioeconomic benefits, projecting USD 3.9 to 8.8 billion in GDP contributions and 14,000 to 30,000 jobs per year by 2050 across the hydrogen value chain. 

It identifies regulatory gaps and recommends enabling policies to accelerate renewable deployment, reduce capital costs, stimulate demand and establish safety and technical standards. Nine pilot projects across mobility, industry and buildings are proposed to initiate the hydrogen economy and build local capability.

t: New project to create 30,000 jobs a year in South Africa
c: BusinessTech (2022) New project to create 30,000 jobs a year in South Africa, 3 June.
s:
This BusinessTech article reports on government’s progress towards establishing South Africa’s Hydrogen Valley Corridor, a national initiative expected to stimulate large scale job creation and industrial development. 

The Department of Higher Education, Science and Innovation confirms that nine catalytic hydrogen projects have been identified across mobility, industry and buildings, with an estimated implementation cost of USD 1.2 billion. 

The corridor will link Mogalakwena, Johannesburg and Durban, forming an integrated hydrogen ecosystem that supports green hydrogen production, platinum group metal (PGM) beneficiation and the deployment of fuel cell technologies. 

The feasibility study suggests that by 2030 the hydrogen valley could create between 14,000 and 30,000 direct and indirect jobs per year, increasing as the industry matures. 

Job opportunities span the entire hydrogen value chain, including water resource management, platinum mining, electrolyser manufacturing, pipeline and trucking logistics, storageas well as fuel cell system production. 

The article also highlights the investment required to scale green hydrogen, noting that South Africa may need USD 14 billion to build a competitive export oriented industry. 

The initiative aligns with national decarbonisation goals and the broader shift toward renewable energy and electric mobility.

t: Minimum of 14 000 jobs a year from South Africa’s first hydrogen corridor
c: Creamer, M. 2022. Minimum of 14 000 jobs a year from South Africa’s first hydrogen corridor. Mining Weekly, 11 May.
s:
The article outlines the economic and industrial potential of South Africa’s first hydrogen corridor, projected to generate at least 14 000 jobs a year, contribute about $4 billion to GDP and deliver $900 million in annual tax revenue by 2050. 

It highlights South Africa’s comparative advantages for green hydrogen production, including high solar radiation, established platinum group metal reserves.  

These are essential for electrolysers and fuel cells, and long-standing industrial expertise through Sasol’s Fischer-Tropsch processes. 

The Minerals Council and Anglo American emphasise hydrogen’s role in decarbonising heavy-duty transport and mining, demonstrated through Anglo’s hydrogen-powered haul truck prototype and plans to scale the technology across multiple opencast mines. 

The hydrogen valley concept, spanning Limpopo, Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal, is presented as a replicable model that clusters hydrogen production and end-use to reduce costs and build a sustainable ecosystem. 

The article stresses the need for policy support, investment in renewable energy and collaboration with original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) to accelerate commercial deployment. 

It positions green hydrogen as a long-term driver of industrial growth, PGM demand and the just energy transition.

t: South-Africa-UK PACT Green Hydrogen Economy Project: Synthesis Report
c: South African Institute of International Affairs (2022) South-Africa-UK PACT Green Hydrogen Economy Project: Synthesis Report, SAIIA.
s:
The SAIIA South Africa–UK PACT Green Hydrogen Economy Project focuses on preparing the country’s workforce for emerging opportunities in the green hydrogen sector as part of a Just Energy Transition. 

The project aims to strengthen job absorption by aligning government, industry and the TVET college system to produce skills that match real labour market demand. 

It highlights the potential for significant employment growth across the renewable energy and hydrogen value chains, while recognising the need to mitigate job losses in coal dependent regions through structured reskilling and labour mobility pathways. 

The initiative adopts a Just Labour Transition lens, emphasising equitable access to training, improved curriculum relevance and stronger partnerships between training institutions and employers. 

It also seeks to provide policy recommendations on labour planning, skills development, institutional coordination and industry readiness. 

By improving the responsiveness of the TVET system and building a realistic jobs pipeline, the project aims to ensure that South Africa can develop a capable workforce to support hydrogen production, infrastructure development and associated technologies.

t: Launch of Hydrogen Society Roadmap
c: South African Government (2022) Minister Blade Nzimande: Launch of Hydrogen Society Roadmap, 17 February.
s:
Press release from the Department of Higher Education and Training in which the Minister announces the formal launch of South Africa’s Hydrogen Society Roadmap (HSRM)

The roadmap positions hydrogen as a central pillar of economic recovery, industrial revitalisation and long term decarbonisation. 

The Minister emphasises that the roadmap builds on more than a decade of investment through the Hydrogen South Africa (HySA) Programme, which has developed national research capacity, technology platforms and human capital. 

The HSRM aims to support inclusive growth by creating new industries, reducing unemployment and strengthening South Africa’s competitiveness in global green hydrogen markets. 

Key opportunities include leveraging the country’s platinum group metal reserves, renewable energy potential and Fischer Tropsch expertise to expand green hydrogen production and associated manufacturing. 

The roadmap identifies catalytic projects such as the Platinum Valley Corridor, hydrogen powered data centres, and the CoalCO₂ X programme to support industrial decarbonisation. 

It outlines five priority outcomes: export market development, green power and buildings, decarbonised heavy duty transport, decarbonised energy intensive industry and local manufacturing of hydrogen technologies. 

Implementation will be supported by a monitoring and evaluation framework, cross government coordination and partnerships with industry, academia and international organisations.

t: EWSETA Poised to Play Important Role in SA's Hydrogen Roadmap
c: EWSETA (2022) EWSETA poised to play important role in South Africa’s hydrogen roadmap.
s:
The May newsletter outlines the growing importance of hydrogen and fuel cell technologies in South Africa’s energy transition and highlights the central role of the Energy and Water Sector Education and Training Authority (EWSETA) in developing the skills required for a future hydrogen economy. 

It explains that South Africa’s strong renewable energy potential, extensive platinum group metal reserves and existing research capacity position the country to benefit from global hydrogen market growth. 

The EWSETA emphasises the contributions of the Hydrogen South Africa (HySA) Programme, industry partners and universities in advancing research, technology development and early skills pipelines. 

It describes several collaborative initiatives, including training programmes for unemployed graduates, educational outreach in schools and prototype development for hydrogen powered mining equipment. 

The EWSETA stresses that skills shortages could constrain hydrogen sector growth, drawing lessons from Brazil’s stalled fuel cell development. 

The SETA is working with Bambili Energy and other partners to establish accredited hydrogen related qualifications and ensure that TVET colleges and universities can supply the technical skills needed for hydrogen production, fuel cell systems and associated industries.

t: South Africa’s Automotive Industry Master Plan to 2035
c: Department of Trade, Industry and Competition (the dtic) 2018, South Africa’s Automotive Industry Master Plan to 2035, Pretoria.
s:
The South African Automotive Industry Master Plan to 2035 sets out a long-term strategy to expand and transform the automotive sector as a central pillar of national industrialisation. 

The report outlines the global and domestic context, noting the sector’s strong export performance, deep integration into global value chains, and its role as the country’s most significant manufacturing industry. 

Despite these strengths, the sector faces structural challenges including low domestic market growth, high import penetration, limited local content, and global technological shifts. 

The Master Plan proposes an aspirational but achievable vision built around increasing production volumes, raising local content, improving competitiveness, doubling employment, deepening value addition, and accelerating transformation. 

It emphasises coordinated public and private action, supported by targeted incentives, skills development, infrastructure investment, and regional market expansion. 

The plan is structured around six pillars: local market optimisation, regional market development, localisation, infrastructure development, transformation, and technology and skills. 

It positions the automotive industry as a driver of inclusive growth, export expansion, and industrial capability development through to 2035.

t: APDP and the South African Automotive Masterplan summary
c: NAACAM (2019) APDP and the South African Automotive Masterplan summary.
s:
This summary document outlines the relationship between the Automotive Production and Development Programme (APDP) and the South African Automotive Masterplan (SAAM) 2035. 

It explains that the APDP, which replaced the MIDP in 2013, remains the central industrial policy instrument supporting automotive manufacturing, with targeted amendments introduced for the 2021–2035 period. 

The SAAM 2035 provides the long term strategic vision for a globally competitive automotive industry that contributes to sustainable economic development. 

Its objectives include achieving 1% of global vehicle production, increasing local content to 60%, doubling employment, improving competitiveness, deepening value addition and driving transformation. 

The Masterplan is structured around seven pillars: local market optimisation, regional market development, localisation, infrastructure development, industry transformation, technology and skills development and an enabling institutional environment. 

The APDP amendments align with these objectives by shifting incentives toward local value addition, replacing the Volume Assembly Allowance with the Volume Assembly Localisation Allowance, adjusting production incentives and refining investment support through the Automotive Investment Scheme. 

These policy changes are refinements rather than fundamental redesigns, aimed at correcting distortions and strengthening the sector’s long term growth trajectory.

t: Amended Automotive Production and Development Programme Phase 2 (APDP2) Regulations
c: International Trade Administration Commission of South Africa (2022) Amended Automotive Production and Development Programme Phase 2 (APDP2) Regulations, Pretoria.
s:
The Amended Automotive Production and Development Programme Phase 2 (APDP2), effective from July 2022, sets out the regulatory framework governing incentives, localisation and industrial development within South Africa’s light vehicle manufacturing sector. 

The regulations align with the South African Automotive Masterplan vision of creating a globally competitive and transformed industry that contributes to sustainable economic growth. 

APDP2 formalises the structure of rebates, refunds and duty credit mechanisms designed to support local production, deepen value addition and enhance competitiveness. 

Key elements include Production Rebate Certificates (PRCs), calculated from local value addition; the Company Specific Percentage (CSP) which is used to determine the Volume Assembly Localisation Allowance (VALA) as well as strict eligibility criteria for vehicles, components and tooling. 

The regulations introduce rules for declaring imported content, managing transitional arrangements from APDP1 and addressing exceptional circumstances such as national disasters. 

Participation is voluntary and requires compliance with B BBEE, SARS registration and full data submission for monitoring. 

APDP2 strengthens localisation incentives, standardises treatment across the value chain and reinforces the policy shift toward value added manufacturing rather than import offset mechanisms.

t: Hydrogen Society Roadmap for South Africa
c: Department of Science and Innovation (2021) Hydrogen Society Roadmap for South Africa, Pretoria.
s:
The Hydrogen Society Roadmap for South Africa (2021) sets out a national framework for developing a competitive, inclusive and sustainable hydrogen economy that is aligned with the country’s decarbonisation and economic recovery goals. 

Hydrogen is a strategic enabler for reducing emissions in heavy transport, energy intensive industries and the power sector, while creating new industrial opportunities and export markets. 

The roadmap builds on South Africa’s strong renewable energy potential, extensive platinum group metal reserves, Fischer Tropsch expertise and existing Hydrogen Society (HySA) research platforms. 

It outlines global trends, domestic competitive advantages and regulatory considerations, and identifies catalytic projects such as the Hydrogen Valley, CoalCO₂ X, Boegoebaai export hub and sustainable aviation fuels. 

The roadmap proposes a theory of change supported by long term policy signals, demand creation, risk mitigation, innovation and harmonised standards. 

It emphasises human capital development, TVET system strengthening, gender equality and social inclusion, and the establishment of a monitoring, evaluation and learning framework. 

Hydrogen as a pathway to a just transition that supports economic diversification, industrial development and job creation.

t: Proposed South African Green Hydrogen Commercialisation Strategy: Summary of Panel Report
c: Green Hydrogen Commercialisation Panel (2022) Proposed South African Green Hydrogen Commercialisation Strategy: Summary of Panel Report, Pretoria.
s:
The proposed South African Green Hydrogen Commercialisation Strategy (GHCS) outlines a national plan to accelerate the development of a competitive green hydrogen industry that supports economic growth, export expansion and a just transition. 

Building on the Hydrogen Society Roadmap and earlier HySA investments, the strategy focuses on six core elements: prioritising export markets, stimulating domestic demand, supporting localisation, securing finance, driving socio economic development and ensuring strong policy and regulatory support. 

It identifies South Africa’s competitive advantages, including renewable energy resources, platinum group metals, Fischer Tropsch expertise and established petrochemical capabilities. 

The strategy proposes coordinated government action across the Presidency, DIRCO, DMRE, the dtic, National Treasury, DSI and DHET to create an enabling environment through regulatory reform, incentives, standards, skills development and infrastructure planning. 

It emphasises early export projects, domestic applications in hard to abate sectors, mobility pilots, manufacturing of electrolysers and fuel cells, and catalytic projects such as hydrogen valleys and sustainable aviation fuels. 

The GHCS positions green hydrogen as a driver of industrialisation, investment attraction, job creation and inclusive development.

t: A quality infrastructure roadmap for green hydrogen
c: IRENA (2024) A quality infrastructure roadmap for green hydrogen. International Renewable Energy Agency, Abu Dhabi.
s:
The IRENA report outlines how a robust quality infrastructure system is essential for scaling a global green hydrogen economy. 

It argues that rapid decarbonisation requires hydrogen and its derivatives for hard to abate sectors, with demand expected to rise sharply by 2050.

The roadmap defines quality infrastructure as the combination of institutions, standards, metrology, testing, certification, accreditation and regulation that ensures safety, reliability and sustainability across the hydrogen value chain. 

It stresses that many countries lack the specialised services required for hydrogen production, transport and trade, particularly for verifying carbon intensity and compliance with emerging international standards. 

To address this, the IRENA proposes a five step roadmap: assessing national hydrogen potential, developing a hydrogen strategy, evaluating existing quality infrastructure, identifying service gaps and creating an action plan. 

It introduces a three level model that distinguishes between basic, medium and advanced quality infrastructure capabilities. 

The roadmap emphasise that quality infrastructure as a prerequisite for investment, international market access and safe deployment of hydrogen technologies, highlighting the need for coordinated national and international action to support emerging producer countries.

t: Green Hydrogen Technology: CPD4E Webinar
c: Pandarum, A. (2025) Green Hydrogen Technology: CPD4E Webinar. The Impact Catalyst, 9 July.
s:
The presentation outlines the global and South African context for green hydrogen as a key technology for achieving net zero emissions. 

It highlights hydrogen’s role across the value chain, from renewable energy based production to applications in transport, industry, power generation and synthetic fuels. 

Hydrogen can support deep decarbonisation in hard to abate sectors such as steel, petrochemicals and heavy transport, while also enabling large scale energy storage. 

Cost projections indicate declining production costs for green hydrogen as renewable energy and electrolyser technologies mature. 

Significant investment is needed, with electrolysers representing the largest share, and there is significant potential for job creation, particularly in renewable energy and manufacturing.

For South Africa, green hydrogen is located within existing policy frameworks including the Hydrogen Society Roadmap, the Green Hydrogen Commercialisation Strategy and the Just Energy Transition. 

It maps major catalytic projects across provinces, covering green ammonia, sustainable aviation fuels, mobility corridors and component manufacturing. 

Recent developments include international financing commitments and growing interest in export oriented projects. 

Skills development is especially necessary in renewable energy, electrolysis and fuel cell technologies, to support a competitive domestic hydrogen economy.

t: African Green Hydrogen Report 2025
c: African Green Hydrogen Alliance (2025) African Green Hydrogen Report 2025.
s:
The African Green Hydrogen Report 2025 examines the continent’s emerging position in the global green hydrogen economy and outlines the strategic, economic and technological factors shaping Africa’s potential. 

The report highlights that green hydrogen is becoming central to global decarbonisation, particularly for sectors such as steel, chemicals, heavy transport and aviation. 

Africa’s competitive advantages include abundant solar and wind resources, large tracts of available land, and growing interest from international markets looking for long term green hydrogen and derivative supply. 

The report emphasises that green hydrogen could support industrialisation, energy security and export diversification while contributing to a just transition. 

It identifies the need for coordinated policy frameworks, investment mobilisation, infrastructure development and regional cooperation to unlock large scale production. 

Skills development, research capacity and local manufacturing are highlighted as enablers for capturing value along the hydrogen value chain. 

Green hydrogen is a transformative economic opportunity for African countries, provided that development is inclusive, aligned with climate goals and supported by robust governance and financing mechanisms.

t:
African Green Hydrogen Report - Potential to Power:
Advancing Green Hydrogen Across Africa
c:
GIZ (2025) African Green Hydrogen Report - Potential to Power:
Advancing Green Hydrogen Across Africa. Eschborn: Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH.
s:
The report assesses Africa’s readiness to develop a competitive green hydrogen economy and highlights the continent’s strong renewable energy potential, growing project pipeline as well as its strategic position in global decarbonisation. 

It shows that Africa could become a major producer and exporter of green hydrogen and its derivatives, supported by abundant solar and wind resources and increasing international demand. 

Although more than 110 projects are underway, most remain in concept or feasibility stages, with only a few operational. 

Key barriers include limited infrastructure, regulatory gaps, financing constraints and uneven institutional capacity. Countries such as Egypt, Morocco, Namibia, South Africa, Kenya and Mauritania are emerging as leaders due to clearer strategies and stronger industrial bases. 

The report emphasises the need for coordinated policy frameworks, regional corridors, investment in skills and coordinated standards to ensure inclusive and sustainable growth. 

It concludes that Africa can play a central role in global energy transition if it strengthens governance, accelerates infrastructure development, and builds the technical capabilities required for large-scale deployment.

t: Update on HySA, Hydrogen Society Roadmap and next steps
c: Department of Science and Innovation (2024) Update on HySA, Hydrogen Society Roadmap and next steps.
s:
The report outlines South Africa’s progress towards developing a competitive hydrogen economy through the Hydrogen South Africa (HySA) Programme and the Hydrogen Society Roadmap (HSRM). 

It highlights the country’s strategic advantages, including strong renewable energy potential, established port infrastructure and significant platinum group metal reserves. 

Over three phases, HySA has built national R&D capability, demonstrated hydrogen technologies and advanced commercialisation, supported by substantial public and co funding. 

The programme has produced patents, prototypes, commercial products and a growing skills pipeline, including experiential TVET learning. 

The HSRM aligns national departments around decarbonising heavy industry, transport and power generation while creating export markets and manufacturing capacity. 

Catalytic projects such as Coega Green Ammonia, Sasolburg Green Hydrogen Hub, Boegoebaai SEZ and Saldanha Green Steel aim to stimulate investment and job creation. 

Governance is strengthened through an Inter Ministerial Committee and coordinated workstreams covering production, industry, transport, manufacturing and human capital. 

Immediate next steps focus on implementation planning, skills strategy development and enhanced DSTI–DTIC collaboration to support commercialisation.

t: Briefing on the Green Hydrogen Commercialisation Strategy and other green fuels
c: Department of Trade, Industry and Competition (2024) Briefing on the Green Hydrogen Commercialisation Strategy and other green fuels.
s:
The briefing outlines the dtic’s approach to positioning green hydrogen as a strategic industrial opportunity that supports South Africa’s decarbonisation commitments and long term economic competitiveness. 

Hydrogen can be produced without competing for grid electricity or freshwater, using additional renewable energy and desalinated water. 

The strategy focuses on export markets in Europe and Asia where demand for green hydrogen, ammonia and methanol is expected to rise sharply by 2050. 

Domestically, early applications include green steel, fertiliser production, mobility corridors and sustainable aviation fuel. 

South Africa has a cost advantage because of strong renewable resources and proprietary Fischer-Tropsch capability. 

Local manufacturing capacity for electrolysers, fuel cells and related components must be expanded to leverage PGM resources and support industrialisation. 

Governance is coordinated through the JET IP with workstreams covering supply, demand, infrastructure, finance, regulation and skills.

Twenty one projects have been identified across the value with several already progressing through feasibility stages. 

The briefing concludes that policy alignment, investment mobilisation and skills development are essential to secure a just transition and maximise socio economic benefits.

t: Green Hydrogen Commercialisation Strategy for South Africa: Executive Summary
c: Department of Trade Industry and Competition (2022) Green Hydrogen Commercialisation Strategy for South Africa: Executive Summary (2022).
s:
The executive summary to South Africa’s Green Hydrogen Commercialisation Strategy positions the country to compete in a rapidly expanding global market by building export capacity, stimulating domestic demand and supporting industrial development. 

The strategy highlights that green hydrogen is still a nascent market but could grow to supply up to a fifth of global energy by 2050. 

South Africa’s strong renewable resources, mineral endowments and industrial base create opportunities across production, manufacturing and decarbonisation. 

The strategy proposes early export development, targeted domestic pilots in hard to abate sectors and investment frameworks that attract foreign capital without relying on large state subsidies. 

It emphasises coordinated policy, regulatory reform and infrastructure planning to reduce costs and accelerate project development. 

Local manufacturing potential is significant, particularly for electrolyser and fuel cell components linked to platinum group metals. 

Skills development, research partnerships and social dialogue are identified as essential to support a just transition and ensure inclusive economic benefits. The strategy is a foundation for a future sector master plan that will require detailed modelling, stakeholder alignment and long term investment planning.

t: Green Hydrogen Commercialisation Strategy for South Africa: Final Report
c: Department of Science and Innovation (2023), Green Hydrogen Commercialisation Strategy for South Africa: Final Report, Government of South Africa, Pretoria.
s:
The report sets out a commercialisation strategy to position green hydrogen as a new pillar of South Africa’s low carbon industrial development. 

It frames green hydrogen as both a decarbonisation tool for sectors where reduction is a challenge and a driver of export growth, industrialisation and employment. 

South Africa’s strong renewable resources, platinum group metals and existing hydrogen capabilities are presented as key advantages for building a competitive value chain. 

The strategy explicitly links green hydrogen to the just energy transition, emphasising the need to support vulnerable workers and communities as coal-based value chains decline. 

It highlights opportunities to reskill and redeploy technical and vocational workers into emerging hydrogen related occupations across production, infrastructure and manufacturing. 

Skills planning, social dialogue and alignment with national development and climate commitments are essential to secure inclusive benefits. 

It calls for coordinated policy, regulation, finance and infrastructure to enable phased market driven growth of a green hydrogen sector that advances energy security, competitiveness and a just transition.

t: The development of green hydrogen in South Africa
c: Pandarum, A (2023) The development of green hydrogen in South Africa. Paper presented at the 11th CIGRE Southern Africa Regional Conference, CSIR International Convention Centre, Pretoria, 24–27 October.
s:
South Africa’s green hydrogen development is presented as a pathway to decarbonise hard to abate (decrease) sectors and support a just energy transition. 

The paper explains that electricity sector decarbonisation alone cannot meet national and global net zero targets, making green hydrogen essential for sectors such as steel, chemicals, shipping and aviation. 

South Africa’s strong solar and wind resources, land availability, platinum group metal reserves and long-standing Fischer-Tropsch capability position the country as a potential global exporter of green hydrogen and its derivatives. 

National strategies, including the Hydrogen Society Roadmap, the Just Energy Transition Investment Plan and the draft commercialisation strategy, outline the enabling environment and catalytic projects required to build a viable ecosystem. 

Pandarum highlights constraints such as limited grid capacity, water requirements, land competition, technology cost assumptions and the scale of skills development needed to support new value chains. 

He concludes that South Africa can build a competitive green hydrogen economy with significant job creation and inequality reduction if policy, infrastructure, financing and skills planning are aligned and implemented effectively.

t: Integrated Resource Plan 2025
c: Department of Electricity and Energy (2025) Integrated Resource Plan 2025. Pretoria: Government of South Africa.
s:
The Integrated Resource Plan (IRP) 2025 sets out South Africa’s long term approach to securing reliable electricity supply while reducing environmental impact. 

It is a statutory planning instrument under the Electricity Regulation Act and is updated as conditions in the power system and economy change. 

The IRP emphasises least cost generation expansion, system adequacy and alignment with national policy objectives. 

It highlights the shift from a coal dominated system towards a more diverse mix that includes renewable energy, nuclear, gas and storage technologies. 

The IRP outlines the legislative evolution of electricity planning, the role of private generation, and the increasing importance of clean technologies as costs fall and climate commitments strengthen. 

It also notes the need for improved plant performance, timely commissioning of new capacity and investment in transmission infrastructure. 

The IRP 2025 positions the energy transition as central to economic growth, security of supply and long term decarbonisation.

t: South Africa Country Climate and Development Report
c: World Bank Group (2022) South Africa Country Climate and Development Report.
s:
South Africa’s Country Climate and Development Report outlines how the country can align development goals with climate action through three interconnected transitions. 

It highlights that South Africa faces deep structural challenges, including low growth, high inequality and rising climate risks, which threaten long term development. 

The report argues that a low carbon transition centred on renewable energy, improved energy security and reduced dependence on coal is essential for economic competitiveness and resilience. 

It stresses that adaptation is equally urgent, as climate impacts such as droughts, floods and heatwaves already undermine productivity, infrastructure and human wellbeing. 

A just transition is presented as critical to protect vulnerable households, manage labour shifts and support skills development as carbon intensive sectors decline. 

The report identifies priority policy packages that maximise synergies between climate and development objectives, emphasising investment mobilisation, governance reform and targeted support for workers and communities. 

It concludes that South Africa can achieve a more inclusive, resilient and sustainable growth path if climate action is integrated into economic planning and supported by coordinated public, private and external financing.

t: EU’s work in Employment Sector: ILO Information Session with Donors and Partners
c: European Commission (2022) EU’s work in Employment Sector: ILO Information Session with Donors and Partners, 20 May 2022.
s:
The presentation outlines the European Union’s employment related cooperation with South Africa, focusing on skills development, youth employability and support for small enterprises. 

It highlights ongoing programmes such as Education for Employability, the Capacity Building Programme for Employment Promotion and the Ecosystem Development for Small Enterprises, all aimed at improving labour market readiness, strengthening TVET systems and supporting SMMEs. 

The Team Europe Initiative on Jobs for the Future is presented as a coordinated effort by EU member states to address high youth unemployment by promoting inclusive labour market policies, preparing young people for future jobs and fostering job creation in green and digital sectors. 

The initiative leverages European companies operating in South Africa, technical exchanges and blended finance. 

A forthcoming Youth Action programme will further support TVET reform, digital learning, entrepreneurship and lifelong learning. 

The presentation emphasises the need for stronger skills ecosystems, improved access to training and greater alignment between education and labour market needs to support South Africa’s just transition and reduce inequality.

t: Assessment of local skills for the South African renewable energy value chain
c: GreenCape (2022) Assessment of local skills for the South African renewable energy value chain. Department of Science and Innovation and SANEDI, Cape Town.
s:
The report assesses South Africa’s current and future skills needs across the renewable energy value chain, focusing on utility scale solar PV and wind, battery storage, rooftop PV, as well as transmission and distribution. 

It finds that the shift to Independent Power Producers (IPPs) and distributed generation is creating strong demand for highly skilled engineers, technical specialists and project managers, alongside growing needs for blue collar technicians during construction, operations and manufacturing. 

Industry interviews highlight persistent shortages in high voltage engineering, grid integration, solar PV design, wind turbine maintenance and specialised manufacturing trades. 

Companies report challenges in retaining skilled staff, limited alignment between training institutions and industry needs, and uncertainty caused by delays in Renewable Energy Independent Power Producer Procurement Programme (REIPPPP) procurement rounds. 

Although skills were previously imported through work visas, this has declined as local capacity improves. 

Future demand will include cyber security, drone operations, energy storage engineering and software development. 

The report recommends stronger collaboration between industry, universities, TVET colleges and SETAs, improved curriculum alignment, expanded apprenticeships and bursaries, and structured pathways for HV electricians, solar PV designers, welders and electrical line workers. 

It also proposes using REIPPPP to support skills planning and establishing a national register of trainees in priority occupations.

t: Labour market reform options to boost employment in South Africa
c: Duval R, Ji Y and Shibata I (2021) Labour market reform options to boost employment in South Africa. IMF Working Paper WP/21/165.
s:
South Africa’s labour market is marked by persistently low employment, weak labour force participation and extremely high structural unemployment. 

These outcomes stem from a combination of historical legacies, weak labour market institutions and limited flexibility in wage setting. 

Collective bargaining is fragmented, often uncoordinated and dominated by sector level agreements that do not adequately reflect firm level conditions. 

Minimum wages are high relative to median wages in emerging markets, which improves income protection but may constrain low skilled employment. 

Employment protection legislation is complex and not widely enforced, creating uncertainty for employers and limiting job creation. 

They recommend strengthening coordination in wage bargaining, improving representativeness in bargaining councils, introducing firm level flexibility clauses and streamlining dispute resolution. 

They also note the need for complementary reforms in education, transport and product markets to raise returns to work. 

These measures would disproportionately benefit disadvantaged groups, particularly youth, who face the highest unemployment rates.

t: Economic and Employment Indicators and Trends in South Africa: Issue 03
c: NEDLAC (2022) Economic and Employment Indicators and Trends in South Africa: Issue 03 (March 2022).
s:
South Africa’s economic performance in 2021 reflected a fragile recovery shaped by weak investment, uneven sectoral output and persistently high unemployment. 

Real GDP per capita increased for the first time since 2013, supported by stronger household and government consumption and lower imports, although gross capital formation remained a major drag on growth. 

Public corporations recorded the sharpest fall in fixed investment, contributing to the lowest investment-to-GDP ratio on record. 

Employment conditions deteriorated further, with both official and expanded unemployment reaching new highs and a marked rise in unemployed matriculants and graduates. 

Most sectors operated below pre-COVID levels, although agriculture, finance and community services outperformed. 

Rising global commodity prices following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine had limited direct impact on South Africa because of its small trade exposure to both Russia and Ukraine. 

Government debt per capita continued to rise and the yield curve signalled heightened medium-term uncertainty. 

Overall, the data point to structural weaknesses that constrain growth and employment.

t: The Productivity Ecosystem for Decent Work
c: Radic, D. (2022) The Productivity Ecosystem for Decent Work. International Labour Organization, 13 May.
s:
Radic outlines the ILO’s Productivity Ecosystem approach, which positions productivity as central to decent work, higher wages and sustainable economic growth. 

It highlights a decade of stagnating global productivity growth, widening gaps between frontier firms and the rest, and the lower productivity of small economic units that employ most workers. 

The ILO argues that productivity constraints are systemic and span regulatory burdens, weak innovation systems, limited skills supply, poor infrastructure, unstable macroeconomic conditions and ineffective workplace practices. 

Its ecosystem model integrates macro, meso- and micro factors, emphasising social dialogue, skills, technology, management practices and supportive policies. 

The approach is adaptive and evidence-driven, with interventions emerging from consultation rather than predetermined templates. 

In South Africa, productivity challenges include declining manufacturing, weak investment, falling labour productivity and high unemployment. 

The country component aims to strengthen public-private platforms for evidence-based productivity policy and improve SME access to value chains and supporting functions to enable decent job creation.

t: South Africa Economic Outlook: Sustainable options to plug the energy deficit
c: PwC (2022) South Africa Economic Outlook: Sustainable options to plug the energy deficit (29 November).
s:
South Africa’s economic outlook highlights the urgent need to address the country’s energy deficit through sustainable, decentralised and market enabling measures. 

The report shows how load shedding, declining coal use, and rising renewable uptake are reshaping the energy landscape while exposing weaknesses in governance and infrastructure. 

Municipalities emerge as central actors in closing the supply gap by enabling small scale embedded generation, microgrids, rooftop solar, and improved distribution management. 

Climate resilience and decarbonisation are now strategic imperatives for businesses, requiring action across operations, supply chains, capital allocation and ESG reporting. 

Regulatory reforms, including the Electricity Regulation Amendment Bill, are expected to open the market to new entrants, expand renewable energy procurement, and support South Africa’s just energy transition. 

However, persistent regulatory uncertainty continues to slow large scale renewable deployment. 

The report concludes that coordinated public and private action is essential to stabilise energy supply, accelerate decarbonisation, and strengthen social and economic outcomes.

t: Skills supply and demand in South Africa: Labour Market Intelligence research programme summary report.
c: Department of Higher Education and Training (2022) Skills supply and demand in South Africa: Labour Market Intelligence research programme summary report. Pretoria: DHET.
s:
South Africa continues to face persistent skills shortages alongside high unemployment, driven by a structural mismatch between labour market needs and the skills profile of the workforce. 

The summary report outlines how weak economic growth, a services dominated economy and declining labour intensive sectors have limited job creation and deepened unemployment, particularly among young people. 

The labour market remains largely formal, yet total employment fell between 2018 and 2021, with the greatest losses in medium skilled occupations. 

Although the stock of skills has improved gradually, with more individuals completing secondary education and entering higher education, the pandemic disrupted enrolments and slowed progress in the skills pipeline. 

Higher education institutions produced increasing numbers of graduates, especially at undergraduate level, while private institutions also expanded output. 

However, demand for skills has not kept pace with supply, and employment growth has been uneven across industries. 

The report highlights ongoing occupational shortages, mismatches between qualifications and jobs, and rising graduate unemployment. 

These trends reinforce the need for responsive skills planning and stronger alignment between the post school education and training (PSET) system and labour market requirements.

t: The role of dual VET in the just green transition
c: DC dVET (2024) The role of dual VET in the just green transition. Zurich: Donor Committee for Dual Vocational Education and Training.
s:
This policy brief explains how dual vocational education and training can support a just green transition by integrating economic, social and ecological sustainability. 

It highlights that the transition to a carbon neutral and circular economy has uneven social impacts, making fairness and inclusion essential. 

Dual VET is well placed to respond because it links public and private actors, enables green skills development, and supports reskilling in sectors undergoing structural change. 

The brief emphasises a holistic view of transformative VET that considers stakeholder needs, justice dimensions, and the interdependence of skills systems. 

It outlines the roles of business, which must align sustainability with value chain skills needs, and TVET institutions, which should green campuses, curricula and institutional cultures. 

Effective implementation requires social dialogue, sound data on future skills, and cascading training models. 

The brief concludes that dual VET can drive sustainable change when stakeholders collaborate around shared green values and long term commitment to sustainability.

t: An inclusive green transition: aligning skills and jobs for impact
c: Swisscontact (2025)An inclusive green transition: aligning skills and jobs for impact. Zurich: Swisscontact
s:
This position paper sets out Swisscontact’s approach to an inclusive green transition, emphasising that climate change is reshaping economies and labour markets in ways that demand systemic, not just skills focused responses. 

They define an inclusive green transition as a shift towards environmentally sustainable, resilient and more equitable societies, requiring structural economic change, not isolated training interventions. 

Swisscontact argues that most green employment will emerge from transforming existing sectors rather than creating new ones, and that green skills must be understood through their contribution to adaptation, mitigation and environmental conservation. 

Their model highlights three layers of competence: a green mindset, transversal skills and technical skills. 

The paper stresses the need for labour market aligned, evidence based and context specific interventions, supported by strong private sector engagement and local system anchoring. 

Case studies from Ghana, Kosovo, Bangladesh, Bolivia, Mozambique and Laos illustrate how market realities, incentives and systemic constraints shape green job creation. 

Swisscontact sees itself as a learning organisation committed to adaptive management, decent work and principled engagement to ensure that green transitions are inclusive and economically grounded.

t: Green jobs for social inclusion and sustainable transformation (GESIT)
c: GIZ (2024) Green jobs for social inclusion and sustainable transformation (GESIT). Jakarta: Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH.
s:
This GIZ publication outlines Indonesia’s efforts to link climate action with inclusive employment through the Green Jobs for Social Inclusion and Sustainable Transformation (GESIT) project. 

Indonesia faces rising emissions and significant environmental pressures, while lacking demand driven and inclusive upskilling systems to support a socially just green transition. 

GESIT responds by strengthening national, sectoral and local capacities to promote green jobs. 

At national level, it supports the operationalisation of the Green Jobs Roadmap, advises ministries and sector associations, and builds the evidence base for future skills needs. 

The project pilots inclusive upskilling and reskilling programmes for emerging green occupations, particularly in manufacturing, e mobility and the circular economy, and works with training providers to integrate proven modules into the TVET system. 

At subnational level, GESIT enables multi stakeholder platforms in pioneer provinces to coordinate strategies, develop measures and share learning across regions. 

The project aims to ensure that Indonesia’s green transition is both economically viable and socially inclusive by aligning skills development, employment promotion and policy reform.

t: Skills Gap or Signalling Gap? Insights from LinkedIn in emerging markets of Brazil, India, Indonesia and South Africa. Solutions for Youth Employment
c: S4YE & LinkedIn (2020) Skills Gap or Signalling Gap? Insights from LinkedIn in emerging markets of Brazil, India, Indonesia and South Africa. Solutions for Youth Employment, Washington DC and LinkedIn, Mountain View CA.
s:
The report analyses LinkedIn data from Brazil, India, Indonesia and South Africa to understand youth employment dynamics, skills demand and the nature of skills gaps. 

It finds that employers increasingly seek entry level workers with a mix of technical, soft and computer literacy skills, with technical skills dominating job postings across the three countries where data was available. 

The study shows that the severity and nature of skills gaps differ by country, and employer perceptions are inconsistent, highlighting measurement challenges. 

A major insight is the presence of a skills signalling gap: young people often possess soft skills but fail to highlight them in their LinkedIn profiles, despite employers valuing them. 

The report also finds that youth underutilise LinkedIn even though most job postings on the platform target entry level roles. 

It recommends strengthening labour market intermediation, improving career guidance, promoting digital professional engagement, and integrating soft, ICT and Fourth Industrial Revolution skills into training. 

The report emphasises the need for real time labour market information systems that combine big data with traditional sources.

t: Green Economy Bulletin: Trends, developments and data
c: TIPS (2022) Green Economy Bulletin: Trends, developments and data. Pretoria: Trade & Industrial Policy Strategies.
s:
The Green Economy Bulletin provides a national overview of South Africa’s progress towards a sustainable, low carbon and inclusive economy. 

It tracks 14 indicators across economic development, social progress and environmental sustainability to assess whether the country is shifting towards the goals set out in the National Development Plan and the Low Emission Development Strategy 2050. 

This Bulletin shows that progress has been slow, with unemployment, inequality and household vulnerability remaining high, and the COVID 19 crisis worsening these pressures. 

Although energy intensity has improved, the dominance of coal persists, and renewable energy uptake has not yet significantly reduced emissions. 

South Africa continues to overshoot its ecological footprint, and water security remains a concern. 

However, recent policy commitments, increased climate finance and forthcoming legislation such as the Climate Change Act may accelerate progress. 

Investments in renewable energy, green industrial capabilities and just transition financing are expected to support improvements over the next decade. 

The Bulletin establishes a baseline for monitoring South Africa’s transition and highlights areas requiring urgent action.

t: South Africa Country Climate and Development Report
c: World Bank Group (2022) South Africa Country Climate and Development Report. Washington, DC: World Bank Group.
s:
South Africa’s Country Climate and Development Report sets out how it can align its development goals with the demands of a low carbon, climate resilient and socially just transition. 

The report underlines the scale of South Africa’s economic and social challenges, including slow growth, high inequality and persistent unemployment, all of which are intensified by climate risks. 

It argues that climate action is in the country’s development interest, particularly given the vulnerability of infrastructure, water systems and human capital to rising temperatures and extreme weather. 

The report proposes three interconnected transitions: a low carbon shift driven by reduced reliance on coal and expanded renewable energy; a resilience transition to manage climate impacts; and a just transition that protects poor and vulnerable households. 

It stresses the need for urgent, prioritised policy action, stronger governance and effective mobilisation of public, private and external finance. 

The report also identifies areas requiring further research, including labour market impacts, skills needs and the operationalisation of just transition strategies in coal dependent regions.

t: National Employment Vulnerability Assessment: Analysis of potential climate change related impacts and vulnerable groups
c: Makgetla, N., Maseko, N., Montmasson Clair, G. and Patel, M. (2019) National Employment Vulnerability Assessment: Analysis of potential climate change related impacts and vulnerable groups. Pretoria: Trade & Industrial Policy Strategies (TIPS).
s:
This assessment examines how climate change will affect employment across key South African value chains and identifies which workers, communities and small businesses are most vulnerable. 

It evaluates vulnerability through four forms of capital: financial, physical, human and social. 

The report shows that climate related impacts differ sharply across coal, metals, petroleum based transport, agriculture and tourism, with each sector facing distinct risks linked to declining demand, technological shifts, extreme weather and policy changes. 

Coal dependent municipalities in Mpumalanga face concentrated exposure due to undiversified local economies and high reliance on mining jobs. 

Metals value chains confront structural change as global markets shift and energy intensive processes become less competitive. 

Transport workers, especially informal operators, mechanics and petrol attendants, face income insecurity as electric vehicles expand. 

Agriculture is highly exposed to drought, heat and rainfall variability, with farmworkers having limited assets, low pay and weak social protection. 

Across all sectors, vulnerable groups typically have low education levels, limited savings, precarious employment and restricted access to social networks. 

The report highlights the need for targeted support, skills development and transition planning to reduce inequality and protect livelihoods.

t: Sector Jobs Resilience Plan: Agriculture Value Chain
c: Makgetla, N., Maseko, N., Montmasson Clair, G. and Patel, M. (2020) Sector Jobs Resilience Plan: Agriculture Value Chain. Pretoria: Trade & Industrial Policy Strategies (TIPS).
s:
This Sector Jobs Resilience Plan outlines how climate change threatens employment and livelihoods across South Africa’s agricultural value chain, particularly among low income and marginalised groups. 

Agriculture must deal with rising temperatures, more frequent droughts and increasingly erratic rainfall which impacts both livestock and crop production. 

Farmworkers are highly vulnerable due to low wages, limited savings, weak social protection and housing tied to employment. 

Emerging farmers and gardeners in historic labour sending regions face declining production, limited access to irrigation, and constrained ability to invest in adaptive technologies. 

This plan proposes strengthening institutional responsibility for implementation, accelerating the diffusion of climate resilient technologies, and supporting diversification in communities that depend on farming. 

It also recommends active labour market policies to help displaced workers transition to new livelihoods, alongside income support and drought relief during severe climate events. 

Given the uncertainty of localised climate impact, the plan emphasises the need for monitoring systems and adaptive management. 

Overall, the plan aims to reduce climate related job losses, protect vulnerable households and support a more resilient agricultural sector.

t: Sector Jobs Resilience Plan: Coal Value Chain
c: Patel, M., Makgetla, N., Maseko, N. and Montmasson Clair, G. (2020) Sector Jobs Resilience Plan: Coal Value Chain. Pretoria: Trade & Industrial Policy Strategies (TIPS).
s:
The Sector Jobs Resilience Plan for the coal value chain examines how climate change mitigation and the transition to cleaner energy will affect workers, communities and local economies that depend on coal. 

Coal has long been central to South Africa’s energy system and industrial development, with employment concentrated in a small number of Mpumalanga municipalities. 

These areas face significant vulnerability because their economies are highly undiversified and rely heavily on coal mining, Eskom power stations and Sasol’s coal to liquids operations. 

Climate related impacts arise primarily from declining demand for coal as countries reduce greenhouse gas emissions and as domestic policy expands renewable energy and carbon pricing. 

Miners are the most vulnerable because of limited mobility, relatively low formal qualifications and dependence on a single industry. 

The plan proposes strengthening institutional capacity to manage the transition, reforming Social and Labour Plans to support diversification, promoting new economic activities in coal towns, and improving active labour market policies to help workers shift to alternative livelihoods. 

It also recommends enhanced social protection and public employment schemes to cushion income losses during the transition.

t: Sector Jobs Resilience Plan: Metals Value Chain
c: Trade & Industrial Policy Strategies (TIPS) 2020 Sector Jobs Resilience Plan: Metals Value Chain. Pretoria: TIPS.
s:
The Sector Jobs Resilience Plan for the metals value chain assesses how climate change pressures will reshape mining, refining and downstream manufacturing. 

It stresses that South Africa’s metals sector is exposed to rising input costs, regulatory changes and market shifts linked to decarbonisation. 

Vulnerability is concentrated in gold, platinum group metals (PGMs), iron ore, manganese and chrome, with nine districts heavily dependent on mining. 

Workers face risks due to specialised skills, limited alternative employment and the geographic concentration of operations. 

The plan proposes five interventions: establishing a coordinated oversight structure; strengthening Social and Labour Plans and rehabilitation requirements; promoting technological adjustments to reduce emissions and improve competitiveness; supporting economic diversification in mining towns; and improving labour market and social protection measures for workers affected by climate related downsizing. 

These interventions aim to protect livelihoods, stabilise regional economies and support a just transition across the metals value chain.

t: Sector Jobs Resilience Plan: Tourism Value Chain
c: Trade & Industrial Policy Strategies (TIPS) 2020 Sector Jobs Resilience Plan: Tourism Value Chain. Pretoria: TIPS.
s:
The Sector Jobs Resilience Plan (SJRP ) for the tourism value chain outlines how climate change impacts threaten both the supply and demand sides of South Africa’s tourism economy. 

Nature based attractions face risks from heat, drought, floods, biodiversity loss and rising sea levels, while long distance travel may decline as measures slow climate change down, increase costs and consumers shift behaviour. 

The value chain is dominated by accommodation and catering, which employ mostly women in low paid, low skill and often insecure jobs. 

Because tourism is not a standalone statistical category, identifying vulnerable groups and towns is challenging, but catering and accommodation workers serve as a reliable proxy. 

The proposed SJRP focuses on strengthening coordination across government, protecting environmental attractions, supporting technological adjustments, identifying tourism dependent towns, and establishing active labour market measures for workers who may lose their livelihoods. 

The plan emphasises early warning systems, diversification strategies and targeted support to ensure a just transition for workers and communities reliant on tourism.

t: Sector Jobs Resilience Plan: Petroleum based Transport Value Chain
c: Trade & Industrial Policy Strategies (2020) Sector Jobs Resilience Plan: Petroleum based Transport Value Chain. Pretoria: TIPS.
s:
The Sector Jobs Resilience Plan (SJRP) for the petroleum based transport value chain assesses how the transition away from internal combustion engine vehicles will reshape employment, business models and technological requirements across the sector. 

With more than 1.2 million workers in road transport services, auto maintenance, petrol stations, sales and assembly, the value chain faces significant disruption as global and domestic policy shifts accelerate the adoption of electric and hybrid vehicles. 

The timing of this transition remains uncertain, but its impacts will be far reaching, particularly for mechanics, taxi operators and auto industry workers. 

Vulnerabilities arise from low formal qualifications, high levels of informality, ageing workforces and limited financial buffers. 

The SJRP proposes measures to incentivise local electric vehicle production, support taxi owners to adopt cleaner technologies, and strengthen active labour market policies to help mechanics and other workers transition to new occupations. 

The plan emphasises coordinated action across government, industry and labour to manage risks, protect livelihoods and ensure a just transition for affected groups.

t: The SJRP Toolbox: Summary for Policy Makers
c: Trade & Industrial Policy Strategies (TIPS) 2020, The SJRP Toolbox: Summary for Policy Makers, TIPS, Pretoria.
s:
The Sector Jobs Resilience Plans (SJRPs) Toolbox outlines cross-cutting measures required to protect vulnerable workers, small producers and communities from climate related employment shocks across five value chains: coal, metals, petroleum-based transport, agriculture and tourism. 

It emphasises that climate impacts cannot be forecast with precision, making institutional readiness more important than detailed plans. 

The toolbox identifies five strategic pillars.  

The first, a high level coordination structure (ideally the Presidential Climate Change Coordination Council), secondly, promoting technological adjustment to reduce exposure to carbon pricing and climate risks.  

In addition, economic diversification in vulnerable mining, farming and historic labour sending towns must be supported and the active labour market policies for retraining, placement and small enterprise support should be strengthened.  

Finally, social protection for workers facing prolonged transitions needs to be enhanced.

The report notes the fragmentation across government spheres, weak diffusion of climate adaptive technologies, limited municipal capacity, and gaps in skills and social protection systems. 

It concludes that SJRPs must prioritise monitoring, resilience-building and risk management, with implementation dependent on institutional alignment, stakeholder engagement and targeted support for vulnerable groups.

t: Green meets digital: how technology is accelerating sustainable change
c: CEDEFOP (2024) Green meets digital: how technology is accelerating sustainable change Thessaloniki: CEDEFOP.
s:
The article shows how the green and digital transitions are converging, with technologies such as AI, big data and IoT.  

This is sustainability practices across sectors while creating demand for new digital green skill sets.

CEDEFOP stresses that VET systems must adapt through interdisciplinary learning and stronger partnerships to equip workers for emerging roles in a low carbon, tech driven economy.

t: Green skills wanted: how the green transition is reshaping the labour market
c: CEDEFOP (2024) Green skills wanted: how the green transition is reshaping the labour market. Thessaloniki: CEDEFOP.
s:
The article explains how the accelerating green transition is transforming both new and existing jobs across Europe, driving strong demand for upskilling and reskilling in technical, environmental and digital competences. 

VET systems, lifelong learning and close partnerships between policy-makers, providers and industry are essential.  Green skills should be embedded in curricula to create a workforce that can support a more sustainable and resilient economy.

t: One transition, many realities: how sectors are tailoring their green responses
c: CEDEFOP (2024) One transition, many realities: how sectors are tailoring their green responses. Thessaloniki: CEDEFOP.
s:
The article explains that although all sectors are moving towards sustainability, each faces distinct pressures, technologies and workforce needs, requiring tailored green responses. 

CEDEFOP argues that sector specific skills strategies, stronger collaboration and targeted training are essential to support workers and industries through the wide-ranging realities of the green transition.

t: People power: the workforce behind the green transition
c: CEDEFOP (2024) People power: the workforce behind the green transition. Thessaloniki: CEDEFOP.
s:
The article highlights that Europe’s workforce is central to the green transition, with rising demand for green skills creating new opportunities while posing risks for workers in carbon intensive sectors. 

CEDEFOP stresses that a just transition depends on reskilling, upskilling, strong social dialogue and adaptable education and training systems that embed sustainability and lifelong learning.

t: TVET Quarterly Updates April–May 2024
c: Department of Higher Education and Training (2024) TVET Quarterly Updates April–May 2024. Pretoria: DHET.
s:
An overview of key developments in the TVET sector between April and May 2024, with a strong focus on youth unemployment, just energy transition priorities and system readiness. 

It notes that in his state of the nation speech, the President outlined the Presidential Employment Stimulus, SAYouth.mobi and the Youth Employment Service. 

Energy transition updates included increased financing for the Just Energy Transition Investment Plan and plans to expand transmission infrastructure to support renewable energy. 

The Minister of Higher Education and Training comments on declining real budgets, reduced enrolments and ongoing efforts to strengthen PSET responsiveness, infrastructure and workplace placements. 

Other articles cover the deregistration of Educor institutions due to regulatory non-compliance, the launch of the National Artisan Development Academy to boost artisan production, and the introduction of the Higher Education Innovation Fund to support entrepreneurship and innovation. 

The newsletter also notes ongoing entrepreneurship competitions and the transition to revised QCTO qualifications by the June 2024 enrolment deadline.

t: TVET College Times: December 2023–January 2024, Volume 72
c: Department of Higher Education and Training (2023) TVET College Times: December 2023–January 2024, Volume 72. Pretoria: DHET.
s:
