The December 2023–January 2024 issue of TVET College Times highlights major developments across the TVET sector, emphasising expansion, funding reforms and strengthened skills pipelines.

 Minister Nzimande’s update on the Comprehensive Student Funding Model outlines the introduction of a loan scheme for missing middle students, supported by NSFAS and SETAs, alongside continued investment in PSET infrastructure and readiness for the 2024 academic year. 

The edition showcases the official opening of the Msinga Campus, part of a broader national programme to expand TVET capacity and deliver occupationally aligned programmes such as mechatronics. 

Several articles profile artisan development initiatives, including the Decade of the Artisan campaign, Centres of Specialisation and multiple entrepreneurship competitions that promote self employment and innovation. 

Colleges across the country report achievements in social inclusion, alumni development, international partnerships, graduate success stories and participation in WorldSkills competitions.

t: College and SETA Times: February–April 2024
c: Department of Higher Education and Training (2024) College and SETA Times: February–April 2024, Volume 73. Pretoria: DHET.
s:
The central focus of the February–April 2024 issue of College and SETA Times is the Department of Higher Education and Training’s R1 billion investment in new Community College infrastructure, launched at the Tjheseho Skills Development Centre in the Free State. 

Minister Blade Nzimande emphasises the role of Community Colleges in addressing unemployment, poverty and inequality through expanded skills provision, particularly for young people not in employment, education or training. 

It also reports on the WorldSkills South Africa National Competition, showcasing excellence in artisanal and technical skills, and the launch of new TVET and CET facilities across several provinces. 

Other features include leadership development initiatives, campaigns against illegal colleges, civic education programmes, and strengthened partnerships between colleges, SETAs and industry. 

The issue reflects a sector-wide effort to expand access, improve infrastructure, enhance governance, and align training with labour market needs. 

It also documents achievements in student performance, artisan development, entrepreneurship promotion, as well as international collaboration, underscoring the sector’s commitment to building a capable, future ready workforce.

t: Directive on the implementation and transitional arrangements for pre 2009 qualifications (under SAQA Act, 1995)
c: Department of Higher Education and Training (2024) Directive on the implementation and transitional arrangements for pre 2009 qualifications (under SAQA Act, 1995). Government Gazette No. 50742, 3 June. Pretoria: Government Printer.
s:
This 2024 Ministerial Directive sets out new implementation and transitional arrangements for pre 2009 qualifications registered under the former SAQA Act (1995). 

It explains that the shift from the eight level NQF to the current ten level system requires all older qualifications to be replaced or realigned in line with the Occupational Qualifications Sub Framework. 

The Directive notes that 1 475 pre 2009 qualifications reached their registration end date in June 2023, with the final enrolment date set for June 2024. 

It notes that many SETAs have not prioritised the development or realignment of replacement qualifications despite repeated instructions since 2009. 

The Directive therefore introduces a structured process for this transition: 1 101 qualifications will be deregistered, while 374 will receive limited extensions of one to two years where realignment or regulatory requirements justify it. 

It also confirms that listed trades without occupational qualifications will receive temporary extensions, and that regulatory unit standards will remain recognised until replaced. 

SETAs are held accountable for completing development work, supported by DHET, SAQA and QCTO through monitoring, reporting and roadshows. 

The Directive emphasises that the transition affects only a small proportion of NQF qualifications and aims to ensure relevance, quality and alignment with current labour market needs.

t: CPD4E TVET Quarterly Updates: April–July 2024
c: Department of Higher Education and Training (2024) CPD4E TVET Quarterly Updates: April–July 2024. Pretoria: DHET.
s:
This newsletter focuses on technology adoption, renewable energy skills, governance changes and budget priorities. 

It reports on Africa Day activities that showcased the role of science, innovation and TVET colleges in preparing students for digital and green economy opportunities. 

The Ministerial Directive on pre 2009 qualifications is summarised, outlining the deregistration of outdated programmes, limited extensions for 374 qualifications and the requirement for SETAs to accelerate realignment to the Occupational Qualifications Sub Framework. 

It also covers DHET’s drive to revitalise technology and science skills through 4IR aligned curricula, supported by partnerships with industry and government departments. 

It profiles EWSETA’s collaboration with Chinese partners to strengthen renewable energy training and establish local solar PV production capacity in TVET colleges which will be a major contribution to the just energy transition. 

Additional sections outline leadership changes in the Department, the 2024/25 budget allocations and parliamentary assessments of DHET’s performance and priorities.

t: Quarterly Labour Force Survey, Quarter 2: 2024
c: Statistics South Africa (2024) Quarterly Labour Force Survey, Quarter 2: 2024. Pretoria: Stats SA.
s:
The Quarterly Labour Force Survey for Q2 2024 reports a weakening labour market, with employment falling by 92 000 to 16,65 million and unemployment rising by 158 000 to 8,38 million. 

The unemployment rate increased to 33,5% as the labour force grew by 66 000. 

Employment losses occurred mainly in the formal sector, agriculture and private households, while the informal sector grew by 48 000 jobs. 

Industry level declines were most notable in trade, agriculture and construction, whereas manufacturing, community and social services, utilities and transport recorded gains. 

Year on year, total employment increased by 306 000, driven by finance, manufacturing, transport and private households. 

Occupational shifts show large quarterly losses among plant and machine operators, sales and services, professionals and clerks, while elementary, technician and managerial roles expanded. 

Provincial trends were mixed: Western Cape, KwaZulu Natal, Mpumalanga, Northern Cape and North West recorded quarterly declines, while Gauteng, Limpopo, Eastern Cape and Free State showed increases. 

The working age population grew by 137 000, and discouraged work seekers increased by 147 000. 

Overall, the data reflect persistent structural challenges, with rising unemployment, uneven sectoral performance and continued pressure on young people entering the labour market.

t: Climate Change Act 22 of 2024
c: South Africa. (2024) Climate Change Act 22 of 2024. Pretoria: Government of South Africa.
s:
South Africa’s Climate Change Act 22 of 2024 establishes an overarching legal framework for responding to climate change. 

It coordinates national, provincial and municipal action to support a long term just transition to a low carbon, climate resilient economy and society. 

The Act requires government departments and municipalities to assess climate risks, develop response plans and align policies to reduce vulnerability across sectors. 

It mandates the Minister of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment to publish greenhouse gas lists, set sectoral emissions targets and allocate carbon budgets to major emitters. 

The Act also provides for a national adaptation strategy and sector adaptation plans to strengthen resilience and guide investment. 

Its emphasis on a just transition ensures that climate measures do not disadvantage vulnerable communities and that economic restructuring supports inclusive development. 

The Act’s implementation is phased with several sections scheduled to take effect after March 2025.

t: CPD4E TVET quarterly updates: July–September 2024
c: CPD4E. (2024) CPD4E TVET quarterly updates: July–September 2024. Pretoria: CPD4E.
s:
The CPD4E TVET Quarterly Updates for July to September 2024 reports on the signing of the Climate Change Act, which establishes a phased national response to climate risks but faces implementation challenges linked to regulatory readiness and cooperation from major emitters. 

The Municipal JET Conference emphasised the central role of municipalities in electricity reform, grid upgrades and inclusive transition planning, supported by investment, capacity building and improved governance. 

Cabinet’s restructuring of the energy and mineral portfolios aims to streamline oversight of electricity, gas and nuclear legislation. 

Labour market data show rising unemployment, persistent youth vulnerability and uneven sectoral performance. 

International partners, particularly Germany, have signalled financial support for renewable energy expansion, although grid constraints and delays remain barriers. 

TVET related updates include inter SETA initiatives to strengthen renewable energy skills, international training partnerships and leadership development programmes for women in the energy sector. 

The DHET budget vote reaffirmed commitments to student funding, artisan development and institutional support despite fiscal pressures.

t: CPD4E TVET quarterly updates: July–September 2024
c: CPD4E. (2024) CPD4E TVET quarterly updates: July–September 2024. Pretoria: CPD4E.
s:
The CPD4E TVET Quarterly Updates for July to September 2024 outline major developments in climate policy, energy transition planning and post school education. 

The signing of the Climate Change Act marks a significant policy milestone, although its impact will depend on enforcement, regulatory strength and cooperation from major emitters. 

The Municipal JET Conference highlighted the central role of municipalities in electricity reform, grid modernisation and inclusive transition planning, supported by investment, capacity building and improved governance. 

Cabinet’s restructuring of the energy and mineral portfolios aims to streamline oversight of electricity, gas and nuclear legislation. 

Labour market data show rising unemployment, persistent youth vulnerability and uneven sectoral performance across industries. 

International partners, particularly Germany, have indicated readiness to support renewable energy expansion, although grid constraints and institutional delays remain barriers. 

TVET related updates include inter SETA initiatives to strengthen renewable energy skills, international experiential learning programmes and leadership development for women in the energy sector. 

The DHET budget vote reaffirmed commitments to student funding, artisan development and institutional support despite fiscal pressures.

t: Quarterly employment statistics (QES), June 2024: Statistical release P0277
c: Statistics South Africa. (2024) Quarterly employment statistics (QES), June 2024: Statistical release P0277. Pretoria: Stats SA.
s:
The Quarterly Employment Statistics (QES) release for June 2024 provides payroll based measures of employment, earnings and labour trends across South Africa’s formal non agricultural sector. 

The survey draws data from VAT registered businesses and public institutions and covers eight major industries, including mining, manufacturing, electricity, construction, trade, transport, business services and community services. 

The document outlines quarterly and annual changes in total employment, distinguishing between full time and part time workers. 

It reports modest overall employment growth quarter on quarter, driven mainly by increases in community services, while several industries recorded declines. 

Earnings data show mixed movements, with gross earnings decreasing slightly over the quarter but rising year on year. Basic salaries increased across most industries, while bonus payments fell sharply. Overtime payments rose in several sectors. 

The release also highlights differences between the QES and the household based Quarterly Labour Force Survey, noting that the QES excludes agriculture, private households and informal work.

t: CPD4E quarterly newsletter: January–March 2025
c: CPD4E. (2025) CPD4E quarterly newsletter: January–March 2025. Pretoria: CPD4E.
s:
The CPD4E Newsletter for January to March 2025 highlights major national and international developments shaping South Africa’s just energy transition and skills landscape. 

South Africa’s G20 Presidency focuses on solidarity, equality and sustainability, with priorities including disaster resilience, debt sustainability, climate finance mobilisation and equitable use of critical minerals. 

The second JET Progress Report shows continued momentum, with significant international financing pledged, growing private sector investment in renewables and progress across electricity, municipal, skills, NEV and green hydrogen portfolios. 

The 2025 State of the Nation Address emphasised education reform, expanded student funding, digital learning, renewable energy expansion, job creation and large-scale skills development initiatives. 

The 2025 Budget Speech reinforced these commitments through targeted investments in energy infrastructure, education, apprenticeships and green economy skills. 

The South Africa-EU Summit strengthens cooperation on trade, investment, green hydrogen, critical minerals and skills development. 

The newsletter also reports on the USA’s withdrawal from the JETP, reducing total pledges and prompting efforts to secure alternative grant funding.

t: CPD4E quarterly newsletter: August–October 2025
c: CPD4E. (2025) CPD4E quarterly newsletter: August–October 2025. Pretoria: CPD4E.
s:
The CPD4E Newsletter for August to October 2025 highlights major developments in South Africa’s skills, TVET and energy transition landscape. 

The period saw strong emphasis on green hydrogen, renewable energy and future focused skills. 

Minister Buti Manamela underscored the need for a skills led transition at the Pan African Green Hydrogen Skills Conference, calling for youth readiness to support a growing hydrogen economy. 

The HRDC advanced implementation of the Reconceptualised HRD Strategy and Master Skills Plan, while the Free State launched its Provincial HRD Council to strengthen alignment between provincial priorities and national skills agendas. 

TVET readiness for 2026 was confirmed, with expanded enrolment capacity and new occupational qualifications under development. 

In the energy sector, Eskom announced a long term shift from coal to renewables, supported by international financing and new programmes such as the Renewable Energy Offtake initiative. 

Collaboration with the Chinese company, BYD, signalled growing momentum in electric mobility. 

Employment creation efforts focused on SMMEs, youth interventions and economic recovery measures. 

Numerous JET related events and new research resources enriched national dialogue on skills, resilience and transition planning.

t: Annual solar outlook 2023
c: AFSIA. (2023) Annual solar outlook 2023. Kigali: Africa Solar Industry Association.
s:
The AFSIA Annual Solar Outlook 2023 reviews global and African solar trends, highlighting strong growth in global installed capacity and steady expansion across the continent. 

Globally, solar PV additions reached an estimated 220–260 GW in 2022, pushing total capacity beyond 1 TW and confirming solar as the fastest growing energy technology. 

Africa added 949 MW of new capacity, reflecting a 14 percent annual increase, with large scale projects dominating installations. 

Angola led the continent with two major utility scale plants, while South Africa, Egypt, Ghana and Mozambique followed with notable contributions. 

The report shows that solar deployment is spreading beyond traditional leaders, with 30 African countries installing more than 1 MW in 2022. 

Commercial and industrial systems grew rapidly, supported by rising demand for energy security and private investment. 

Mini grids experienced a decline due to limited financing, while solar home systems continued to expand. 

AFSIA also identifies more than 10 GW of documented solar projects across Africa and a growing pipeline of future developments, signalling increasing diversification and market maturity.

t: Anticipating Skill Needs and Adapting Higher Education: From Insight to Alignment
c: OECD 2026, Anticipating Skill Needs and Adapting Higher Education: From Insight to Alignment, OECD Publishing, Paris. https://doi.org/10.1787/827b3ca4-en.
s:
The report examines how skills assessment and anticipation (SAA) exercises can better inform higher education systems across OECD and EU countries. 

It highlights persistent skills mismatches in the EU, where 21% of workers are over-qualified and 25% over-skilled, while 10% are under-qualified and 9% under-skilled. 

Mismatches reduce productivity, wages and life satisfaction, underscoring the need for accurate, forward-looking skills intelligence. 

Drawing on 17 national SAA exercises, the report identifies key design features including unit of analysis, sectoral and geographical coverage, time horizon, data sources and methodological choices. 

It finds that most systems rely on occupational analysis, often supplemented by skills or qualification-level insights. 

Quantitative approaches dominate but are increasingly complemented by qualitative methods to capture emerging trends. 

Effective SAA systems depend on strong stakeholder engagement, sustainable funding and integration into broader governance structures. 

The report emphasises the importance of translating SAA results into higher education planning, programme design and student decision-making through regulatory mechanisms, financial incentives and targeted information provision.

t: Skills for a Just Transition to a Green Future: Measuring the South African TVET System and providing input to support its development
c: Freimann K and Magnus G (2023) Skills for a Just Transition to a Green Future: Measuring the South African TVET System and providing input to support its development. GIZ, Pretoria.
s:
This discussion paper assesses how South Africa’s TVET system must evolve to support a just transition to a green economy. 

It emphasises the need for coherent policy alignment between national development strategies, sustainability goals and skills planning. 

Although structures such as the Presidential Climate Commission provide coordination, major policy gaps remain, particularly in linking green industrial strategies with skills development. 

Demand for green skills is rising, driven by renewable energy expansion, regulatory shifts and the energy crisis, yet job creation remains uneven across sectors and heavily influenced by temporary construction roles. 

The TVET system faces persistent weaknesses, including limited labour market linkages, funding misalignment and insufficient lecturer capacity. 

Nonetheless, progress has been made through new occupational programmes, renewable energy curricula and emerging short skills programmes. 

The Career Path Development for Education (CPD4E) project demonstrates an integrated approach that strengthens policy capacity, supports SMMEs, improves employability and links skills forecasting to curriculum reform. 

The paper concludes that without a responsive, well resourced TVET system, South Africa cannot achieve an equitable and inclusive Just Transition.

t: The transition of youth from school to work: issues and policies
c: Atchoarena D (ed.) (2000) The transition of youth from school to work: issues and policies. UNESCO International Institute for Educational Planning, Paris.
s:
This UNESCO volume reviews international evidence on how young people move from school into work and examines the role of technical and vocational education 

in improving their prospects. It highlights that global economic restructuring, demographic pressures and labour market volatility have made transitions longer and more uncertain, with youth unemployment rising even in growing economies. 

It analyses diverse national experiences, including OECD countries, Latin America, Korea, Kenya and South Africa, showing that effective transitions require coordinated policies across education, labour markets and social protection. 

Key themes include the importance of well organised pathways linking education and employment, targeted support for youth at risk, stronger partnerships between training institutions and employers, and the need to address the realities of informal labour markets in developing countries. 

The volume argues that technical and vocational education can support employability only when aligned with economic demand, delivered through flexible and responsive systems and embedded in broader strategies for inclusive growth. 

It concludes that youth transitions require integrated, context specific interventions rather than reliance on education reforms alone.

t: Supported work experience and its impact on young people with intellectual disabilities, their families and employers
c: Real Opportunities Project (2015) Supported work experience and its impact on young people with intellectual disabilities, their families and employers. Wales.
s:
This study evaluates the Real Opportunities project, a supported work experience initiative designed to improve employment prospects for young people with intellectual disabilities or Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). 

It responds to longstanding evidence that these groups face extremely low employment rates, limited access to supported employment and significant personal, social and structural barriers. 

The project provided vocational profiling, job coach supported placements, family engagement, independence training and social inclusion support across nine regions in Wales. 

Data from 297 participants and 405 placements show that young people successfully undertook a wide range of entry level roles and that most gained measurable improvements in key work related skills, particularly communication, concentration, initiative and independent working. 

Employers reported high satisfaction with both the support provided and the performance of the young people, with many indicating willingness to host future placements or offer employment. 

Interviews with young people and families revealed increased confidence, positive workplace experiences and greater belief in the possibility of paid work. 

The findings demonstrate that structured, well supported work experience can enhance skills, shift expectations and create more inclusive employment pathways for young people with intellectual disabilities or ASD.

t: Transitions from school to work: UNICEF technical note
c: UNICEF (2019) Transitions from school to work: UNICEF technical note. United Nations Children’s Fund, New York.
s:
This UNICEF technical note outlines how governments and partners can strengthen young people’s transition from school to decent work. 

It highlights the scale of global exclusion, with millions of adolescents out of school and many more leaving without foundational skills. 

The paper identifies a persistent skills gap and mismatch, driven by poor quality schooling, limited access to technical and vocational training and gendered barriers that restrict girls’ participation. 

It emphasises that employability depends on both capability and opportunity, requiring young people to develop foundational, transferable, digital and job specific skills while also accessing labour markets that recognise and reward these skills. 

The note stresses that transitions are non linear and shaped by structural constraints such as weak labour demand, informal employment, limited job matching services and inadequate social protection. 

UNICEF proposes an integrated approach that expands equitable access to skills development, improves the relevance and quality of training, strengthens links between training providers and employers and builds enabling ecosystems that support decent work. 

The technical note positions UNICEF as a convener able to scale programmes and ensure continuity of support for vulnerable adolescents.

t: Illustrating school to work transition through drawings: An exploratory study with a sample of South African students
c: Harry T and Chinyamurindi WT (2020) Illustrating school to work transition through drawings: An exploratory study with a sample of South African students. SA Journal of Human Resource Management, University of Fort Hare, South Africa.
s:
This study explores how final year students at a historically disadvantaged South African university experience the transition from university to work, using drawings as a participatory visual method. 

Despite nearing graduation, students reported feeling unprepared for the labour market, largely because their programmes emphasised theory over practical experience. 

Three dominant narratives emerged. 

First, students felt “blind but determined”, expressing confusion and anxiety about entering the labour market without work experience. 

Second, they were “excited but scared”, recognising the value of their qualifications but fearing rejection due to institutional stigma and South Africa’s high youth unemployment. 

Third, some felt “ready to explore”, yet still struggled with inferiority linked to race, institutional disadvantage and rural location. 

The study highlights how structural inequalities, limited labour market exposure and low confidence shape students’ perceptions of employability. 

It also demonstrates the value of visual participatory methods for eliciting nuanced insights from vulnerable groups. 

The authors argue that universities, counsellors and policymakers must better support students’ work readiness and address systemic barriers affecting transitions into employment.

t: Making sense of jobs in South Africa’s just energy transition: Managing the impact of a coal transition on employment
c: Hermanus L and Montmasson-Clair G (2021) Making sense of jobs in South Africa’s just energy transition: Managing the impact of a coal transition on employment. Pretoria: Trade & Industrial Policy Strategies.
s:
This policy brief examines how South Africa can manage the employment impacts of its coal transition in a planned and equitable way. 

It notes the absence of a coherent national just transition strategy despite clear evidence that demand for coal is declining due to climate commitments, market shifts and ageing infrastructure. 

Coal-dependent regions in Mpumalanga face concentrated risks, with most direct and indirect jobs tied to mining, transport and coal-based industries. 

Around 150 000 direct jobs are at stake, most of which are held by semi-skilled workers with limited formal qualifications. 

It stresses the need for detailed, site-specific data to guide retirement planning, reskilling and re-employment. 

The authors argue that debates about job losses and renewable energy jobs are often distorted by inconsistent metrics and false comparisons. 

They emphasise that re-employment should extend beyond the energy sector to broader local economic development. 

Without active planning, the social and economic costs of unmanaged decline will be severe and long lasting. 

The brief calls for consensus-building, credible evidence and coordinated policy to support workers and communities through the transition.

t: Greening TVET Colleges Initiative in South Africa: From individual competence development to institutional change
c: GIZ (2014) Greening TVET Colleges Initiative in South Africa: From individual competence development to institutional change. Pretoria: Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH.
s:
This is a guide to a structured approach for transforming South African TVET colleges into institutions that actively support a green economy. 

TVET plays a central role in developing the skills, values and behaviours needed for sustainable development, and greening must extend beyond technical training to institutional culture, management and community engagement. 

The guide presents a holistic framework built on green campus operations, green curriculum, green research, green community and green culture, supported by integration into management systems. 

It emphasises organisational development, leadership commitment, stakeholder involvement and systematic processes such as environmental reviews, policy development and monitoring. 

Practical examples from participating colleges demonstrate progress in energy and water efficiency, waste management, renewable energy training and awareness initiatives. 

The guide positions greening as both a skills development imperative and a catalyst for behavioural change, enabling colleges to become role models for sustainability and contributors to regional development.

t: The impact of work integrated learning on student work readiness: Final report
c: Smith, C., Ferns, S. and Russell, L. (2014) The impact of work integrated learning on student work readiness: Final report. Sydney: Office for Learning and Teaching.
s:
This report investigates how work integrated learning (WIL) influences student work readiness across Australian universities. 

It draws on five linked studies that examine placements and simulations, comparing their respective contributions to employability. 

The research shows that WIL has a clear and measurable impact on students’ professional capability, confidence and ability to apply theory in practice. 

Placement based WIL consistently produces stronger outcomes than simulation, although both contribute to employability. 

The report identifies six dimensions of work readiness: professional practice, integration of theory and practice, lifelong learning, collaboration, informed decision making and commencement readiness. 

High quality WIL depends on authenticity, structured preparation, supervision, aligned assessment and facilitated reflection. 

Employers confirm that WIL improves communication, self awareness, motivation and adherence to professional standards. 

The report recommends embedding WIL across curricula, strengthening partnerships with industry and developing national benchmarks for employability. 

It concludes that WIL is a critical mechanism for producing graduates who can transition effectively into the labour market.

t: The African Journal for Work Based Learning, Volume 4
c: Brink, R. (2015) The African Journal for Work Based Learning, Volume 4. Johannesburg: Southern African Society for Cooperative Education.
s:
This journal issue provides an overview of work based learning developments in South Africa, with a strong focus on the role of work integrated learning in strengthening employability and improving the relevance of technical and vocational education. 

It highlights the growing national and international recognition of WIL as a core component of effective skills development and presents contributions from practitioners, researchers and industry partners. 

The foreword emphasises the importance of aligning human capital needs with graduate readiness and notes the increasing policy attention given to WIL. 

Articles in the issue examine the state of WIL in the TVET sector, employer perspectives, partnership models, workplace learning in specialised fields and comparative international practices. 

Across these contributions, the journal underscores the need for stronger collaboration between education institutions and employers, improved workplace exposure for students and more coherent national frameworks to support WIL. 

It positions work based learning as essential for bridging the gap between institutional learning and labour market expectations.

t: Guidelines for a just transition towards environmentally sustainable economies and societies for all
c: International Labour Organization (2015) Guidelines for a just transition towards environmentally sustainable economies and societies for all. Geneva: ILO.
s:
These ILO guidelines set out a global policy framework for achieving a just transition to environmentally sustainable economies and societies. 

They emphasise that decent work, social inclusion and environmental sustainability must be pursued together and anchored in the Decent Work Agenda. 

They outline a shared vision in which the greening of economies becomes a driver of job creation, poverty reduction and resilience. 

The guidelines identify major opportunities, including new employment in sustainable sectors, improved job quality and greater social inclusion, alongside challenges such as economic restructuring, job displacement and rising costs for vulnerable households. 

They also present core principles for managing the transition, including strong social dialogue, respect for rights at work, gender-responsive policies and coherent economic, social and environmental strategies. 

They define key policy areas such as macroeconomic planning, industrial policy, enterprise support, skills development, social protection and active labour market measures. 

The guidelines stress that countries must tailor approaches to their own contexts and that cooperation between governments, employers and workers is essential for effective implementation.

t: The relationship between work readiness skills, career self efficacy and career exploration among engineering graduates: A proposed framework
c: Makki, B.I., Salleh, R., Memon, M.A. and Harun, H. (2015) The relationship between work readiness skills, career self efficacy and career exploration among engineering graduates: A proposed framework. Research Journal of Applied Sciences, Engineering and Technology, 10(9), pp. 1007–1011.
s:
This article proposes a conceptual framework linking work readiness skills, career self efficacy and career exploration among engineering graduates. 

It argues that rapid industrial and technological change requires graduates to possess a broad set of employability skills beyond technical knowledge, including higher order thinking, communication, teamwork and personal qualities. 

The authors note that Malaysian employers report persistent skills gaps and low confidence among graduates entering the labour market. 

Drawing on existing models, the paper groups work readiness skills into three domains: personal qualities and people skills, professional knowledge and skills and technology related skills. 

It suggests that these domains influence career self efficacy, which in turn affects graduates’ willingness and ability to explore career options. 

The proposed framework positions self efficacy as a mediating factor that shapes how graduates translate their skills into proactive career behaviour. 

The authors recommend empirical testing of the model and highlight its potential value for curriculum design, graduate assessment and targeted interventions to strengthen work readiness.

t: Energy2Equal Africa: Women’s participation in the renewable energy workforce in Sub Saharan Africa
c: IFC (2015) Energy2Equal Africa: Women’s participation in the renewable energy workforce in Sub Saharan Africa. Washington, DC: International Finance Corporation.
s:
This report examines women’s participation in the renewable energy workforce in Sub Saharan Africa and identifies barriers and opportunities for improving gender equality across the sector. 

It highlights the rapid growth of renewable energy as a major job creator and stresses that women remain under represented, particularly in technical and leadership roles. 

Although women make up around one third of the workforce, they are concentrated in administrative and support functions, with far fewer in STEM and technical positions. 

The study identifies three main barriers: restrictive social norms and stereotypes that limit girls’ access to STEM education, workplace policies that do not support recruitment, retention or advancement of women and legal constraints in some countries that restrict women’s access to industrial jobs. 

Gender diversity strengthens company performance, innovation and resilience and outlines recommendations for companies to improve gender balance, including leadership commitment, gender responsive policies, targeted recruitment, mentoring, training and stronger monitoring. 

Women’s inclusion is essential for a just and inclusive energy transition.

t: Guidelines on mainstreaming gender equality and social inclusion into the National Adaptation Plan process in Viet Nam
c: Department of Climate Change (2025) Guidelines on mainstreaming gender equality and social inclusion into the National Adaptation Plan process in Viet Nam. Hanoi: Ministry of Agriculture and Environment.
s:
This manual provides structured guidance for integrating gender equality and social inclusion (GESI) into Viet Nam’s National Adaptation Plan (NAP) processes. 

Women and vulnerable groups face disproportionate climate risks due to socio economic constraints, limited access to information and traditional gender roles. 

Although Viet Nam’s policy framework increasingly recognises gender responsive adaptation, practical implementation remains uneven across ministries and provinces. 

The manual clarifies key concepts such as gender responsive adaptation, gender sensitive approaches and intersectionality, and outlines international and national mandates that require GESI integration. 

It presents tools and approaches for analysing vulnerabilities, ensuring inclusive participation and embedding GESI considerations into planning, implementation and monitoring. 

The guide details step by step actions for mainstreaming GESI across background assessments, strategy development, implementation and reporting, including the use of gender disaggregated data and tailored indicators. 

Overall, the manual aims to strengthen institutional capacity and ensure that adaptation policies deliver equitable benefits and enhance resilience for all social groups.

t: Policy brief on integrating care work into just transition strategies
c: Bernard, C., Lakshminarayanan, S.N., Bencurikova, S., Prabakaran, V.V. & Perdomenico, J. (2025) Integrating care work into just transition strategies. Policy brief, 13 July. School of Public Affairs, Policy-Making Initiative for Sustainability in partnership with the European Chair for Sustainable Development and Climate Transition, Sciences Po, Paris.
s:
This policy brief argues that a just energy transition cannot succeed without recognising and supporting unpaid care work, which overwhelmingly falls on women. 

It shows that coal transition regions experience severe social impacts such as rising domestic violence, food insecurity and mental health strain, with women absorbing these burdens through unpaid care. 

Because reskilling programmes rarely account for care responsibilities, women are excluded from transition benefits and from emerging opportunities in the renewable energy sector. 

The brief recommends integrating care into Just Energy Transition Partnerships through gender responsive diagnostics, flexible and accessible training, and investment in community care infrastructure. 

International precedents from Spain, Chile and Bolivia demonstrate workable models, including subsidised childcare, after school programmes and care linked stipends. 

South Africa, as the first JETP recipient, faces acute risks due to coal dependency, weak care systems and gender blind reskilling. 

The brief proposes country specific actions: expanding care funding, co locating childcare with training centres, offering care stipends, and embedding care requirements into JETP financing. 

Multi stakeholder collaboration across government, donors, civil society and the private sector is essential to ensure that women can participate fully in the transition.

t: Gender equality and social inclusion in a just energy transition
c: Buchy, M. & Shakya, S. (2023) Gender equality and social inclusion in a just energy transition. T20 Policy Brief, July. International Water Management Institute.
s:
This policy brief examines how gender equality and social inclusion can be embedded in a just energy transition, with a particular focus on South Asia and Nepal. 

Women and marginalised groups experience disproportionate barriers to accessing clean, affordable energy due to entrenched social norms, limited mobility and structural inequalities. 

Energy poverty affects women more severely because of their domestic responsibilities, exposure to harmful fuels and restricted participation in decision-making. 

Gender-blind energy policies overlook intersectional disadvantages linked to caste, ethnicity and economic status, which further restrict access to modern energy services. 

Nepal’s policy landscape demonstrates slow progress in mainstreaming gender equality and social inclusion (GESI), with fragmented implementation and weak accountability. 

The authors argue that inclusive energy transitions require evidence-based policy design, intersectoral collaboration and investment in a diverse workforce capable of addressing both technological and social challenges. 

They recommend that the G20 promote gender-responsive energy governance, strengthen institutional capacity and support educational reforms that encourage women and underrepresented groups to enter science and engineering fields.

t: Just transition in South Africa: the case for a gender just approach
c: Maseko, N. (2021) Just transition in South Africa: the case for a gender just approach. TIPS Policy Brief 4/2021, June. Trade & Industrial Policy Strategies, Pretoria.
s:
This policy brief argues that South Africa’s transition to a green economy will remain unjust unless it intentionally addresses the structural gender inequalities that shape women’s economic participation. 

Women perform most unpaid care work, are overrepresented in low paid and informal sectors and face higher vulnerability to climate impacts due to limited access to income, assets and decision making spaces. 

Climate related shocks increase unpaid care burdens, reduce women’s ability to seek paid work and heighten exposure to violence during displacement. 

This brief shows that South African women, particularly black women, experience intersecting disadvantages linked to race, geography, contract precarity and limited access to social protection. 

A gender just transition therefore requires deliberate measures to redistribute care work, expand access to childcare, strengthen anti discrimination legislation and ensure women’s inclusion in green sector employment beyond administrative roles. 

It also calls for targeted training in technical fields, improved access to funding and mentorship and structural reforms to address gender segmentation in STEM. 

Without these interventions, the green transition risks reproducing existing inequalities rather than transforming them.

t: A just transition or just a transition: making the case for women in energy
c: Jreich, R. (2024) A just transition or just a transition: making the case for women in energy. RES4Africa Foundation, Rome.
s:
This report argues that the global energy transition will not be just unless women are fully included as beneficiaries, workers, entrepreneurs and decision makers. 

It highlights persistent gender gaps across five dimensions: energy access, education, employment and leadership, entrepreneurship and the policy environment. 

Despite global commitments such as the COP28 Gender Responsive Just Transitions and Climate Action Partnership, women continue to face unequal access to modern energy services, limited representation in STEM fields and low participation in the energy workforce, particularly in technical and leadership roles. 

Energy poverty, conflict, climate shocks and economic crises disproportionately affect women and girls, deepening existing inequalities. 

The report calls for a shift from viewing women solely as end users to recognising them as active agents in energy planning, rural electrification and innovation. 

Multi stakeholder approaches are emphasised, including gender responsive policies, targeted skills development, improved access to finance for women led enterprises and stronger institutional mechanisms for gender mainstreaming. 

The report concludes that without deliberate action, the energy transition risks reinforcing structural inequalities rather than delivering a genuinely just transition.

t: A just transition or just a transition: making the case for women in energy – infographics
c: RES4Africa Foundation (2024) A just transition or just a transition: making the case for women in energy – infographics. RES4Africa Foundation, Rome.
s:
This infographic report highlights the persistent gender gaps across Africa’s energy sector and argues that women’s full participation is essential for a just energy transition. 

It shows that women continue to bear the brunt of energy poverty, limiting their time for education and income generating activities. 

Expanding decentralised renewable energy is presented as a key opportunity to improve women’s wellbeing and create new economic pathways. 

The report illustrates the severe underrepresentation of women in STEM fields, technical roles and senior management, despite growing demand for skills in renewable energy. 

It also notes that women led enterprises remain a minority, particularly in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region, where structural barriers restrict entrepreneurship. 

Policy measures are identified as critical drivers for gender responsive energy transitions, including mainstreaming gender in energy planning, linking electrification to wider development programmes and ensuring women’s participation in decision making. 

The report concludes that multi stakeholder approaches are required to promote women as end users, workers, entrepreneurs and leaders, ensuring that the transition is genuinely just rather than reinforcing existing inequalities.

t: Women led coal transitions: background brief. Climate Investment Funds
c: Kolybashkina, N. & Kanter, E. (2024) Women led coal transitions: background brief. Climate Investment Funds, Washington DC.
s:
This background brief explains why coal transition planning must explicitly address gender inequality and strengthen women’s leadership. 

It shows that women experience the social, economic and environmental impacts of coal phase outs more severely due to existing structural inequalities. 

Women are concentrated in informal and low paid mining related work, making them ineligible for formal compensation, retraining or social protection when mines close. 

Mine closures increase women’s unpaid care work, reduce income security and heighten exposure to gender based violence. 

Renewable energy investments can also disadvantage women through land loss, disrupted livelihoods and reduced access to services. 

Women remain largely absent from decision making in coal transition processes, resulting in gender blind policies that fail to address their needs. 

The Women Led Coal Transitions (WOLCOT) mechanism seeks to correct this by promoting women’s leadership at community, employment and entrepreneurship levels. 

It adopts a transformative, intersectional approach to build women’s agency, skills and influence in transition planning. 

The brief outlines the benefits of women’s leadership and identifies key action pillars to close leadership gaps and ensure coal transitions are equitable and effective.

t: Electricity privatisation vs just energy transition in South Africa: A critical analysis
c: Bantsijang, M. (2025) Electricity privatisation vs just energy transition in South Africa: A critical analysis. Unpublished manuscript.
s:
This paper analyses the tension between electricity privatisation and a just energy transition in South Africa, arguing that neither approach alone can address the country’s structural energy, social and economic challenges. 

It outlines the perceived benefits of privatisation, including improved efficiency, reduced political interference and increased investment, but highlights significant risks such as higher consumer costs, deepening inequality, job losses and weakened social responsibility. 

In contrast, the just energy transition framework prioritises climate action, economic diversification, energy security and social equity, particularly for coal dependent communities. 

The paper stresses that although a just transition offers long term sustainability, it faces barriers including high upfront costs, social disruption and the need for equitable benefit distribution. 

A balanced approach is proposed, centred on community participation, transparency and deliberate measures to reduce inequality. 

The author concludes calling for an energy future that safeguards vulnerable communities while ensuring reliable, affordable supply and supporting South Africa’s climate commitments.

t: Just energy transition in Africa: Towards social inclusion and environmental rights based imperatives
c: Agbaitoro, G.A. and Ekhator, E.O. (2025) Just energy transition in Africa: Towards social inclusion and environmental rights based imperatives. Business and Human Rights Journal, 10(1), 34–55.
s:
The article examines how African countries can pursue a just energy transition by embedding social inclusion and an environmental rights based approach into policy and practice. 

It argues that although energy transition is essential for climate goals, many African communities hosting energy projects experience exclusion, rights violations and unequal distribution of benefits. 

The authors note that social inclusion requires early and meaningful participation of local communities, recognition of their land and resource rights and protection from negative socio economic impacts. 

They show that several African states, including Kenya, South Africa and Nigeria, have introduced transition related laws and policies, yet gaps remain in community engagement and accountability. 

The article also emphasises the value of environmental rights as a tool for addressing injustices linked to renewable energy projects, noting the growing use of litigation by communities to challenge harmful practices. 

It concludes that a just transition in Africa depends on strong legal frameworks, transparent governance, corporate responsibility and institutional capacity that centres the needs and rights of vulnerable groups.

t: Delayed retirement and digitalization drive energy efficiency in China’s low carbon transition
c: Wang Y and Sun M (2026) Delayed retirement and digitalization drive energy efficiency in China’s low carbon transition. Academia Green Energy, 3. https://doi.org/10.20935/AcadEnergy8214
s:
The paper examines how China’s delayed retirement policy and rapid digitalisation jointly improve operational energy efficiency across buildings, transport depots and the steel industry. 

It argues that demographic change, particularly the retention of experienced workers after 2025, enhances the effectiveness of digital tools such as building management systems, energy management systems and digital process twins. 

These workers reduce manual overrides, improve tuning and strengthen the application of digital controls. 

Digital platforms in turn deliver measurable efficiency gains, including 5–20% energy savings in buildings, 15–30% peak-load reduction in transport depots and 15–20% reductions in unit energy consumption in hydrogen ready DRI EAF steel pilots. 

The study proposes a D3 framework linking demography, digitalisation and decarbonisation, showing that operational improvements can be achieved at near zero capital cost by converting demographic pressure into human capital assets. 

It concludes that aligning retirement reform with pricing mechanisms and digital infrastructure development can support energy security and accelerate China’s low carbon transition.

t: Power system stability enhancement using wind battery hybrids in the GADA Special Economic Zone
c: Gebre, MT and Biru, G (2026) Power system stability enhancement using wind battery hybrids in the GADA Special Economic Zone. Academia Green Energy, 3. https://doi.org/10.20935/AcadEnergy8129
s:
This paper investigates how a hybrid power system combining grid supply, a 42 MW wind farm and a 40 MW battery can improve voltage and frequency stability in Ethiopia’s GADA Special Economic Zone. 

The study responds to persistent reliability challenges in Ethiopia’s power system, where industries face outages, voltage instability and dependence on diesel backup. 

Using MATLAB and DigSILENT modelling, the authors test system behaviour under grid faults, wind generation drops and sudden load changes. 

Results show that grid only and grid wind configurations experience significant instability during grid faults, leading to load disconnection. By contrast, the wind battery grid hybrid maintains stability by supplying 61.3 MW from wind and storage while shedding non critical loads to protect system frequency and voltage. 

During wind faults, the grid meets full demand without disconnections, and under 50 percent load reduction the system rebalances power flows effectively. 

The findings demonstrate that hybrid systems enhance resilience, support critical loads and offer a practical pathway for industrial zones in emerging economies to strengthen energy security.

t: South Africa’s Industrial Development Strategy
c: Department of Trade, Industry and Competition (2026) South Africa’s Industrial Development Strategy. Pretoria: the dtic.
s:
South Africa’s Industrial Development Strategy sets out a coordinated plan to reverse de industrialisation, strengthen productive capacity and position the economy for long term competitiveness. 

It responds to global shifts driven by climate change, supply chain reconfiguration and digitalisation, while addressing domestic constraints such as weak growth, declining investment, and infrastructure backlogs. 

The strategy is built around three pathways: decarbonisation, diversification, and digitalisation. 

Decarbonisation focuses on securing affordable energy, scaling renewables, reforming energy intensive value chains, and leveraging critical minerals for green technologies. 

Diversification aims to expand value added production in agriculture, health industries, services, and advanced manufacturing, supported by regional integration through the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). 

Digitalisation promotes productivity through expanded ICT infrastructure, automation and strengthened science and innovation systems. 

Enablers include improved logistics, SEZ reform, regulatory efficiency, blended finance and targeted incentives linked to measurable outcomes. 

The strategy emphasises coordinated implementation, institutional capability and partnerships with business and labour to drive investment, job creation and export growth.

t: Research Agenda 2023–2028

s:
The DHET Research Agenda 2023–2028 sets out the Department’s priority research needs to strengthen the Post School Education and Training system. 

It positions research as essential for improving policy, planning and institutional performance across universities, TVET colleges and CET colleges, as well as SETAs and quality assurance bodies. 

The Agenda outlines six focus areas: system integration, expanded access, responsiveness to labour market needs, stronger links between education and work, improved quality, and enhanced efficiency. 

It highlights the need for evidence to support articulation pathways, curriculum relevance, lecturer development, student success and the alignment of programmes with economic demand. 

The Agenda emphasises partnerships between researchers, institutions and government to maximise limited resources and ensure research informs policy decisions. 

It also stresses the importance of addressing barriers to access, improving workplace based learning, strengthening governance and enhancing the quality of teaching and learning. 

In essence, the Agenda aims to guide coordinated research that supports a more inclusive, effective and responsive PSET system.

t: Vocational education and training (VET), green and STEM jobs: Insights from job vacancy data
c: OECD (2026) Vocational education and training (VET), green and STEM jobs: Insights from job vacancy data. Paris: OECD Publishing.
s:
This OECD paper analyses how vocational education and training contributes to skills supply for green and STEM jobs in Australia, Canada and the United Kingdom. 

Using online job vacancy data, it examines employer demand, qualification requirements and the extent to which green roles rely on STEM knowledge. 

The study finds strong overlap between green and STEM occupations, with many green jobs requiring advanced technical skills. 

Demand for green jobs is growing, although they remain a small share of total vacancies. 

Employers value VET pathways differently across countries, and apprenticeships play a varied role in meeting green and STEM labour needs. 

The paper highlights that VET systems must update curricula, strengthen green competences and expand upskilling opportunities to address skills gaps. 

It also identifies the need for clearer skill signalling, better alignment between VET qualifications and emerging green requirements and stronger use of apprenticeships as inclusive pathways into technical green roles. 

The findings underscore the importance of targeted reskilling to support workers affected by the transition and ensure a skilled workforce for low carbon industries.

t: Energy Performance Certificate Guideline
c: South African National Energy Development Institute (SANEDI) (2022) Energy Performance Certificate Guideline. Sandton: SANEDI.
s:
The EPC Guideline is a quick and easy referencing guide, compiled from various regulations and acts. The EPC Guideline aims to support accounting officers and building owners by explaining South Africa’s approach to energy efficiency. It outlines relevant energy efficiency regulations, details the national Energy Performance Label for Buildings, explains building classification, describes how to assess and measure a building’s energy use, clarifies the Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) process, addresses issues related to non-compliance and sets out the requirements for certificate display and validity.

The EPC Guideline sets out a clear, step by step compliance process through which South African buildings can get Energy Performance Certificates (EPC). 

The guideline establishes a national standard for building energy consumption and encourages greater energy efficiency throughout the built environment.

The guideline explains who is required to comply, outlines the responsibilities of the South African National Energy Development Institute (SANEDI) and the South African National Accreditation System (SANAS), and specifies the data and measurements needed. 

It also details the seven-grade energy performance scale, which is measured in kilowatt hours per square metre per year (kWh/m² per year).

The guideline makes the building owner or accounting officer responsible for registering the building on the National Building Energy Performance Register and for supplying accurate energy data to a SANAS accredited inspection body which conducts the assessment. 

The guideline clarifies how to measure the net floor area, adjust for spaces that are not in use, include all types of energy sources, convert fuel usage into kilowatt hours, and apply reference values from SANS 10400 XA to assess a building’s energy performance.

The process culminates in a printed certificate that must be displayed at the building entrance and uploaded to the national register; certificates are valid for five years and non compliance carries significant penalties.
