t: Green Hydrogen Training: Module 1: Introduction
c: GIZ International PtX Hub 2024, Renewable Power to X Training: Module 1 Introduction, GIZ, Berlin.
s:
This introduces learners to why Renewable Power to X (technology) is central to global decarbonisation and the just energy transition. 

It explains that increasing greenhouse gas emissions, escalating climate impacts and the economic cost of inaction create an urgent need to shift from fossil fuels to renewable energy carriers. 

PtX enables the conversion of renewable electricity into green hydrogen and synthetic fuels for sectors that cannot electrify directly, such as heavy industry, aviation and shipping. 

The module stresses the scale of current emissions, the role of energy efficiency and the need for renewable electricity expansion to meet future hydrogen demand. 

It also introduces sustainability considerations, including environmental, social and governance dimensions that shape responsible PtX deployment. 

PtX is a strategic pathway for moving and industrial systems away from fossil fuel based energy, supporting economic resilience and enabling countries to participate in emerging green value chains. 

This introduction prepares learners to understand PtX technologies, markets and policy frameworks in later modules.

t: Green Hydrogen Training: Module 2: Production Pathways
c: International PtX Hub and GIZ (2024) Green Hydrogen Training: Module 2: Production Pathways. Berlin: International PtX Hub/GIZ.
s:
Module 2 of the Renewable PtX Training outlines production pathways for renewable Power to X with a focus on hydrogen production, carbon sourcing and downstream synthesis routes. 

The module explains electrolysis technologies (alkaline, AEM, PEM and SOEC) and compares their operating temperatures, efficiencies, pressures and material constraints. 

It describes the colour coding of hydrogen including green, grey, blue and turquoise variants and presents lifecycle considerations for blue hydrogen. 

The simplified PtX value chain is mapped from renewable power and carbon inputs through electrolysis and synthesis to fuels and chemicals, and details carbon sourcing options such as biogenic streams and direct air capture with associated cost considerations. 

Technical system elements and balance of plant for alkaline electrolysers are shown alongside water use metrics and technology readiness notes. 

The module also presents synthesis processes including methanation, Fischer Tropsch and Haber Bosch for methanol ammonia and synthetic hydrocarbons, and it outlines project development steps from feasibility and permitting through front end engineering, EPCM and operations.

t: Green Hydrogen Training: Module 3 - Economics
c: GIZ & International PtX Hub 2024, Renewable PtX Training: Module 3 – Economics, Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit, 7 February.
s:
Module 3 outlines the economics of Renewable PtX, focusing on cost drivers for green hydrogen and the factors shaping future competitiveness. 

It explains how renewable energy costs have declined sharply, with global weighted average LCOE for utility scale solar PV falling from 0.417 USD/kWh in 2010 to 0.048 USD/kWh in 2021, and onshore wind decreasing by 68% over the same period. 

Regions with strong wind and solar resources can achieve hydrogen production costs below USD 1.5/kg by 2030. 

It classifies LCOH cost drivers, noting the influence of electricity prices, capital expenditure (CAPEX), full load hours, electrolyser efficiency and financing conditions. 

Electrolyser CAPEX remains a major component but could fall by 60–70% by 2030 as manufacturing capacity expands and learning curves accelerate. Material requirements differ across alkaline, Proton Exchange Membrane Electrolysis (PEM) and Solid Oxide Electrolysis Cell (SOEC) technologies, with implications for supply risk and diversification. 

Economic viability depends on low cost renewable electricity, reduced electrolyser costs, high operating hours and effective transport and storage solutions.

t: Green Hydrogen Training: Module 4 –  Infrastructure
c: GIZ International PtX Hub 2024, Green Hydrogen Training: Module 4 – Infrastructure, Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit, viewed 2024.
s:
Module 4 focuses on how Power to X products move from production sites to end users. 

It explains the role of hydrogen as a feedstock and energy carrier, then examines transport options over different distances, including pipelines, liquefied hydrogen, ammonia and liquid organic hydrogen carriers. 

These carriers are compared in terms of energy losses, storage density, conversion and reconversion needs, as well as technological maturity and cost implications. 

The module also draws attention to how global hydrogen and ammonia trade is expected to grow, with seaborne shipping and long-distance pipelines enabling large scale flows between regions. 

It links this to the wider carbon cycle, emphasising closed renewable loops that avoid tapping fossil carbon. 

Significant new infrastructure, retrofitting of existing assets and careful choice of carriers will be essential to support a just transition to low carbon fuels across industry, power and mobility.

t: Green Hydrogen Training: Module 5 Demand and Markets
c: International PtX Hub and GIZ (2024) Renewable PtX Green Hydrogen Training: Module 5 Demand and Markets. Berlin: International PtX Hub/GIZ.
s:
This is the presentation that accompanies Module 5 of the Renewable PtX Training which deals with market demand and use cases for green hydrogen and Power to X (renewable energy) products and links those market signals to skills and training priorities. 

The module explains that current hydrogen use is limited and concentrated in oil refining and ammonia production.  

However, projections show substantial growth by 2050 with industry as the main user. 

It maps PtX opportunities such as green methanol, green ammonia, sustainable aviation fuel and green steel, and assesses competitiveness using electricity costs, technology readiness and marginal abatement cost curves. 

The module looks at with “no regret” applications where hydrogen is clearly competitive and compares them with low value uses.

t: Green Hydrogen Training: Module 6 -  Sustainability Criteria for Renewable PtX
c: GIZ International PtX Hub 2024, Renewable PtX Training: Module 6 – Sustainability Criteria for Renewable PtX, Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit, 7 February.
s:
Module 6 introduces sustainability as a core requirement for Renewable PtX and explains how the EESG framework guides responsible development. 

It traces the evolution of sustainability from early ecological concepts to broader social and economic dimensions, highlighting frameworks such as Doughnut Economics and the SDGs. 


PtX strategies must align with national climate commitments while managing risks such as water scarcity, land use conflicts, ecosystem impacts, corruption and energy poverty. 

It outlines opportunities for local value creation, skills development and improved energy access. 

The EESG framework is described as four dimensions: environmental (renewable electricity, carbon cycles, water use, land impacts, biodiversity and critical raw materials); social (human rights, labour standards, jobs and a just transition); economic (decoupled growth, innovation and circularity); and governance (transparency, participation and the rule of law).

The module stresses that PtX sustainability must be assessed at policy, production and product levels using tools such as standards, certification and due diligence.

t: PtX Training – Deep Dive: Green Shipping,
c: GIZ International PtX Hub 2024, PtX Training – Deep Dive: Green Shipping, Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit, viewed 2024.
s:
The Deep Dive into green shipping outlines the scale of global maritime activity and the urgent need to decarbonise a sector that responsible for 3% of global emissions. 

It emphasises the ageing fleet, rising greenhouse gas output and the regulatory measures introduced through the International Maritime Organisation (IMO), International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships (MARPOL) and regional systems such as the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS). 

The training addresses the shift from fossil fuels to alternative marine fuels including green methanol, ammonia and hydrogen, noting their different energy densities, safety profiles and emissions.

It shows how shipping and hydrogen production are interdependent, with ports positioned as critical hubs for future green fuel supply. 

The training also looks at South Africa’s potential role as a producer of green shipping fuels, supported by strong renewable resources and targeted PtX Hub initiatives. 

Planned studies, training programmes and stakeholder engagement aim to build capacity, assess port infrastructure and identify opportunities for zero carbon bunker fuels.

t: Career opportunities in the energy and water sectors
c: Energy and Water Sector Education and Training Authority (EWSETA) 2022, Career opportunities in the energy and water sectors, EWSETA, Johannesburg.
s:
The EWSETA Career Opportunities in the Energy and Water Sectors guide introduces a wide range of green careers essential to South Africa’s transition to a sustainable and climate resilient economy. 

Green jobs reduce environmental harm, improve resource efficiency and support adaptation to climate impacts. 

The shift to a greener economy requires new and upgraded skills across energy, water and environmental fields. 

It outlines career pathways in air quality management, climate science, soil science, hydrology, hydrogeology, water treatment, wastewater operations, plumbing, irrigation and water governance. 

Each role is described in terms of core functions, required competencies, study routes and typical employers, with strong emphasis on scientific, technical and analytical skills. 

The guide stresses that skills shortages in renewable energy, environmental services and water management present opportunities for young people entering the labour market. 

Green careers are vital for protecting ecosystems, ensuring sustainable water supply, improving environmental health and enabling a just energy transition that supports inclusive development.

t: Solar PV installation guidelines
c: SAPVIA. (2017) . Johannesburg: South African Photovoltaic Industry Association.
s:
The Solar PV Installation Guidelines provide a comprehensive technical framework to support safe, standardised and high quality solar PV installations in South Africa. 

Developed with international partners, the guidelines respond to the rapid growth of small scale embedded generation and the need for consistent installation practices. 

They outline the fundamentals of electricity, PV components, system design and sizing, and the operational behaviour of solar technologies under real conditions. 

The guidelines emphasise the importance of certified components, accurate yield assessments and proper mechanical and electrical installation techniques. 

They also highlight legal requirements, including compliance with national electrical codes and grid connection standards. 

The guidelines align with the National Solar PV Service Technician Qualification and aim to strengthen installer competence through structured training and adherence to best practice. 

They further address safety considerations, working at heights, commissioning, documentation and ongoing maintenance. 

The guidelines support the professionalisation of the PV sector and contributes to a reliable, safe and scalable solar industry that underpins South Africa’s transition to cleaner energy.

t: Criteria and guidelines for the implementation of Artisan Recognition of Prior Learning
c: Department of Higher Education and Training (2016) Criteria and guidelines for the implementation of Artisan Recognition of Prior Learning. Pretoria: Government Printer.
s:
The Criteria and Guidelines for the Implementation of Artisan Recognition of Prior Learning ARPL) set out a national framework to support experienced workers to gain access to a trade test through a structured, fair and quality assured process. 

They position ARPL as a developmental pathway that broadens access for non contracted candidates in both formal and informal sectors. 

They establish standardised admission requirements, including a minimum of three years verifiable workplace experience, and outline the responsibilities of DHET, QCTO, NAMB, accredited Trade Test Centres as well as Skills Development Providers. 

The guidelines define the evaluation process, which includes compiling a portfolio of evidence, theoretical and practical assessments, workplace observation and gap closure where required.

A readiness grid guides decisions on whether candidates may proceed to a trade test or need further development. 

The framework aims to strengthen artisan development, improve consistency across sectors and ensure credible assessment practices that support national skills priorities.

t: PV GreenCard user manual
c: South African Photovoltaic Industry Association (SAPVIA) 2020 PV GreenCard user manual. SAPVIA, Johannesburg.
s:
This manual guides solar PV installation companies to register, manage profiles and complete PV GreenCard documentation within the SAPVIA system. 

It outlines the online company registration process, including data entry, annual payment and uploading required certificates. 

Administrators can add or remove installers, with each installer receiving system generated login details. 

The manual provides detailed guidance on completing the PV GreenCard form, which requires full completion of system information, components, design and documentation before submission. 

Administrators review submitted cards, pay the processing fee and release the document to customers for approval. 

Customer sign off determines whether the installation receives a green or red status. 

The manual also explains the red card process, where unresolved customer complaints trigger escalation to ECASA for investigation and potential installer deregistration. 

Completed PV GreenCards are stored in the company profile with clear status indicators for draft, submitted, rejected or approved installations.

t: Occupational Certificate: Solar Water Heater Installer. Curriculum Code 642602001
c: Quality Council for Trades and Occupations (QCTO) (n.d.) Occupational Certificate: Solar Water Heater Installer. Curriculum Code 642602001. Pretoria: QCTO.
s:
The curriculum sets out the full occupational requirements for a Solar Water Heater Installer, in terms of the knowledge, practical skills and workplace experience needed to install, test, maintain and repair domestic solar water heating systems of up to 500 litres. 

It defines the occupational purpose, key tasks and contexts, and provides a structured set of modules at NQF Levels 2 to 4. 

Knowledge modules address water behaviour, tools, system types and installation theory, while practical modules develop competence in planning, mounting, pipework, system installation and maintenance. 

Work experience modules ensure exposure to real installations across different configurations, including thermosyphon, pumped, direct and indirect systems. 

The curriculum aligns with national regulations, SANS codes and safety requirements, and emphasises correct system selection, site assessment, risk management and compliance. 

It also outlines accreditation requirements for providers and workplaces. 

The qualification supports progression within the plumbing and related construction occupations and responds to national energy and regulatory drivers that promote renewable water heating technologies.

t: External Assessment Specifications: Occupational Certificate – Solar Water Heater Installer (Curriculum Code 642602001)
c: Quality Council for Trades and Occupations (QCTO) (n.d.) External Assessment Specifications: Occupational Certificate – Solar Water Heater Installer (Curriculum Code 642602001). Pretoria: QCTO.
s:
The External Assessment Specifications (EAS) set out the national requirements for assessing learners completing the Occupational Certificate: Solar Water Heater Installer. 

They define the external assessment model, which combines a written examination and a practical task conducted at an accredited centre in a single working day. 

They outline the qualification purpose, expected occupational outcomes and the assessment standards used to judge competence in planning, installing, testing, repairing and maintaining domestic solar water heating systems up to 500 litres. 

The specifications detail the integrated assessment focus areas, including preparation and planning, system installation and fault diagnosis and repair. 

They also set the criteria for assessor registration, emphasising the need for qualified plumbers with relevant experience and professional registration. 

The EAS confirm that no phase tests, part qualifications or external assignments apply. 

Eligibility for the external assessment requires proof of completed knowledge modules, practical skills modules and a signed Statement of Work Experience. 

Foundational learning competence is mandatory for certification.

t: Curriculum Document: Solar Photovoltaic Service Technician (Curriculum Code 313109000)
c: Quality Council for Trades and Occupations (QCTO) (n.d.) Curriculum Document: Solar Photovoltaic Service Technician (Curriculum Code 313109000). Pretoria: QCTO.
s:
This curriculum sets out the full occupational framework for the Solar Photovoltaic Service Technician: installation, commissioning, maintenance and repair of PV systems across domestic, commercial and utility scale settings. 

It defines the occupational purpose, tasks and contexts for PV installers, mounters and service technicians, and provides a structured set of knowledge, practical skills and work experience modules from NQF Levels 2 to 5. 

Knowledge modules span workplace fundamentals, tools, electrical systems, wiring, protection, renewable energy and detailed PV system components. 

Practical modules develop competence in hazard mitigation, working at height, electrical and mechanical installation, system interconnection and advanced maintenance of panels, inverters, transformers, batteries, cabling and control systems. 

Work experience modules ensure exposure to planning, installation, commissioning and complex diagnostic processes. 

The curriculum also supports multiple part qualifications, enabling progression from PV mounter to installer and service technician. 

It responds to national energy needs by preparing a technically capable workforce able to support safe, compliant and efficient PV deployment.

t: External Assessment Specifications: Solar Photovoltaic Service Technician (Curriculum Code 313109000)
c: Quality Council for Trades and Occupations (QCTO) (n.d.) External Assessment Specifications: Solar Photovoltaic Service Technician (Curriculum Code 313109000). Pretoria: QCTO.
s:
The External Assessment Specifications (EAS) for the Solar Photovoltaic Service Technician qualification set out the national requirements for assessing competence across planning, installation, maintenance and diagnostic functions in PV systems. 

The EAS outline the external integrated assessment model, which combines written and practical tasks conducted in a simulated environment at accredited centres under registered MerSETA assessors. 

They define the qualification’s purpose, describing the technician’s role in maintaining PV systems in line with Department of Energy regulations, isolating systems safely, conducting fault finding and performing repairs across stand alone and PV farm installations. 

The EAS cover planning and preparation, mechanical and electrical installation, as well as advanced maintenance of panels, inverters, transformers, batteries, cabling and control systems. 

Eligibility for assessment include successful completion of all prescribed knowledge modules, practical skills modules and a signed Statement of Work Experience. 

The EAS also set criteria for assessor registration, emphasising technical qualifications, industry experience and assessment competence. 

No external assignments or internal reassessments apply.

t: Skills Programme: Renewable Energy Workshop Assistant (SP 210602)
c: Quality Council for Trades and Occupations (QCTO) (2021) Skills Programme: Renewable Energy Workshop Assistant (SP 210602). Pretoria: QCTO.
s:
The Skills Programme Renewable Energy Workshop Assistant provides foundational technical preparation for learners entering renewable energy occupations. 

It is an NQF Level 4, 24 credit programme delivered over 30 days and designed to support entry into roles such as Solar Photovoltaic Service Technician, Solar Water Heater Installer, Wind Turbine Service Technician and Electrician. 

The programme rationale notes the growing national demand for renewable energy skills and the need to upskill both employed and unemployed individuals, including those previously in low skilled work. 

The curriculum covers introductory renewable energy concepts, legislative and economic frameworks, occupational health and safety, hazard identification, environmental protection and safe working practices. 

Learners develop competence in selecting, using and maintaining hand tools, power tools and measuring instruments, as well as performing marking off, riveting, soldering and lifting tasks. 

Exit outcomes focus on tool selection, preparation, use, maintenance, reporting of defects and safe working conduct. 

Assessment includes written tests, practical tasks and supervised demonstrations, with RPL available for access and credit transfer. 

Successful learners gain employability in the renewable energy sector and may progress to full occupational qualifications.

t: Unit Standard 113890: Design a wind/solar hybrid system
c: South African Qualifications Authority (SAQA) (2018) Unit Standard 113890: Design a wind/solar hybrid system. Pretoria: SAQA.
s:
This unit standard covers the design of a hybrid wind and solar system for use in electrical engineering, construction and renewable energy environments. 

It prepares learners to identify system components, interpret symbols, understand circuit behaviour and construct photovoltaic circuits in a simulated environment. 

learners must analyse wind and solar resource data, adjust data for height, determine available energy and assess compatibility between wind and solar profiles. 

It includes developing daily and annual load profiles and evaluating their suitability for hybrid system design. 

Learners calculate photovoltaic array and wind turbine ratings, test cost effectiveness and refine results through iterative processes. 

Embedded knowledge includes safety precautions, electrical principles, renewable energy system components, data processing and regulatory requirements. 

The unit standard supports mobility within the electrical engineering and construction sectors and contributes to skills development for renewable energy applications. 

It forms part of elective components in NQF Level 4 electrical engineering qualifications and is aligned with national standards and statutory requirements.

t: Unit Standard 113888: Design a stand alone renewable energy system
c: South African Qualifications Authority (2018) Unit Standard 113888: Design a stand alone renewable energy system. Pretoria: SAQA (2018).
s:
This unit standard sets out the competencies required to design a stand alone renewable energy system at NQF Level 4. 

It focuses on the practical and theoretical skills needed to identify electrical symbols and components, understand circuit behaviour, and construct basic photovoltaic circuits in a controlled environment. 

Learners must analyse solar and wind resource data, calculate household or school energy loads and determine appropriate ratings for batteries, solar arrays and wind turbines. 

The standard also covers wire sizing, system losses, seasonal variation and safety requirements aligned with SABS, NRS and the OHS Act. 

Embedded knowledge includes electrical principles, safe working procedures, defect reporting and the operation of renewable energy components. 

The unit standard supports skills development in the renewable energy sector and contributes to mobility and progression within electrical engineering and construction fields. 

It also reinforces problem solving, teamwork, communication and the application of science and technology in safe system design.

t: Advanced Diploma in Mechanical Engineering in Renewable Energy (SAQA ID 101562
c: South African Qualifications Authority (2021) Advanced Diploma in Mechanical Engineering in Renewable Energy (SAQA ID 101562). Pretoria: SAQA.
s:
This qualification provides advanced, industry aligned training in mechanical engineering with a strong focus on renewable energy technologies. 

It equips learners with the theoretical grounding, analytical capability and applied engineering skills required to design, evaluate and optimise wind, solar and biofuel energy systems across utility, commercial and domestic contexts. 

The programme develops competence in engineering mathematics, heat transfer, fluid mechanics, strength of materials and project management, supported by specialised modules in renewable energy technologies. 

Learners gain the ability to diagnose and solve engineering problems, design systems within regulatory and technical constraints, conduct investigations, use modelling tools and communicate effectively in professional environments. 

The qualification responds to South Africa’s transition away from fossil fuel based electricity by preparing technologists with the skills needed for a rapidly expanding renewable energy sector. 

It also provides the educational base for registration with the Engineering Council of South Africa and offers articulation into Level 8 engineering programmes. 

Stakeholder engagement from industry, academia and national bodies ensures relevance to labour market needs.

t: Higher Certificate in Renewable Energy Engineering (SAQA ID 110936)
c: South African Qualifications Authority (2019) Higher Certificate in Renewable Energy Engineering (SAQA ID 110936). Pretoria: SAQA.
s:
The Higher Certificate in Renewable Energy Engineering provides foundational training for learners who aim to support artisans, technicians and engineers in the renewable energy sector. 

It develops pre artisan competence across core areas including solar, wind and hydro systems, electrotechnology, mechanotechnology and renewable energy project work. 

The qualification responds to the rapid expansion of renewable installations across South Africa and the need for better trained assistants who can improve installation quality, safety and system reliability. 

It equips learners with applied knowledge in mathematics, natural science and engineering principles, enabling them to diagnose problems, perform basic design tasks, conduct tests and use modern engineering tools. 

The programme also builds communication, ethical awareness and an understanding of the societal and environmental impacts of renewable energy. 

Successful learners can progress into employment as assistants in installation, design, manufacturing, energy surveying and general electrical work, or articulate into engineering diplomas and degrees. 

The qualification strengthens the skills pipeline for the just energy transition by improving technical capability at entry level and supporting wider uptake of renewable energy systems.

t: Unit Standard 113869: Fault find a photovoltaic supplied system
c: South African Qualifications Authority (2018) Unit Standard 113869: Fault find a photovoltaic supplied system. Pretoria: SAQA. (2018)
s:
A learner credited with this unit standard can plan, prepare, fault find and maintain a stand alone photovoltaic system in line with statutory requirements and workplace procedures. 

The standard focuses on safe isolation, interpretation of electrical drawings and the correct use of testing instruments and tools. 

Learners must identify faults logically, repair them safely and restore systems to operational condition while complying with the OHS Act, SABS and NRS standards. 

The unit standard also emphasises accurate reporting, quality checks and responsible housekeeping. 

It supports skills development in the electrical engineering environment by strengthening competence in maintenance planning, system diagnostics and safe operational practices. 

The outcome contributes to improved reliability of small scale renewable energy systems and supports broader workforce readiness for the growing photovoltaic sector.

t: Unit Standard 113892: Design a solar pump system
c: South African Qualifications Authority (2018) Unit Standard 113892: Design a solar pump system. Pretoria: SAQA.
s:
This unit standard sets out the competencies required to design a solar pump system for use in electrical engineering and construction settings. 

It covers the identification of symbols and components, the functioning of circuits and the ability to sketch and construct renewable energy circuits. 

Learners must calculate loads for typical solar applications, assess solar and wind resources and determine appropriate ratings for battery banks, solar arrays and wind turbines. 

The standard also requires accurate selection of wire sizes in line with NRS and SABS specifications. 

Embedded knowledge includes safety procedures, electrical principles, renewable energy components and relevant statutory requirements. 

The unit standard supports skills development for renewable energy applications and contributes to mobility within the sector. 

It forms part of qualifications at NQF Level 4 and is delivered by accredited providers across South Africa.

t: Unit Standard 116678: Install and maintain a solar hot water system
c: South African Qualifications Authority (2018) Unit Standard 116678: Install and maintain a solar hot water system. Pretoria: SAQA.
s:
This unit standard sets out the competencies required to install, connect, service and maintain solar hot water systems in compliance with statutory, manufacturer and work site requirements. 

It trains learners to plan installations by interpreting job instructions, drawings and safety procedures, and to select appropriate tools, equipment and personal protective equipment. 

Learners prepare the work area, inspect components, identify hazards and coordinate with other trades before installation. 

They must install the solar water heater, mounting bracket and peripheral equipment correctly, ensuring correct orientation and adherence to operational and safety standards. 

The unit standard also covers the connection of associated electrical devices, including pumps and valves, and the safe use of tools and protective equipment. 

Maintenance tasks include isolation, inspection, cleaning, repair and replacement of components, followed by correct disposal of waste, restoration of the work area and completion of records. 

The standard supports skills development in renewable energy installation and contributes to workforce readiness in the transition to sustainable energy technologies.

t: Unit Standard 244499: Install and maintain solar water heating systems
c: South African Qualifications Authority (2018) Unit Standard 244499: Install and maintain solar water heating systems. Pretoria: SAQA.
s:
This unit standard defines the competencies required to install and maintain solar water heating systems within the plumbing and building construction environment. 

It trains learners to understand solar energy as a heat source, identify system components and plan installations in line with drawings, specifications and statutory requirements. 

Learners must size systems correctly, assess roof structures, consider climatic conditions and understand the effects of water quality on system performance. 

The standard covers the installation of solar collectors, cylinders, pipes and fittings across various roof types, including the use of heat transfer fluids, pressure testing and commissioning. 

Maintenance tasks include identifying faults, repairing or replacing components and ensuring systems operate within manufacturer and industry codes of practice. 

Embedded knowledge includes plumbing principles, safety procedures, regulatory frameworks and the characteristics of solar heating technologies. 

The unit standard supports skills development for the renewable energy and plumbing sectors and contributes to workforce readiness for expanding solar water heating applications.

t: Unit Standard 258926: Inspect service and maintain a photovoltaic supplied pump
c: South African Qualifications Authority (2018) Unit Standard 258926: Inspect service and maintain a photovoltaic supplied pump. Pretoria: SAQA.
s:
This unit standard outlines the competencies required to inspect, service and maintain a stand alone photovoltaic supplied pump. 

It sets out the knowledge and practical skills needed to plan, prepare and carry out maintenance activities in line with workplace procedures, manufacturers’ specifications and relevant safety legislation. 

Learners must understand task instructions, select appropriate personal protective equipment and identify correct cleaning materials, solvents and tools. 

The standard emphasises safe isolation and lockout of photovoltaic components before work begins. 

It details the inspection, cleaning, repair and replacement of components such as batteries, regulators, inverters and pumps, as well as the correct handling, storage and disposal of solvents and defective parts. 

Accurate recording and reporting of defects, housekeeping and re energising procedures form part of the concluding activities. 

The unit standard supports skills development in the renewable energy sector by promoting safe, competent maintenance of photovoltaic pumping systems.

t: Unit Standard 258927: Install and commission photovoltaic supplied water pump
c: South African Qualifications Authority (2018) Unit Standard 258927: Install and commission photovoltaic supplied water pump. Pretoria: SAQA.
s:
This unit standard sets out the competencies required to install, connect and commission a photovoltaic supplied water pump. 

It covers the interpretation of job instructions and electrical drawings, the selection and inspection of tools, equipment and personal protective equipment, and the application of statutory and work site safety procedures. 

Learners must identify and prepare the pump, photovoltaic array, mounting structures and associated electronic control devices in line with manufacturer specifications. 

The standard details the correct installation, connection and testing of DC and single phase inverter supplied pumps, including the safe use of measuring instruments such as multimeters, insulation testers and clip on ammeters. 

It also requires learners to conduct functional tests, apply fault finding procedures and verify that the system operates to required performance standards. 

Completion activities include restoring the work area, caring for tools, reporting defects and recording test results. 

The unit standard supports skills development in renewable energy installation and contributes to safe, compliant deployment of photovoltaic pumping systems.

t: Unit Standard 262784: Mount solar water heating system
c: South African Qualifications Authority (2018) Unit Standard 262784: Mount solar water heating system. Pretoria: SAQA.
s:
This unit standard sets out the knowledge and practical skills required to mount a solar water heating system under the supervision of a qualified plumber. 

To ensure safe and compliant installation, it covers the theory of solar water heating technologies, including system types, configurations and associated risks. 

Learners must understand roof truss structures, relevant building regulations and safety legislation, and apply this knowledge when preparing roofs for installation. 

The standard details the selection and correct use of hand and power tools, personal protective equipment and installation materials. 

It also outlines the steps for positioning, assembling and securing system components across different roof types, filling collectors and heat exchangers with appropriate fluids, installing controls and conducting pressure tests. 

Emphasis is placed on following plumber instructions, complying with SANS codes and ensuring safe, efficient system operation. 

The unit standard supports skills development in renewable energy technologies and contributes to the expansion of solar water heating capacity.

t: National Certificate: Electrical Engineering (SAQA ID 72051)
c: South African Qualifications Authority (2019) National Certificate: Electrical Engineering (SAQA ID 72051). Pretoria: SAQA.
s:
This qualification provides the intermediate knowledge and practical skills required to work effectively in electrical engineering environments at NQF Level 3. 

It equips learners to install, commission, maintain and repair electrical equipment and integrated circuits while applying scientific and technological principles. 

The qualification strengthens understanding of safety, health, environmental and quality systems and prepares learners to work without direct supervision. 

It supports mobility across sectors such as manufacturing, energy, mining, chemical and transport, and enables progression toward more advanced electrical occupations. 

Learners develop competence in interpreting drawings, constructing basic electronic circuits, applying protection principles and solving familiar operational problems. 

The qualification also promotes responsible work practices, effective communication, teamwork and adherence to statutory requirements. 

It contributes to national skills development priorities by expanding the pool of technically skilled workers and improving access for previously disadvantaged groups. 

The structure includes compulsory fundamental and core components, with elective specialisations that allow learners to align their training with industry needs.

t: Further Education and Training Certificate: Electrical Engineering (SAQA ID 72052)
c: South African Qualifications Authority (2019) Further Education and Training Certificate: Electrical Engineering (SAQA ID 72052). Pretoria: SAQA.
s:
This qualification defines the advanced knowledge and skills required to work as a skilled electrical worker at NQF Level 4 across multiple industrial sectors. 

It prepares learners to understand electrical equipment and protection technology, interpret integrated system schematics and install, commission, maintain and repair electrical equipment on integrated systems. 

The qualification emphasises application of scientific and technological principles, adherence to safety, health, environmental and quality systems and the ability to work without direct supervision. 

It forms the third step in a learning pathway, building on NQF Level 3 and leading towards artisan status or further study at NQF Level 5. 

Qualification rules combine fundamental communication and mathematical literacy with core electrical engineering competencies and elective specialisations in areas such as mining, electrical construction, distribution, generation, transport and renewable energy. 

Exit level outcomes focus on integrated system installation and commissioning, fault finding and maintenance, advanced electrical theory, problem solving and responsible, autonomous work practice.

t: National Certificate: Electrical Engineering (SAQA ID 73313)
c: South African Qualifications Authority (2019) National Certificate: Electrical Engineering (SAQA ID 73313). Pretoria: SAQA.
s:
This qualification provides the foundational knowledge and practical skills required to work in the electrical engineering environment at NQF Level 2. 

It equips learners to use engineering tools and measuring instruments, interpret basic electrical drawings and apply hand skills for installation, maintenance and repair of designated circuits and electrical machines. 

The qualification introduces basic electrical theory and its application in workplace tasks, enabling learners to participate safely and effectively in routine activities. 

It forms the first step in a three level learning pathway that progresses to integrated circuits at NQF Level 3 and artisan level competence at NQF Level 4. 

The rationale highlights the qualification’s role in meeting industry needs across sectors such as manufacturing, energy, mining, chemical and transport. 

It supports national strategies to expand scarce skills, improve productivity and enhance employability, particularly for previously disadvantaged groups. 

Qualification rules include compulsory communication and mathematical literacy, core electrical engineering competencies and elective specialisations aligned to industry contexts, including renewable energy. 

Exit outcomes focus on installation procedures, routine maintenance, basic electrical theory, safe working practices and problem solving in familiar contexts.

t: Higher Certificate in Renewable Energy Technologies (SAQA ID 91825)
c: South African Qualifications Authority (2021) Higher Certificate in Renewable Energy Technologies (SAQA ID 91825). Pretoria: SAQA.
s:
This qualification prepares learners to work as technicians or technologists in the renewable energy sector by providing a structured foundation in mathematics, physics, engineering principles and practical installation skills. 

It aims to develop graduates who can support the growing demand for renewable energy technologies in South Africa’s urban and rural contexts. 

The qualification equips learners to apply engineering principles to diagnose and solve narrowly defined problems, design basic components or processes, conduct tests and measurements and use established engineering tools. 

It also develops competence in communication, health and safety, engineering management and ethical practice. 

Compulsory modules cover mathematics, life skills, physics of energy conversion, power plant systems, health and safety, electrical installation principles and storage of converted electricity. 

Elective modules allow specialisation in solar, wind or biogas installation and maintenance. 

The rationale highlights the national need for technical capacity to support the transition to cleaner energy systems and reduce the country’s carbon footprint. 

The qualification also provides a pathway to further study at diploma or degree level.

t: Higher Occupational Certificate: Solar Photovoltaic Standalone Service Technician (SAQA ID 120863)
c: South African Qualifications Authority (2023) Higher Occupational Certificate: Solar Photovoltaic Standalone Service Technician (SAQA ID 120863). Pretoria: SAQA.
s:
This qualification prepares learners to work as Solar Photovoltaic Standalone Service Technicians responsible for maintaining, testing, repairing and replacing components in stand alone PV systems. 

It focuses on ensuring safe, efficient operation of off grid installations across domestic, urban and rural contexts. 

The purpose notes the need for technicians who demonstrate integrity, attention to detail, risk awareness and technical competence. 

The rationale emphasises the growing importance of renewable energy in supporting economic growth, environmental protection and national development goals. 

It addresses the lack of standardised qualifications in this expanding sector and forms the highest level in a structured career pathway. 

The curriculum comprises knowledge modules on power conditioning, rotating machinery, mechanics, PV system design and maintenance, supported by practical skills modules and extensive work experience. 

Exit outcomes require learners to apply technical knowledge to maintain and replace PV panels, inverters, transformers, cables, switchgear, batteries and charge controllers. 

The qualification supports professionalisation of the sector and contributes to building a skilled workforce capable of installing and maintaining safe, sustainable energy infrastructure.

t: National Occupational Certificate: Solar Photovoltaic Standalone Systems Installer (SAQA ID 120883)
c: South African Qualifications Authority (2023) National Occupational Certificate: Solar Photovoltaic Standalone Systems Installer (SAQA ID 120883). Pretoria: SAQA.
s:
This qualification prepares learners to install stand alone solar photovoltaic (PV)systems safely and competently across a range of domestic, urban and rural settings. 

It equips installers to plan system configurations, assess site conditions, assemble support structures, install modules and connect electrical components in line with building codes, standards and regulatory requirements. 

Learners are trained to activate, test and maintain PV systems and to apply weatherproofing and safety measures during installation. 

The purpose emphasises the need for effective communication, problem solving, compliance orientation and physical stamina.

The rationale emphasises the growing importance of renewable energy in supporting economic growth, environmental protection and resilience, and identifies the qualification as a pathway for new entrants, existing workers and unemployed community members seeking employability or self employment. 

The curriculum integrates knowledge modules, practical skills and structured work experience covering workplace fundamentals, tools, electrical systems, protection systems, renewable energy and PV components. 

Exit outcomes focus on planning, mechanical installation, electrical installation and basic maintenance of PV panels.

The qualification supports national efforts to expand safe, sustainable energy infrastructure and build a skilled workforce for the renewable energy sector.

t: Occupational Certificate: Solar Photovoltaic Standalone System Mounter (SAQA ID 120885)
c: South African Qualifications Authority (2023) Occupational Certificate: Solar Photovoltaic Standalone System Mounter (SAQA ID 120885). Pretoria: SAQA.
s:
This part qualification prepares learners to work as Solar Photovoltaic (PV) Standalone System Mounters who form part of an installation team and take responsibility for the safe, accurate mounting of pre designed PV systems. 

Work is carried out under supervision and according to detailed instructions, with emphasis on risk awareness, compliance and correct use of tools. 

Learners are trained to inspect installation sites, interpret mounting instructions and diagrams, use hand tools effectively and report on completed work. 

The rationale highlights the qualification’s role as an entry point into the renewable energy sector and its alignment with national priorities to expand safe, sustainable energy infrastructure. 

It supports upskilling of new and existing workers and provides opportunities for unemployed community members to gain employable skills or pursue self employment. 

The curriculum integrates knowledge modules on workplace fundamentals, tools and PV components with practical skills in hazard mitigation, working at height, tool use and mechanical installation. 

Work experience modules reinforce planning, communication and installation processes. 

The qualification contributes to building a competent workforce capable of supporting the growing demand for renewable energy installations.
